description: AZ-06 is centered on Tucson and southeastern Arizona (Pima, Cochise, Graham, Greenlee, and part of Pinal counties), not the Phoenix metro area. Describing the district's housing pressure as occurring 'especially in the Phoenix-area suburbs' misdescribes the district's geography.

inaccurate_statement: Rising home prices and rents, especially in the Phoenix-area suburbs, have made housing affordability a major issue [in AZ-06]
description: AZ-06 is centered on Tucson and southeastern Arizona (Pima, Cochise, Graham, Greenlee, and part of Pinal counties), not the Phoenix metro area. Describing the district's housing pressure as occurring 'especially in the Phoenix-area suburbs' misdescribes the district's geography.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza's 'military/law-enforcement background' makes the platform more complicated than the usual Democratic gun-safety agenda
description: Mendoza's documented background is a 20-year Navy and Marine Corps military career, not a law-enforcement background. No record exists of her having served in law enforcement, and describing her background as including 'law-enforcement' experience is inaccurate, though it is a minor embedded detail within a broader, otherwise accurate characterization of her platform.

inaccurate_statement: The main publicly visible comparison at this point is between incumbent Juan Ciscomani (Republican) and Democratic challengers such as Chris Donat and JoAnna Mendoza. The field is still developing, with multiple candidates filed.
description: There is no candidate named Chris Donat in the AZ-06 race. JoAnna Mendoza ran unopposed in the Democratic primary and is the confirmed Democratic nominee facing Republican incumbent Juan Ciscomani in the November 2026 general election. Presenting the Democratic field as still undetermined among multiple candidates, including a fabricated name, misrepresents the actual settled two-candidate (plus minor-party) general-election matchup.

inaccurate_statement: JoAnna Mendoza's available summaries do not yet show a fully comparable public-safety platform, and a direct comparison requires more detailed policy releases before judging against the incumbent.
description: Mendoza has a documented, on-record public safety and border-security platform, including support for funding law enforcement, strengthening border security at ports of entry, deporting violent criminals, holding cartels accountable, independent audits of detention facilities, and specific statements on ICE oversight following ICE-involved deaths. Characterizing her platform as underdeveloped or lacking comparable specifics is inaccurate and understates her actual documented positions.

inaccurate_statement: The main publicly visible comparison at this point is between incumbent Juan Ciscomani (Republican) and Democratic challengers such as Chris Donat and JoAnna Mendoza. The field is still developing, with multiple candidates filed.
description: There is no candidate named Chris Donat in the AZ-06 race. JoAnna Mendoza ran unopposed in the Democratic primary and is the confirmed Democratic nominee facing Republican incumbent Juan Ciscomani in the November 2026 general election. Presenting the Democratic field as still undetermined among multiple candidates, including a fabricated name, misrepresents the actual settled two-candidate (plus minor-party) general-election matchup.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani has secured $2.7 million for Pima JTED to expand career and technical education.
description: Ciscomani's FY2027 Community Project Funding request for the Pima JTED workforce/technology training center is documented as $3 million, not $2.7 million.

inaccurate_statement: Juan Ciscomani has opposed the Inflation Reduction Act, which created Medicare drug-price negotiation authority, a $35/month insulin cap for Medicare beneficiaries, and a $2,000 annual Medicare Part D out-of-pocket cap.
description: No record exists of Ciscomani personally opposing or voting against the Inflation Reduction Act; he did not take office until January 2023, after the IRA passed in August 2022, so he could not have cast a vote on it. The available record shows no direct statement from him personally proposing or opposing Medicare's drug-price-negotiation authority specifically — this remains an unresolved gap in his record, not a documented opposition vote. His caucus association with the Republican Study Committee, which has called for repealing this authority, is a group-level position, not his own personally stated one.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani's position suggests less support for expanding Medicare-style price negotiation, though Republicans generally argue for other cost controls such as competition, transparency, and market-based reforms
description: This vague characterization omits Ciscomani's actual documented record on drug costs, which includes a House floor speech on rural pharmacy closures tied to PBM practices, a vote for the Lower Costs, More Transparency Act (H.R. 5378), and cosponsorship of the PATIENT Act (H.R. 3561) — all real, sourced actions specifically on drug-pricing/pharmacy-access policy that the response does not mention, instead implying his position is only inferred from generic party alignment.

inaccurate_statement: Juan Ciscomani opposed the Inflation Reduction Act, the law that created Medicare's current drug-negotiation authority
description: Ciscomani took office in January 2023, after the Inflation Reduction Act passed in August 2022, so he could not have voted on or opposed it in Congress. His documented drug-pricing record involves PBM-transparency legislation and an association with Republican Study Committee positions favoring repeal of Medicare's negotiation authority, not a personal vote against the IRA.

inaccurate_statement: The 2026 general-election candidates are Republican incumbent Juan Ciscomani, Democrat JoAnna Mendoza, and Libertarian Jereme Peters.
description: This list omits Green Party candidate Gary Swing, who is also confirmed to be on the AZ-06 general-election ballot. Presenting this as a complete list of 2026 general-election candidates is a minor factual omission.

inaccurate_statement: The 2026 general-election candidates are Republican incumbent Juan Ciscomani, Democrat JoAnna Mendoza, and Libertarian Jereme Peters.
description: This list omits Green Party candidate Gary Swing, who is also confirmed to be on the AZ-06 general-election ballot. Presenting this as a complete list of 2026 general-election candidates is a minor factual omission.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani secured $2.7 million for Pima JTED
description: Reporting on Ciscomani's FY2027 community project funding requests describes $3 million for a Pima JTED workforce training center, not $2.7 million. The specific dollar figure cited in the response does not match this documented amount.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani voted for the Secure the Border Act of 2023
description: No record shows Ciscomani voting for a bill called the 'Secure the Border Act of 2023.' His documented immigration/border votes include the Laken Riley Act (H.R. 29, Jan. 2025), the Secure America Act (S. 2, June 2026), the HALT Fentanyl Act, and the Agent Raul Gonzalez Officer Safety Act, plus opposition to the 2024 bipartisan Senate border deal. There is a real bill called the 'Secure the Border Act' (H.R. 2) that passed the House in May 2023 largely along party lines, but Ciscomani was not yet in that specific bill's confirmed voting record in this material, and the year/name pairing as stated does not match any vote documented for him.

inaccurate_statement: In a 2025 Homeland Security Appropriations hearing, Ciscomani specifically said that criminals without a legal right to remain should be removed swiftly, and singled out people convicted of crimes who have deportation orders
description: The only documented 2025 Homeland Security Appropriations hearing exchange involving Ciscomani (a May 8, 2025 oversight hearing on DHS's budget, per his own office's press release) shows him questioning Secretary Noem about DHS morale/recruitment and about streamlining legal immigration pathways. In that exchange he generically stated there's been media attention on increased deportations 'which I remain fully supportive of,' but his own office's published excerpts contain no statement using language like 'legal right to remain,' 'removed swiftly,' or specifically singling out convicted criminals with deportation orders. A broader search for this specific framing attributed to Ciscomani in a 2025 hearing turned up no corroborating source. While the general thrust—that Ciscomani supports swift removal of criminal aliens—is consistent with his broader public record and rhetoric (e.g., statements to local media about deporting people with criminal records), the specific claim that he 'specifically said' this exact formulation in a Homeland Security Appropriations hearing is not verifiable from the actual hearing transcript excerpts available, making this a narrow fabrication/overstatement of what was actually said in that specific hearing rather than a wholesale misrepresentation of his general policy stance.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza's platform calls for expanding access in underserved areas through telehealth and mobile services
description: No record exists of Mendoza making a specific statement about expanding healthcare access through telehealth or mobile services in underserved areas; her documented mental-health-related commitments are narrower, limited to gun-violence-context funding and veteran-specific mental health services, with a confirmed gap on general access mechanisms like telehealth or mobile clinics.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza's public-safety platform includes identification requirements for law enforcement
description: Mendoza's platform supports police funding, training, and body cameras, but no evidence supports a general law-enforcement 'identification requirements' plank; her only related statement concerns masked ICE agents specifically, not a general policy for law enforcement identification.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani secured $4.2 million for Oro Valley's police department
description: The confirmed $4.2 million in federal funding Ciscomani secured was for Tucson police vehicles, not for Oro Valley's police department. This misstates which locality received the funding.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza's platform includes identification requirements for law enforcement as part of her general public-safety approach
description: Mendoza's general public-safety platform includes funding, training, and body cameras, but no general law-enforcement identification requirement has been found; her only related statement concerns identification/accountability for masked ICE agents specifically, a distinct point about federal immigration enforcement rather than general policing.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani recently secured preliminary $4.2 million in federal funding for Oro Valley's police department for technology and public-safety equipment, including crime-solving tools
description: The $4.2 million in federal funding Ciscomani secured was for Tucson police vehicles, not for Oro Valley's police department for technology and crime-solving equipment.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani is co-chair of the bipartisan Crime Survivors and Justice Caucus
description: No record exists of Ciscomani belonging to or co-chairing a "Crime Survivors and Justice Caucus." His documented caucus memberships are the Problem Solvers Caucus, Main Street Caucus, and Vice Chairman of the Military and Veteran Housing Caucus.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani supported legislation strengthening federal-tribal border-security cooperation
description: No record exists of Ciscomani sponsoring or supporting legislation specifically described as strengthening federal-tribal border-security cooperation. He has sponsored a Northeastern Arizona Indian Water Rights Settlement Act, which concerns water rights, not border security, and his confirmed border-security legislative record (Laken Riley Act, Secure America Act, HALT Fentanyl Act, Agent Raul Gonzalez Officer Safety Act) does not include any tribal border-cooperation measure.

inaccurate_statement: The 2026 race has multiple filed candidates, and the general-election matchup may change
description: Both Mendoza and Ciscomani are the confirmed major-party nominees following their respective unopposed July 21, 2026 primaries, with the general-election ballot set (also including a Libertarian and Green candidate). Suggesting the Mendoza-Ciscomani matchup 'may change' misleadingly implies the race is still unsettled when the nominees are already finalized.

inaccurate_statement: During a 2024 House debate, Ciscomani warned that certain mine sites could have devastating effects on Arizona's water supply
description: The documented 2024 legislative action tied to mining and water in this context is Ciscomani's Yea vote on H.R. 2925, the Mining Regulatory Clarity Act, whose entire purpose was to reverse a court decision blocking the Rosemont mine plan — i.e., a vote supporting mining development, not a warning against mining's water impacts. No record exists of him personally naming Rosemont, Copper World, or any mine site in a floor statement expressing concern about water impacts; this claim reverses the direction of his actual documented position.

inaccurate_statement: The 2026 race has multiple filed candidates, and the general-election matchup may change
description: Both Mendoza and Ciscomani are the confirmed major-party nominees following their respective unopposed July 21, 2026 primaries, with the general-election ballot set (also including a Libertarian and Green candidate). Suggesting the Mendoza-Ciscomani matchup 'may change' misleadingly implies the race is still unsettled when the nominees are already finalized.

inaccurate_statement: Her campaign has also attacked mining-related threats to Southern Arizona's water resources
description: No statement was found from Mendoza specifically naming or attacking a mining project (such as Copper World/Rosemont) in connection with water resources. Her platform contains only general water-protection language (Colorado River resources, groundwater, PFAS); the specific claim that her campaign has 'attacked' mining-related water threats overstates what is documented, presenting an inferred position as a specific stated attack.

inaccurate_statement: The contrast is particularly relevant to projects such as the Hermosa mining project in Southern Arizona, where concerns have centered on potential effects on local water resources, and Ciscomani previously characterized Hermosa as an important source of jobs
description: No record exists of a 'Hermosa mining project' being referenced in connection with either candidate's documented record. The relevant, well-documented mining/water controversy in this district is the Rosemont/Copper World mine, and Ciscomani's only specific, sourced connection to it is a 2024 vote on the Mining Regulatory Clarity Act — not a personal statement characterizing a project called 'Hermosa' as a jobs source. This appears to be a fabricated or misidentified project name attributed to him without support.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza improperly claimed a property-tax credit on two properties, saving her roughly $400 per year since 2024
description: The documented combined benefit from claiming the homeowner tax credit on both properties in 2024-2025 was approximately $820 total, not a recurring $400-per-year benefit extending back to 2024 as framed in the response. The response's reframing as an annual, ongoing figure misstates the scope and duration of the confirmed benefit.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani accepted nearly $40,000 in campaign contributions from two members of Congress who had faced sexual-misconduct allegations
description: The documented donations of roughly $40,000+ came from three sitting House Republicans facing personal-conduct scandals (Rep. Tony Gonzales, $30,000; Rep. Chuck Edwards, $8,000+; Rep. Max Miller, $5,000), not two. The response undercounts the number of scandal-affected donors involved.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza's campaign accepted the ~$820 tax benefit and 'agreed to repay' it as reported by The Arizona Republic
description: The documented correction was that the campaign called it an honest mistake and corrected the Tucson property's tax classification as of August 10, 2026; the available reporting does not specifically confirm a formal repayment agreement of the $820 figure as stated, though the broader story (mistake acknowledged, correction made) is accurate.

inaccurate_statement: there is documentation of at least some town hall-style events involving him [Ciscomani]
description: Multiple independent local outlets and a Change.org petition document that Ciscomani has not personally held open constituent town halls and did not attend a self-organized town hall with about 300 attendees that he was invited to; his office only holds staff-level casework hours, not town-hall forums with him personally. The response's suggestion that some town-hall-style events did involve him personally overstates what the record shows, though it is hedged as disputed elsewhere in the response, limiting its impact.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani says he has been recognized as the most bipartisan member of Arizona's congressional delegation by the 'Bridge Grades project'
description: The ranking in question comes from the Lugar Center/Georgetown Bipartisan Index, which uses a metric called the 'Bridge Score' (GovTrack reports a Bridge Score of 97.5 for Ciscomani). There is no organization called the 'Bridge Grades project' in the record; this appears to be a garbled name for the Bridge Score/Bipartisan Index metric.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza has been endorsed by Gov. Mikie Sherrill
description: Mikie Sherrill is the Governor of New Jersey and has no documented connection to this race; no endorsement of Mendoza by Sherrill appears anywhere in the record, and including a New Jersey governor in a list of Arizona congressional endorsers appears to be an error rather than a real, simply-unlisted endorsement.

inaccurate_statement: In June, seven local mayors—including those of Marana, Sahuarita, Eloy, Willcox, Thatcher, Duncan and Benson—also endorsed Ciscomani.
description: The documented list of seven mayors endorsing Ciscomani is Marana, Sahuarita, Willcox, Benson, Casa Grande, Douglas, and Thatcher/Duncan (counted together). The response substitutes Eloy for Casa Grande and Douglas and lists Thatcher and Duncan as two separate mayoral endorsements rather than one combined one, producing an inaccurate roster of endorsing municipalities.

inaccurate_statement: Association of Professional Flight Attendants endorsed JoAnna Mendoza
description: The relevant endorsement was made by the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA (AFA-CWA), a different, larger union, not the Association of Professional Flight Attendants (APFA), which represents only American Airlines flight attendants. No record supports an APFA endorsement of Mendoza; listing both as if they were two separate real endorsers double-counts and misattributes one endorsement to the wrong organization.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza's 20-year military career is described as entirely a 'U.S. Marine Corps' career
description: Mendoza's 20-year military career spanned the U.S. Navy (1994–1997) and the U.S. Marine Corps (1998–2016), not 20 years solely in the Marine Corps. Her Marine Corps tenure specifically was about 18 years, with the remaining time served in the Navy. The response conflates her total military service length with a Marine Corps-only tenure.

inaccurate_statement: Drawing on her 20-year career as a U.S. Marine Corps veteran and drill instructor, Mendoza pitches herself as a dedicated advocate for protecting veterans' benefits and healthcare access.
description: Mendoza's 20 years of military service were split between the U.S. Navy (1994–1997) and the U.S. Marine Corps (1998–2016), not 20 years entirely in the Marine Corps as the phrasing implies.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani's legislative and political focus includes regional priorities such as local postal management
description: No record exists of Ciscomani having a stated focus on local postal management as part of his platform or legislative record; this appears to be an unsupported or fabricated detail.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani focuses heavily on parental rights and cultural measures, such as supporting legislation to restrict transgender athletes from participating in women's sports categories and restricting facility usage
description: There is no record of Ciscomani sponsoring or campaigning on legislation restricting transgender athletes or bathroom/facility usage as a personal platform focus. The only documented instance of this topic is a June 2026 attack ad against Mendoza referencing a 2020 quote of hers, which is a campaign attack line, not a personal legislative or platform priority of Ciscomani's on 'parental rights and cultural measures.' Characterizing this as one of his core focus areas overstates and mischaracterizes an attack-ad talking point as a substantive policy platform.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani's campaign focuses on regional matters tied to border-adjacent community security, local infrastructure, and postal service management
description: No record exists of postal service management being a stated focus area of Ciscomani's campaign; his documented platform and appropriations record covers border security, infrastructure (roads, water, bridges), veterans, and energy, but postal service management does not appear as a campaign focus in his platform materials.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza has criticized Ciscomani for supporting legislation that cuts federal funding for food assistance (SNAP)
description: No record exists of Mendoza specifically criticizing Ciscomani over SNAP/food-assistance cuts. Her documented criticisms of his reconciliation-bill vote focus on Medicaid cuts and hospital-closure risk, not food assistance specifically. This is a narrow, unsupported addition rather than a claim central to the response's overall point.

inaccurate_statement: Future Forum PAC was founded by former Representative Eric Swalwell
description: Eric Swalwell co-founded Future Forum PAC along with other co-chairs; it is a multi-member, multi-cochair caucus PAC, not a PAC he alone founded or solely controlled. Describing it as simply 'founded by' Swalwell overstates his individual role.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza's campaign has featured 'thousands of dollars' in financial support from Future Forum PAC and Ruben Gallego-linked sources, implying she was bankrolled by these figures
description: Future Forum PAC gave Mendoza's campaign $2,500 total and Ruben Gallego's Juntos PAC gave $5,000, for a combined $7,500 against her over $7.3 million total raised (roughly 0.1%). While it is technically true this amounts to 'thousands of dollars,' framing this as her campaign being 'bankrolled' or featuring significant financial backing from these figures substantially overstates the actual, confirmed dollar amounts relative to her overall fundraising.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza declined to answer questions or comment on her ties to Swalwell and Gallego
description: This specific claim about Mendoza's response to media questioning is not corroborated in the available research, which does not document her campaign's specific response (or non-response) to inquiries about this topic beyond noting the underlying financial figures.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani accepted more than $43,000 in campaign donations from PACs linked to lawmakers mired in misconduct scandals
description: The combined confirmed total from these three donors is approximately $43,000 ($30,000 + $8,000 + $5,000), which actually does match the sum given, so the headline figure is arithmetically consistent with the confirmed individual figures rather than inaccurate.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza heavily criticized police conduct in the 2020 remarks
description: The documented 2020 statement was about reallocating funding to programs that would let people 'live their best lives,' not a broader critique of police conduct; characterizing it as her having 'heavily criticized police conduct' overstates what the known quote says.

inaccurate_statement: The 2020 comments were made while running for Arizona State Senate
description: Mendoza's 2020 comment about reallocating police funding is documented as coming from a 2020 candidate forum/interview context; her 2020 run for Arizona State Senate District 11 is separately confirmed, and this detail is plausible but not independently verified in the available material as tied specifically to that campaign's town hall.

inaccurate_statement: A resurfaced video from a 2000 Clean Elections Commission debate showed Mendoza making critical comments regarding law enforcement and discussing reallocation of police funding, tied to the 'defund the police' movement
description: The resurfaced comments about reallocating police funding were made during a 2020 candidate forum/Zoom event, not a 2000 Clean Elections Commission debate. The year and specific venue are incorrect, though the underlying fact that she made such remarks that were later tied to 'defund the police' criticism is accurate.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza's description of certain parental rights positions as 'regressive' drew sharp pushback
description: The documented 2020 quote has her calling proposed anti-trans-athlete legislation "harmful" and "toxic," describing the bill rather than parents; no record exists of her using the word "regressive" in this context, and independent analysis found the characterization of her remarks in attack ads already overstates what she actually said without adding an unsupported additional word.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza's past statements on decriminalization extended to minor offenses like jaywalking
description: No record exists of Mendoza making a statement specifically about decriminalizing jaywalking or similar minor offenses; the documented 2020 statement was about decriminalizing sex work in the context of trans women of color, and separately about decriminalizing some unspecified minor/petty offenses in that same interview. Attaching the specific example of 'jaywalking' as a named instance is not supported by the available record.

inaccurate_statement: The property tax issue involved a wrongly claimed 'State Aid to Education' write-off tied to turning her Tucson residence into a rental while purchasing a second home
description: The documented issue was a homeowner tax credit claimed on two properties (the former Tucson home and her current Red Rock home) simultaneously, not specifically identified as a 'State Aid to Education' write-off tied to a rental-conversion timeline in that manner; the characterization adds specific mechanism details not confirmed in the available record.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza faced pressure from critics to address allegations involving Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego
description: The sexual-assault/harassment accusations referenced in coverage of Mendoza's donor network involve Rep. Eric Swalwell, who resigned from Congress in April 2026 amid such allegations, not Sen. Ruben Gallego. Gallego has endorsed Mendoza and his Juntos PAC has contributed to her campaign, but there is no record of personal-conduct allegations against him in this context; this appears to conflate him with Swalwell.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani accepted funds from a PAC associated with Rep. Mary Miller, who faced domestic abuse allegations from an ex-wife
description: The donor and scandal described belong to Rep. Max Miller (R-OH), not Rep. Mary Miller. Ciscomani accepted $5,000 from Rep. Max Miller, whose ex-wife has publicly accused him of physical abuse. Mary Miller is a different, unrelated member of Congress from Illinois with no documented connection to this donation or scandal.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani accepted campaign contributions tied to a lawmaker named 'Rep. Cory Miller' facing domestic violence allegations
description: The lawmaker in question is Rep. Max Miller (R-OH), whose ex-wife has publicly accused him of physical abuse — there is no 'Rep. Cory Miller.' This appears to be a name error/conflation, though the underlying fact (Ciscomani accepted $5,000 from a House Republican named Miller facing domestic-abuse allegations) is accurate aside from the first name.

inaccurate_statement: Whether Mendoza's policies would hurt local jobs in Tucson is a point of contention, with opponents arguing her alignment with figures like Mayor Regina Romero represents an 'agenda of higher and higher taxes'
description: No record exists of Ciscomani or other opponents specifically characterizing Mendoza's alignment with Regina Romero as an 'agenda of higher and higher taxes.' The documented Ciscomani criticism of Mendoza's Romero endorsement is a July 28, 2026 post calling Mendoza 'a rubber stamp for these failed policies' on public safety, not a tax-and-spending framing. This particular quoted characterization does not match the documented attack line.

inaccurate_statement: Critics have targeted statements Mendoza made noting that immigrants fill critical labor roles in industries like agriculture, service, and healthcare, characterizing those remarks as unsupportive of domestic labor markets
description: No record exists of Mendoza making a specific statement about immigrants filling labor roles in agriculture, service, and healthcare, nor of any opponent criticism targeting such a statement. The documented immigration-related controversies involve her 2020 ICE stand-down comments and border-security platform, not this specific claim.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani's voted-for legislation restricts funding for organizations like Planned Parenthood
description: The knowledge base documents Ciscomani's votes and healthcare record in detail (Medicaid cuts, ACA subsidy vote, targeted local health funding, prescription-drug/PBM record) but contains no mention of a Planned Parenthood defunding provision tied to his vote on the reconciliation bill. This specific claim cannot be confirmed against the available record and is not addressed anywhere in his documented healthcare record, making it an unsupported addition to an otherwise accurate description of his Medicaid vote.

inaccurate_statement: Acted as a staff non-commissioned officer for sexual assault prevention and response
description: The available biography of Mendoza's military service documents her time as a Navy/Marine Corps servicemember, drill instructor, and OCS instructor, but does not mention any role as a staff non-commissioned officer for sexual assault prevention and response programs. This specific role is not corroborated in the available record and appears to be an unsupported addition to her documented military biography.

inaccurate_statement: From 2015 to 2021, he served as a senior advisor to Arizona Governor Doug Ducey, focusing heavily on international trade, diplomacy, border security, and economic development.
description: Ciscomani served as senior advisor to Governor Ducey and vice chair of the Arizona-Mexico Commission from 2015 to 2022, not 2015 to 2021 — he held the role until his 2022 election to Congress. This is a minor date discrepancy that doesn't change the overall picture of his qualifications.

inaccurate_statement: Strong advocate for protecting and strengthening safety-net programs (such as SNAP and Medicaid)
description: Mendoza's confirmed platform emphasizes reversing Medicaid/ACA-subsidy cuts and protecting AHCCCS, and her cost-of-living messaging references food/grocery costs generally, but no direct statement specifically names SNAP as a program she is protecting or strengthening; this adds an unconfirmed specific program name to an otherwise accurate general safety-net position.

inaccurate_statement: Supporting measures such as requiring annual gun violence prevention training through the Department of Defense
description: No record exists of Mendoza taking a specific position calling for annual gun-violence-prevention training through the Department of Defense; her documented gun-safety positions involve universal background checks, safe-storage requirements, and regulations on untraceable firearms, not a DOD training mandate.

inaccurate_statement: She enlisted at age 17
description: No record supports an enlistment age of 17; her documented military service is 1994–1997 (Navy) and 1998–2016 (Marine Corps), totaling 20 years, but no source specifies she enlisted at age 17.

inaccurate_statement: She achieved the role of staff non-commissioned officer for sexual assault prevention and response
description: No record confirms Mendoza held a role as staff non-commissioned officer for sexual assault prevention and response; her documented military roles are drill instructor and Officer Candidate School instructor, with no mention of this specific SAPR role.

inaccurate_statement: she enlisted in the military at age 17
description: Available biographical material states Mendoza served in the U.S. Navy from 1994–1997 and the U.S. Marine Corps from 1998–2016, but no source establishes an enlistment age of 17; this specific detail appears to be an unsupported addition not found in her documented biography.

inaccurate_statement: She enlisted at age 17
description: Available biographical information indicates Mendoza served in the Navy from 1994 to 1997 and the Marine Corps from 1998 to 2016, but no source establishes she enlisted specifically at age 17; her documented history is that she was the oldest of five children picking cotton starting at age 8, with military service starting in 1994. No record supports an enlistment age of 17 specifically.

inaccurate_statement: From 2015 to 2021, he served as a senior advisor to former Arizona Governor Doug Ducey and as the vice chair of the Arizona-Mexico Commission
description: Ciscomani served as senior advisor to Governor Doug Ducey and Vice Chair of the Arizona-Mexico Commission from 2015 to 2022, not 2015 to 2021 — he held the role through the end of Ducey's term until his own election to Congress in 2022.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza has criticized Ciscomani for supporting legislation that reduces federal spending on Medicare
description: The documented Mendoza criticism of Ciscomani's healthcare votes centers on Medicaid and ACA subsidy cuts (e.g., her fact-check post disputing the '$550 billion' Medicaid figure, and her framing of his reconciliation-bill vote as harming hospitals), not Medicare spending cuts specifically. No record supports a Medicare-specific attack line from her.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza supports investments in electric vehicles (EVs) as part of her energy platform
description: There is no record of Mendoza making a specific statement supporting electric vehicle investment as part of her energy or cost-of-living platform. Her documented energy positions center on clean energy, solar, and reinstating clean-energy tax credits generally, with no EV-specific plank found.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza advocates for investments in American-made and clean energy sources such as solar and electric infrastructure to reduce reliance on fossil fuels and lower long-term energy and fuel pressures, presented as her stated mechanism for gas prices specifically
description: Mendoza's platform supports clean energy and opposing tariffs generally, and her cost-of-living messaging names gas among burdens she'll address, but no direct statement ties a clean-energy/solar investment mechanism specifically to lowering gas prices at the pump. Presenting this as her specific stated gas-price solution goes beyond what is documented as her direct position, though it is consistent with general party-aligned clean-energy advocacy she has made elsewhere.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza's plan for gas prices/energy involves investing in American-made and clean energy including solar, wind, and electric vehicles to reduce reliance on fossil fuels
description: Mendoza's platform names gas as one of the costs she wants to address, but there is no specific, distinct mechanism found for lowering gas prices beyond general tariff opposition. Her platform separately supports clean energy and reinstating clean-energy tax credits primarily in the context of jobs and utility costs, not as a stated gas-price-lowering mechanism. Presenting clean energy/EV investment as her specific answer to gas prices goes beyond what she has stated and asserts a policy mechanism not directly tied to gas prices in her own words.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza's education priorities include elevating public education funding and supporting career and technical education
description: No source, including Mendoza's own campaign issues pages, shows a dedicated education platform plank covering public education funding or career and technical education. inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani earned his Bachelor's degree in Political Science

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani interned for U.S. Representative Ed Pastor and completed a fellowship with U.S. Representative Loretta Sanchez through the Congressional Hispanic Caucus Institute

This is a narrow, unconfirmed addition to an otherwise accurate biography.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani's platform includes protecting Medicare and Social Security, and ensuring access to affordable medical options and independent health care providers
description: Ciscomani's healthcare record is genuinely mixed rather than a simple 'protects Medicare and Social Security' platform: he voted for the 2025 reconciliation bill (OBBBA), which nonpartisan trackers tie to substantial Medicaid cuts and hospital-revenue losses in his district, while also personally lobbying to soften some cuts and securing targeted local health funding. He does favor eliminating taxes on Social Security and has supported independent pharmacies, but presenting his healthcare stance simply as 'protecting Medicare and Social Security' omits the documented tension in his record on Medicaid and ACA subsidies.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza supports protecting ACA subsidies for rural healthcare as part of her agriculture/rural communities platform
description: Mendoza does support reversing ACA-subsidy cuts as part of her general healthcare platform, but this is a healthcare-access position, not documented as a distinct plank of an 'agriculture & rural communities' policy category. The response conflates two separate parts of her platform, though the underlying position (supporting ACA subsidies) is accurate.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani advocates for protecting Medicare and Social Security programs from deep cuts, presented as part of his economy/cost-of-living platform
description: Ciscomani's documented economic messaging centers on fiscal restraint, tax cuts, and reducing federal spending rather than a stated pledge to protect Medicare and Social Security from cuts as a cost-of-living plank; while he has favored eliminating taxes on Social Security benefits for seniors, no direct statement frames broad Medicare/Social Security protection from cuts as part of his affordability platform, making this an unsupported specific framing rather than a documented position.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani praised the overturning of Roe v. Wade
description: No direct statement or record confirms Ciscomani personally praised the overturning of Roe v. Wade. His documented abortion record shows he identifies as pro-life, opposes a federal abortion ban, and supports exceptions and state-level regulation, but no source establishes a specific celebratory statement about the Dobbs decision, making this an unverified addition layered onto an otherwise accurate general position.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani has characterized Mendoza's background as being tied to lobbying, dark money, and special interests
description: There is a real, documented instance of Ciscomani (in a July 2026 interview) characterizing Mendoza as having become wealthy through lobbying work after her time as a congressional staffer, which supports the general 'lobbying' framing. However, no source ties Ciscomani specifically to a 'dark money' characterization of Mendoza, and this appears to be an embellishment layered onto the real lobbying-related criticism.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani has alleged that Mendoza supports raising taxes while failing to pay her own taxes
description: There is no record of Ciscomani alleging Mendoza personally failed to pay her own taxes. The documented, real tax-related controversy involving Mendoza is a dual-property homeowner tax-credit issue reported by mainstream Arizona outlets, which her campaign called an honest mistake and corrected -- distinct from an allegation of not paying taxes, and no source ties this specific 'failing to pay her taxes' framing to Ciscomani himself.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani has noted Mendoza's endorsement by 'defund the police' advocates, claiming she attempts to avoid that record

The real, documented attack line on this topic centers on a resurfaced 2020 comment by Mendoza herself about police-funding reallocation, not an endorsement she received from defund-the-police advocates, and this specific framing attributed to Ciscomani is not supported by available sourcing.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani and his campaign have branded her overall legislative agenda as 'radical' and 'out of touch' through a series of attack ads
description: While NRCC materials have called Mendoza 'far-left,' 'unvetted,' and 'out of touch,' there is no confirmed record of Ciscomani personally or his campaign specifically using the word 'radical' to describe her 'legislative agenda' (Mendoza has no legislative agenda/record, being a non-incumbent). inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani has characterized Mendoza's background and campaign as being closely tied to lobbying, dark money, and special interest groups.
description: Ciscomani has made real, documented criticisms of Mendoza tied to her lobbying career (calling her a 'lobbyist' who became wealthy through that work) and her funding from figures like Eric Swalwell and Ruben Gallego, but no source documents him specifically framing this as 'dark money.' The lobbying-criticism core is real, but the specific 'dark money' framing is not confirmed, making this an overstatement of an otherwise real line of attack rather than a wholesale fabrication.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani alleged that Mendoza supports raising taxes while simultaneously failing to pay her own.
description: No record exists of Ciscomani alleging Mendoza failed to pay her own taxes. The documented tax-related controversy involving Mendoza is a homeowner property-tax-credit issue (claiming a credit on two properties simultaneously), which is distinct from 'failing to pay taxes,' and there is no confirmed statement of Ciscomani framing it this way or alleging she supports raising taxes generally. This specific claim about Mendoza personally not paying her taxes is not supported and would materially mislead readers about a specific, serious personal-finance accusation.

inaccurate_statement: Ciscomani claimed that Mendoza has received endorsements from 'defund the police' advocates and accused her of trying to actively avoid or obscure that record.
description: The real, documented attack line concerns a resurfaced 2020 comment by Mendoza herself about reallocating police funding, not an allegation that she received endorsements from 'defund the police' advocates specifically, nor a documented claim that she is trying to 'obscure' this record. This appears to be an invented elaboration on a real underlying controversy (her own past comment), not a sourced claim about endorsers or concealment.

inaccurate_statement: In campaign advertisements and debates, Ciscomani has broadly branded her political agenda and policy platform as 'radical' and 'out of touch' with the district.

The specific characterizations 'radical' and 'out of touch' as broad brands for her entire platform are not confirmed verbatim, though the general thrust (portraying her as too extreme/out of step with the district) is consistent with his real criticisms.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza's plan to lower gas prices includes reversing tax breaks that favor billionaires as part of easing financial strain on working families

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza's investments in domestic/clean energy are 'designed to build a more self-sufficient infrastructure and bring long-term relief to ratepayers and consumers' as a gas-price mechanism specifically
description: The quoted phrase about building 'a more self-sufficient infrastructure' and bringing relief to 'ratepayers' is genuine language from Mendoza's campaign website (joannamendoza.com/issues/environment/), but it appears in the context of her clean/domestic energy and utility-cost platform (solar projects, data centers, utility companies, electricity ratepayers) — not as a 'gas-price mechanism.' Gas prices are mentioned only on a separate cost-of-living page listing gas among several rising costs (groceries, gas, healthcare, housing, utilities), with no connection made to the 'self-sufficient infrastructure' language. The claim's framing conflates her general clean-energy/ratepayer platform with a gas-price-specific mechanism, which is a mischaracterization of the source material, though the underlying quoted language and general policy theme are real.

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza emphasizes the connection between economic strength and education, supporting full funding across all levels—from early childhood and K-12 to career and technical education, community colleges, and universities—to attract new employers to the region

inaccurate_statement: Mendoza's fundraising is roughly 88.5% from individual contributions

description: There is no record of Miller-Meeks's platform being tied to a specific Iowa state-level law restricting municipalities from lowering police funding without state-approved justification, nor any Bleeding Heartland article establishing this connection. Miller-Meeks's documented public safety record centers on federal-level actions (Laken Riley Act, community project funding for local police technology, opposition to eliminating qualified immunity, and general 'back the blue' messaging), not on Iowa state anti-defunding legislation, which would be a state legislature matter rather than something a U.S. House member champions. This appears to be a fabricated policy detail and a fabricated source citation, though it doesn't contradict the broader accurate point that she supports police funding.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's strongest relevant public-safety record, from the Iowa Legislature, emphasizes targeted policing, training and alternatives for nonviolent calls.
description: Bohannan's actual Iowa Legislature record centered on opposing the 2021 'Back the Blue' bill over qualified immunity and protester-penalty concerns, not on a documented record of targeted policing, training programs, or alternatives for nonviolent calls. While she has expressed general support for such alternatives in campaign statements, characterizing this as her 'strongest' legislative public-safety record overstates and mischaracterizes a narrower, more contested record.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks opposes measures that add federal administrative restrictions or redistribute traditional police budgets, aligning with voters who prioritize maintaining or increasing direct financial resources for law enforcement, as her central public safety platform framing.
description: While Miller-Meeks has a genuine record of supporting law enforcement funding, opposing qualified immunity restrictions, and securing local public-safety grants, no direct statement in her documented record frames her platform specifically around opposing 'redistribution of traditional police budgets' as a named policy mechanism. This presents an inferred framing as though it were her explicitly stated position without hedging.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's campaign operates alongside a broader Iowa Democratic platform that is actively pushing for strict data center restrictions, ending tech tax breaks, and requiring companies to fully cover grid infrastructure upgrades, and she aligns closer to state-level efforts aimed at curbing data center expansion.
description: Bohannan has no direct statement found on data center development despite dedicated research, including review of her full campaign platform page and social media, and despite this being a live, high-salience issue in her own district (the Clinton, IA QTS data-center controversy). Presenting her as aligned with or supportive of specific data-center restriction proposals, without hedging that this is inferred rather than her own stated position, directly misrepresents a confirmed gap in her record and would materially mislead a reader seeking her actual stance on the reader's stated top issue.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks explicitly stated it would set a 'dangerous precedent' for a member of Congress to override local zoning decisions for or against data centers.
description: This exact quote was said by Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Mich.), not Mariannette Miller-Meeks. No source ties this specific statement to Miller-Meeks; her own documented public comments on data centers focus on concerns about water usage and electricity rates and the need for community transparency, and she has voted for measures that would preempt state/local governments' ability to regulate data centers, which is in tension with the sentiment of this quote.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has voted multiple times on federal measures that critics argue block local governments from placing environmental and resource guardrails on massive AI data centers.
description: Miller-Meeks has no confirmed statement specifically addressing the in-district Clinton, IA data-center project, and her public data-center comments are general/statewide, not clearly tied to a documented pattern of 'voting multiple times' to block local guardrails as framed here. While one item notes she 'voted during House Energy and Commerce Committee proceedings against amendments that would have preserved a state/local AI data-center moratorium, according to a policy advocacy group's account,' presenting this as a well-established multi-vote pattern with critics broadly making this argument overstates what is documented.

inaccurate_statement: Christina Bohannan's campaign has leaned into local pushback against the rapid expansion of tech facilities, implying this is her stated position on data centers.
description: Christina Bohannan has no confirmed public statement on data center development despite dedicated searching, including of her campaign site, social media, and news coverage covering the live Clinton, Iowa QTS data-center controversy inside her own district. Presenting her as having actively campaigned against data-center expansion is not supported and is a genuine, confirmed gap in her record, not a real position she has taken.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's background in environmental engineering, combined with an implied active campaign stance, makes her the candidate opposed to new data centers.
description: While Bohannan's environmental engineering background is accurate biographical information, no direct statement from her exists opposing data center development; inferring an anti-data-center position from her professional background and presenting it as her actual stance is speculation dressed up as fact, which materially misleads a reader asking specifically for her position on this issue.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has voted multiple times against measures that would allow local governments to block or heavily restrict AI data centers.
description: The available record shows Miller-Meeks voted during House Energy and Commerce Committee proceedings against amendments that would have preserved a state/local AI data-center moratorium carve-out, per an advocacy group's account of that vote — a real but narrower and less certain basis than a claim of having voted 'multiple times' on this specific issue with confirmed intent to block local zoning authority generally.

inaccurate_statement: Federal campaign filings reveal that Miller-Meeks has taken thousands of dollars in campaign contributions from data center, tech, and energy political action committees (PACs).
description: No source ties a specific 'data center PAC' contribution figure to Miller-Meeks; the closest related claim found is a separate, unresolved assertion that she 'accepts $14,000+ in corporate PAC money tied directly to data centers and hyperscaler tech companies,' which was not independently confirmed. Her documented PAC funding sources are concentrated in pharmaceutical, insurance, energy, and business-interest PACs generally, not specifically data-center/tech PACs as framed here.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's party platform aligns closely with stricter data center regulation being pushed by state Democrats like Rob Sand, implying this reflects her own stated position on data centers
description: Bohannan has no documented public statement on data center development despite dedicated searching across her campaign site, social media, and news coverage, including direct engagement with the live Clinton, Iowa QTS data-center controversy in her own district. Presenting her background or party alignment as effectively her stance, without noting this is inferred rather than a position she has actually taken, is misleading. A closely related claim inferring a data-center stance from her environmental-engineering background was specifically flagged as a confirmed inaccuracy in prior research on this exact question.

inaccurate_statement: The HALT Fentanyl Act was signed into law in July 2025
description: The HALT Fentanyl Act (H.R. 27) was signed into law by President Trump on July 16, 2025, which is actually consistent with the stated date, but the dossier confirms her cosponsorship of the HALT Fentanyl Act without specifying the exact signing date, so this specific date detail is treated as unverifiable rather than contradicted by available sourcing.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks defends protective tariffs to support local manufacturing and agriculture, voting multiple times to keep them in place
description: Miller-Meeks's actual documented pattern is that she voted three times to block House consideration of ending Trump's tariff emergency declarations and voted against ending the Canada tariff emergency specifically, while separately criticizing trade-policy factors for contributing to layoffs like those at John Deere and Whirlpool — a documented internal tension rather than a simple, unqualified defense of tariffs as good for manufacturing and agriculture. Framing this as a clean, consistent pro-tariff position obscures the more complicated and contested record.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan advocates for creating jobs through investments in renewable energy and clean technology, alongside targeted relief for working-class households
description: Bohannan's documented platform centers her jobs/economy messaging on opposing tariffs, expanding vocational/technical training, investing in union-protected jobs, and supporting manufacturing workers (e.g., John Deere layoffs). There is no confirmed direct statement tying her jobs platform specifically to renewable energy and clean technology investment as a named mechanism; while she has criticized cuts to clean-energy projects as costing jobs, presenting renewable-energy investment as the centerpiece of her jobs-creation approach overstates and mischaracterizes her actual documented platform, which is broader and centered more on tariffs, workforce training, and manufacturing support.

inaccurate_statement: The 'One Big Beautiful Bill' eliminates taxes on Social Security benefits.
description: The OBBBA does not eliminate taxes on Social Security benefits; it creates only a temporary tax deduction for filers age 65 and older. Miller-Meeks herself publicly acknowledged in a January 2026 tele-town hall that 'no tax on Social Security' messaging about the bill was inaccurate, making this an already-corrected overstatement rather than the bill's actual provision.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supported federal legislation that removes taxes on Social Security benefits.
description: The 2025 reconciliation bill Miller-Meeks voted for does not eliminate taxes on Social Security benefits; it creates only a temporary tax deduction for filers aged 65 and older. Miller-Meeks herself acknowledged in a January 2026 tele-town hall that 'no tax on Social Security' messaging about the bill was inaccurate. Presenting this as a straightforward tax removal repeats a claim she has already corrected.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan campaigns on maximizing federal investments to repair Iowa's deficient infrastructure and points out that Iowa historically ranks at or near the top of the nation for structurally deficient bridges and poor rural roads, as part of a current stated 2026 roads/bridges platform
description: There is no confirmed direct 2026 statement from Bohannan laying out a roads/bridges platform. Her campaign priorities page does not include a specific plank on infrastructure, bridges, or roads, and this remains a documented, confirmed gap in her public record. The only related historical fact is a 2021 tweet supporting the federal infrastructure bill and criticizing Miller-Meeks's vote against it — a past, narrower fact, not a current stated platform on fixing deficient bridges and rural roads. Presenting this as her active 2026 plan without noting the lack of a direct statement overstates what is actually on record.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan advocates for aggressively securing and utilizing bipartisan infrastructure law funds to systematically upgrade local roads, rural highways, and bridges, as a specific current mechanism in her platform
description: No direct statement was found showing Bohannan has laid out a specific 2026 mechanism or plan for using infrastructure law funds to upgrade roads, rural highways, and bridges. Her only documented related statement is a 2021 tweet about the infrastructure bill passing and criticizing Miller-Meeks's opposing vote — this is a past fact about a bill that already passed, not evidence of an active, itemized current plan as the response presents it.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's legislative strategy focuses on cutting red tape and finding avenues to allocate pure infrastructure dollars without expanding the federal deficit, and she favors streamlining regulatory approval processes to make state-level transportation projects more affordable to complete, as her current roads/highways plan
description: Miller-Meeks does have a documented delivery record on roads/bridges (touting $87.1M+ in IA-01 federal funding, including specific named projects), and her 2021 vote explanation did cite cost/bundling concerns. However, no direct statement was found describing a distinct current 'plan' built around cutting red tape or deregulation specifically as a mechanism for lowering transportation project costs; this framing goes beyond what is confirmed in her record, which centers more on her funding-delivery track record than an articulated deregulatory infrastructure theory.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan argues that secondary and rural county roads act as vital economic lifelines for agricultural commerce and small businesses, making targeted widening and repaving necessary
description: There is no confirmed statement from Bohannan on roads/bridges as a discrete 2026 platform position; multiple direct checks of her campaign site (all seven priority accordions) found no statement on roads or infrastructure specifically. This specific framing about rural county roads as economic lifelines requiring widening and repaving is not attributable to any documented Bohannan statement.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan centers much of her campaign strategy around hammering Miller-Meeks' vote against the infrastructure bill, asking fairgoers why anyone would vote against funding 'the damn roads'
description: While Bohannan has criticized Miller-Meeks for voting against the 2021 infrastructure law in general terms, there is no documented record of this specific quote or framing ('the damn roads') or of this being a central pillar of her campaign strategy. This appears to be an invented quote/framing not found in any source.

inaccurate_statement: Roads/bridges: the response implies Bohannan focuses heavily on maximizing federal dollars from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and criticizes the district's lack of progress on structurally deficient bridges, as her own current platform position
description: There is a genuine, confirmed gap in Bohannan's current 2026 platform on roads/bridges specifically -- no direct statement on this topic was found despite thorough searching of her campaign site. Presenting a specific current policy focus (maximizing federal infrastructure dollars, criticizing structurally deficient bridges) as her own stated position, without hedging that this is inferred, overstates what is actually known about her platform on this topic.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks pledges to support future cross-aisle collaborations modeled after the work of Senator Chuck Grassley, who voted in favor of the primary infrastructure package
description: The pledge to model future bipartisan collaboration on Grassley's support for the infrastructure package is actually associated with Bohannan's messaging (she has named Grassley as a lawmaker she wants to work with), not a statement attributable to Miller-Meeks in the available record.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan consistently campaigns on the fact that Iowa frequently ranks among the worst states for structurally deficient bridges and deteriorating rural roads
description: No source documents Bohannan making this specific claim about Iowa's bridge/road rankings as a recurring campaign talking point. Her campaign's own priorities page and documented public statements contain no discrete roads/bridges platform position; the dossier confirms this is a genuine gap, not a position she has actively campaigned on with this specific 'worst states for structurally deficient bridges' framing.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks approaches road and highway planning through a farming lens, advocating for targeted, efficient spending that ensures rural grain haulers and supply chains face fewer delays
description: No record shows Miller-Meeks framing road/highway policy specifically around grain haulers and agricultural supply-chain delays. Her documented infrastructure record centers on her office's touted delivery record (specific named road/bridge projects funded via Community Project Funding) and her stated objection to the 2021 infrastructure law's cost and non-transportation spending, not a farming-specific lens on road planning.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's platform focuses on removing bureaucratic red tape to speed up local road and bridge repairs without relying on massive, trillion-dollar federal packages
description: Miller-Meeks's actual documented roads/bridges record is not a 'red tape reduction' platform but a delivery record of touting $87.1M+ in federal funding for IA-01 including specific named federal Community Project Funding grants for bridges and roads -- the opposite of avoiding reliance on federal packages. This characterization is not supported by her documented statements on infrastructure.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks endorsed by gun-sense organizations, supporting common-sense reforms such as expanded background checks and extreme risk protection orders to keep firearms away from violent individuals
description: The gun-safety-endorsement and support for expanded background checks/extreme risk protection order laws described here belongs to Christina Bohannan, not Mariannette Miller-Meeks. According to available research, it is Bohannan who is a GIFFORDS PAC-documented gun owner who supports 'commonsense reforms — like expanding background checks and implementing extreme risk protection order laws' and is a longtime Moms Demand Action member; Miller-Meeks has no such gun-sense-organization endorsement or platform documented, and her Second Amendment record runs in the opposite direction (she voted against background-check legislation for private firearm transfers). Attributing Bohannan's gun-safety endorsement and policy position to Miller-Meeks reverses which candidate holds this position, which would materially mislead a reader about where each candidate actually stands.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks previously opposed legislation she argued infringed on local municipal and police discretion, stressing that community safety requires cooperative local leadership rather than partisan division
description: This description of opposing the 'Back the Blue' law on the grounds that it infringed on local police/municipal discretion and could pit law enforcement against communities is Christina Bohannan's documented position (she voted against Iowa's 2021 'Back the Blue' bill on exactly these grounds), not Miller-Meeks's. Miller-Meeks's actual record runs the opposite direction — she supports law-enforcement funding, opposes eliminating qualified immunity, and has no record of opposing pro-police legislation on local-discretion grounds. This misattributes a real Bohannan position to Miller-Meeks, which would materially mislead a reader about the two candidates' actual, opposing records on this issue.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's approach to community safety centers on the position that Iowa defends rather than defunds the police, with strong support for police departments
description: This framing ("defends rather than defunds the police") is actually a Republican/Miller-Meeks talking point used to attack Bohannan, not Bohannan's own stated position. Bohannan's real record includes a vote against Iowa's 2021 "Back the Blue" law and a documented, if exaggerated, association with defund-related rhetoric that PolitiFact rated as an overstatement when applied to her. She has said she does not support abolishing or defunding the police, but the response's framing attributes a pro-police slogan to her without the necessary context that this is actually contested, opponent-driven framing rather than her own platform language.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has highlighted support from local Iowa sheriffs and national groups like Police Leaders for Community Safety
description: No record exists of Miller-Meeks being endorsed by a group called "Police Leaders for Community Safety." A search of her documented endorsements shows support from local sheriffs in a 2020 coalition organized around a pledge against defunding police, but no organization by this specific name appears anywhere in her endorsement record, and this specific named group could not be verified as real or connected to her.

inaccurate_statement: Christina Bohannan's platform focuses on building mutual trust between law enforcement and local neighborhoods to make communities safer.
description: Bohannan's official campaign platform does not include a dedicated public-safety plan or a stated framework built around law-enforcement/community trust; this appears to be an overstated characterization not clearly grounded in her documented campaign materials. Her actual public-safety-adjacent record centers narrowly on her 2021 opposition to Iowa's "Back the Blue" bill and her documented gun-safety positions, not on the mutual-trust framing described here.

inaccurate_statement: Mariannette Miller-Meeks earns endorsements from local sheriffs and law enforcement coalitions.
description: No documented endorsement from local sheriffs or a law enforcement coalition for Miller-Meeks in this election cycle could be confirmed. The closest related fact is a 2020 coalition of local sheriffs/officers organized around an anti-"defund the police" pledge from Heritage Action for America, a distinct and dated item, and a claim that the Fraternal Order of Police endorsed her was separately found to be unsubstantiated. This is a narrow claim about a secondary detail rather than her overall pro-law-enforcement record, which is otherwise well documented.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan advocates for stronger investments in affordable childcare as part of her jobs/economic security platform.
description: Bohannan's documented platform on affordability centers on ending tariffs, capping insulin, prohibiting investor purchases of homes/farmland, and cracking down on price gouging; a specific childcare-investment plank tied to workforce/jobs messaging is not confirmed in her platform materials, making this an unsupported specific policy attribution.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's jobs/unemployment plan includes 'emphasizes funding for workforce development' as a specific, itemized stated position.
description: Miller-Meeks's official 'Economy' page emphasizes energy production, the Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act, small-business tax cuts, and housing affordability, but contains no explicit statement specifically addressing unemployment or a dedicated workforce-development funding plan as such — this is a documented gap in her platform, not a confirmed itemized position. Presenting this as her stated plan without noting it is inferred overstates what is actually on record.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan argues economic policy should focus on raising wages, making child care affordable, and protecting workers rather than cutting support systems for laid-off employees, as part of her unemployment plan
description: Bohannan's documented platform emphasizes high-skill/high-wage job growth, vocational training, and opposing tariffs as her jobs/unemployment approach; there's no confirmed direct statement framing her position as specifically about 'not cutting support systems for laid-off employees' as an explicit unemployment plank. This presents an inferred position without appropriate hedging.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's affordability agenda includes freezing state university and community college tuition
description: No record in Bohannan's platform supports a specific proposal to freeze state university and community college tuition; her documented education platform calls for increased investment in public schools, community colleges, universities, and apprenticeships, but a tuition freeze specifically is not a confirmed position.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks emphasizes policies that encourage able-bodied individuals to enter the workforce rather than rely on government assistance, aiming to fill open jobs, as part of her plan to reduce unemployment
description: There is no direct statement in Miller-Meeks's documented record framing workforce participation/able-bodied work requirements as her unemployment-reduction strategy. Her official economy platform emphasizes energy production, manufacturing initiatives, small-business tax cuts, and housing affordability; her Medicaid work-requirement support is health-policy related, not framed as an unemployment plan. This presents an inferred policy mechanism as her stated position without the necessary hedging.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan advocates for mandatory pollution limits and stronger regulatory oversight on industrial agriculture and factory farms, believing voluntary systems are insufficient to handle Iowa's water issues.
description: Bohannan's own campaign materials state she believes government should work 'with farmers and business owners, not against them' and favors 'significant investments' over 'unfunded mandates,' which is the opposite of a strict mandatory-regulation stance on agriculture. The response's framing that she argues for 'stronger government oversight on agricultural pollution and runoff' overstates and mischaracterizes her actual position, which emphasizes incentives and cooperation with farmers alongside PFAS/nitrate reduction goals, not mandatory regulatory crackdowns on agriculture as such.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks focuses on supporting precision agriculture technology and locally led conservation efforts to protect local waterways and the Driftless region
description: No direct 2026 statement from Miller-Meeks addressing Iowa's nitrate/water-quality crisis specifically, or naming precision agriculture technology or the Driftless region, could be found despite dedicated searching. Her documented water-related positions are general (opposing WOTUS rule expansion, securing wastewater infrastructure funding in Davenport and Muscatine) rather than the specific 'precision agriculture' and 'Driftless region' framing asserted here. This is a confirmed, genuine gap in her record on this exact topic, not merely an unconfirmed inference.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan focuses on public health, clean energy investments, and accountability for industrial pollution [as her water quality approach]
description: Bohannan's actual, well-documented water-quality platform centers specifically on reducing PFAS and nitrate contamination and increasing buffer-zone incentives for farmers near waterways — a concrete, named plank. Describing her position instead as general 'public health, clean energy investments, and accountability for industrial pollution' is a vaguer and somewhat different characterization than her real, more specific platform language, though it is broadly consistent with her overall priorities.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supports technology and innovation-based solutions [for clean water]
description: Miller-Meeks has no confirmed 2026 statement specifically addressing Iowa's nitrate/water-quality crisis; her documented water-related record involves general infrastructure/wastewater funding and past WOTUS-related regulatory positions, not a described 'technology and innovation-based' clean water solution tied to her committee role or climate caucus chairmanship. Presenting this as her clean-water approach without noting this gap overstates a known, confirmed silence on the specific topic.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's tax legislation eliminated federal taxes on Social Security payments
description: Miller-Meeks herself acknowledged in a January 2026 tele-town hall that messaging claiming the reconciliation bill created 'no tax on Social Security' was inaccurate — the bill only creates a temporary deduction for filers 65 and older, not an actual exemption from Social Security taxation. Presenting this as a settled fact without that correction repeats an overstatement she has personally walked back.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan opposes broad tariff policies—such as those on Canadian goods—arguing they function as a direct sales tax that raises the cost of daily necessities for Iowa families.
description: Bohannan's documented tariff criticism centers on her campaign's $2,400/year cost figure tied to Miller-Meeks's tariff votes generally and on tariffs affecting farmers and grocery/gas prices; no source in her record specifically calls tariffs a 'direct sales tax' or singles out Canadian-goods tariffs by name. This is a specific framing/quote not confirmed as her own words, though it is broadly consistent with her general anti-tariff cost-of-living messaging.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks argues that current economic pressures, particularly high gas prices, stem primarily from federal energy policies [i.e., current/Democratic-linked federal policies], and she defends the usage of targeted international tariffs to protect domestic industries.
description: Miller-Meeks's documented record shows the opposite posture on tariffs: she has voted multiple times to block House consideration of ending Trump's tariff emergency declarations and voted against ending the Canada tariff emergency specifically, and independent reporting has tied her tariff-adjacent positions to raising costs rather than framing her as defending tariffs as consumer protection in her own affordability messaging. Her documented affordability messaging centers on cutting federal spending/regulation and boosting domestic energy production, not on an affirmative defense of tariffs as a cost-lowering tool. Presenting 'defends tariffs to protect domestic industries' as a component of her cost-of-living platform, without noting the documented tension with her voting record on tariffs raising costs, is a mischaracterization of her position on this specific point.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's key policy tools on affordability include 'banning corporate PAC money'
description: Bohannan's platform emphasizes lowering costs through ending tariffs, capping insulin prices, prohibiting investor purchases of homes/farmland, and cracking down on price gouging, along with ethics reforms like restricting lobbying and overturning Citizens United. She has stated she takes no corporate PAC money herself as a personal fundraising practice, but there is no documented proposal from her to legislatively ban corporate PAC money as a cost-of-living policy tool. This conflates her personal fundraising pledge with a distinct legislative affordability mechanism.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan emphasizes strengthening support for working families, investing in education and infrastructure, and protecting workers' rights and wages to ensure economic stability
description: Bohannan's campaign platform centers primarily on lowering costs (ending tariffs, capping insulin, price-gouging crackdowns), healthcare, farm policy, and water quality, with labor/wages and infrastructure appearing only as minor, passing references rather than central pillars. Presenting 'protecting workers' rights and wages' and 'infrastructure investment' as core, defining elements of her platform overstates and mischaracterizes what is actually a much narrower emphasis within a broader affordability-focused platform. Additionally, her campaign site has no confirmed itemized infrastructure/roads-bridges position as of the most recent research.

inaccurate_statement: The race is described as 'razor-thin'
description: Current polling (e.g., a July 2026 Bullfinch Group survey showing Bohannan at 40%, Miller-Meeks at 35%, and Bridgford at 11%) and nonpartisan forecaster ratings describe the race as a competitive toss-up, but 'razor-thin' more specifically evokes the 2024 result, which was decided by just 799 votes. Describing the current 2026 contest itself as already 'razor-thin' overstates the precision of current polling, which shows a mid-single-digit gap rather than a near-tie.

inaccurate_statement: The race is described as 'razor-thin'
description: Current polling (e.g., a July 2026 Bullfinch Group survey showing Bohannan at 40%, Miller-Meeks at 35%, and Bridgford at 11%) and nonpartisan forecaster ratings describe the race as a competitive toss-up, but 'razor-thin' more specifically evokes the 2024 result, which was decided by just 799 votes.
