Describing the current 2026 contest itself as already 'razor-thin' overstates the precision of current polling, which shows a mid-single-digit gap rather than a near-tie.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan advocates for increasing federal funding to incentivize farmers to adopt conservation practices, such as cover crops, to reduce fertilizer and nitrate runoff, as her general approach to agricultural regulation on water quality.
description: Bohannan's actual stated position on farm conservation practices, per her own 2022 comments and her current 2026 campaign platform, is that she favors incentives and investments to help farmers voluntarily adopt practices like cover crops and buffer zones, explicitly rejecting mandatory pollution limits or mandates on farmers. The framing here is broadly consistent with her platform (increased incentives for conservation, buffer zones, reducing PFAS/nitrates), so this is a narrow, largely accurate characterization; flagging only because some responses conflate this with mandate-based framing elsewhere in the broader research record, though this particular version tracks her actual voluntary-incentive stance reasonably well.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's approach emphasizes expanding mobile cancer screenings to reach underserved rural populations.
description: No record exists connecting Miller-Meeks to a 'mobile cancer screening' initiative or legislation. Her documented cancer-related record centers on the Nancy Gardner Sewell Medicare Multi-Cancer Early Detection Screening Coverage Act, the EARLY Act Reauthorization (breast/cervical cancer screening grants), and a telemammography pilot bill for veterans (MAMMO for Veterans Act) — none of which involve mobile screening units. A real 'Mobile Cancer Screening Act' exists in Congress but is sponsored by a different member (Rep. Raul Ruiz), not Miller-Meeks. This appears to be either a fabrication or a misattribution of another lawmaker's initiative to her.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks utilizes legislative proposals to steer tobacco tax revenues directly into cancer research funds.
description: The 'Cancer Research Trust Fund Act,' which would direct tobacco-tax/customs-duty revenue into a dedicated cancer research fund, is sponsored by Rep. Ashley Hinson (IA-02), not Miller-Meeks. No evidence ties Miller-Meeks to this specific proposal; her cancer-related legislative record focuses on screening and early-detection coverage rather than tobacco-tax revenue redirection.

inaccurate_statement: Critics and Democratic advocates point out Miller-Meeks's support for recent federal budget proposals that included steep cuts to health agencies, including the National Cancer Institute.
description: There is no substantiation for a specific opposition claim that Miller-Meeks's votes on broader federal budget bills reduced National Cancer Institute allocations specifically. Documented opposition criticism of her voting record centers on Medicaid cuts in the reconciliation/tax bill, not NCI-specific funding reductions; in fact, she has touted legislation that expanded Medicare coverage for multi-cancer early detection and other cancer-related funding. This mischaracterizes the actual substance of criticism aimed at her record.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan favors large-scale, bipartisan infrastructure programs like the IIJA, arguing that direct federal spending creates high-paying jobs for local workers and is essential to keeping Iowa's rural economies and agricultural transit corridors competitive.
description: Bohannan has no confirmed 2026 platform statement on roads/bridges/infrastructure specifically; this is a genuine, documented gap in her record. The only related historical fact is a 2021 tweet supporting the federal infrastructure bill and noting Miller-Meeks voted against it. Presenting a specific rationale about 'agricultural transit corridors' and 'rural economies' as her stated position, without hedging that this is inferred, overstates what is actually confirmed.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's infrastructure platform centers heavily on promoting domestic energy production, supporting American manufacturing, and focusing federal resources directly on traditional, core infrastructure projects without expanding federal regulation.
description: Miller-Meeks does not have a documented 'infrastructure platform' framed around domestic energy production and manufacturing in this way. Her actual, confirmed infrastructure record is a delivery-focused one: touting over $87.1 million in federal funding for IA-01 since taking office, including named projects like the Burlington Cascade Bridge replacement and Iowa County road paving. The claim substitutes an energy/manufacturing-centric framing not found in her documented infrastructure statements for her real, itemized funding-delivery record.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has consistently championed the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA), emphasizing that Iowa's rural roads and high number of deficient bridges require substantial, structural federal investment
description: Bohannan's own campaign platform, checked directly against her full 'Priorities' page, contains no current 2026 statement on roads/bridges/infrastructure specifically -- this is a confirmed gap, not a documented position. The only related fact found is a 2021 tweet as a state representative supporting the federal infrastructure bill and noting Miller-Meeks voted against it, which is a narrower and more dated fact than the sweeping 'consistently championed... requires substantial, structural federal investment' framing presented here as her current plan.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan often highlights her past career as an engineer, arguing that her technical background gives her a practical understanding of structural integrity and project management needed to fix deteriorating roads and bridges.
description: Christina Bohannan has an environmental engineering background, but there is no documented statement connecting that background to roads and bridges or structural-integrity expertise. Her own 2026 campaign platform has no stated position on roads, bridges, or infrastructure at all — this is a confirmed gap in her public record, not merely under-covered territory — and her engineering background is instead tied in her public statements to water quality and drinking-water/wastewater regulation, not to structural engineering of roads and bridges. Presenting this as her actual campaign argument fabricates a rationale central to the very question being asked.

inaccurate_statement: Christina Bohannan takes a 'moderate approach' to border security focused on increased operational resources, bipartisan legislation, and reforming the legal processing framework.
description: Characterizing Bohannan's border stance as simply 'moderate' presents a contested political framing as settled fact. Her position does combine support for border security resources with a pathway to citizenship and broader immigration reform, but no neutral source establishes her as objectively 'moderate' on this issue, and this framing glosses over the genuine political dispute over how to characterize her record.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supported enforcement packages aimed at funding an additional 10,000 border agents
description: No record in the available material ties Miller-Meeks to a specific legislative push for '10,000' additional border agents as a distinct figure; her documented border-security record centers on the Secure the Border Act, Laken Riley Act, SAVE Act, and general support for more Border Patrol/ICE funding, without this specific numeric commitment being substantiated.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supports streamlining specific, legal visa pathways—such as those for seasonal agricultural workers—only after the physical border is fully secured
description: Miller-Meeks has supported legal-immigration reforms such as documented Dreamers legislation and general support for legal pathways including agricultural workers, but there is no documented statement from her conditioning these reforms specifically on the border being 'fully secured' first as a sequencing requirement; this specific sequencing claim is not substantiated by her record.

inaccurate_statement: She has also supported state-level initiatives aimed at reforming unemployment systems to incentivize a faster return to the workforce.
description: No record exists of Miller-Meeks supporting or advocating specific state-level unemployment-system reform initiatives. Her official House 'Economy' page and documented platform emphasize energy production, small-business tax cuts, manufacturing, and housing affordability, but do not address unemployment insurance/system reform, and no news coverage or press release ties her to this specific claim. This is a narrow, unsupported addition to an otherwise generally accurate characterization of her economic platform, so it does not undermine the broader accurate framing.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan advocates for shifting tax advantages away from corporations toward hardworking families and small businesses as a specific unemployment-reduction mechanism
description: Bohannan's platform does emphasize taxing corporations/wealthy more and providing middle-class relief generally, but there is no documented statement tying this specifically to an unemployment-reduction plan; presenting it as a defined 'jobs pillar' with this framing overstates what is actually a general affordability/tax position.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's official economy platform contains an explicit, itemized unemployment-reduction plan built around a 'supply-side economics' label
description: Miller-Meeks's official economy page emphasizes energy production, manufacturing, small-business tax cuts, and housing affordability, but there is a confirmed gap: no explicit statement addressing the unemployment rate as such was found, and no source uses the specific 'supply-side economics' label for her platform. Presenting this as her own explicitly stated economic philosophy/plan overstates a real but confirmed gap in her documented record on this specific topic.

inaccurate_statement: Critics state the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' Miller-Meeks voted for slashes billions in funding from the National Cancer Institute
description: No source in the available record ties criticism of Miller-Meeks's vote for the OBBBA to National Cancer Institute funding cuts specifically. Documented criticism of this vote centers on its Medicaid cuts (~$12 billion in cuts, contributing to an estimated 110,000 more uninsured Iowans) and rural hospital closures, not NCI budget reductions. A related note in the record explicitly found that opponents' criticism of her broader budget votes as reducing 'direct National Cancer Institute allocations' could not be substantiated and instead reflects national Trump-administration budget proposals unrelated to her specific vote, making this a mischaracterization of the actual criticism raised against her.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan backs stricter government regulation on carcinogens and environmental factors as part of her cancer-prevention approach.
description: Bohannan's documented position on agricultural/environmental regulation tied to water contamination (a major carcinogen-exposure pathway cited in Iowa's cancer crisis) is the opposite of a push for stricter mandatory regulation. She has said she wants to focus on 'supporting farmers in conserving their land, rather than imposing strict mandates on them,' and her 2026 platform states the government should work 'with farmers and business owners, not against them,' favoring incentives and investment over mandates. While her support for stricter tobacco regulation is accurate, characterizing her broader approach to environmental/carcinogen regulation as favoring 'stricter government regulation' misrepresents her actual voluntary/incentive-based stance on agricultural pollution.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan emphasizes stronger accountability for industrial agricultural pollution, advocating for robust federal oversight, greater transparency, and increased investments in clean drinking water infrastructure and water monitoring to combat high nitrate levels, favoring pollution limits and stricter federal oversight over voluntary measures
description: Bohannan's actual stated approach to water quality favors working with farmers through incentives and investments rather than mandates: her platform pledges to "increase resources and incentives for farmers to boost buffer zones" and take action to reduce PFAS, framed as cooperative and incentive-based rather than as "robust federal oversight" or "pollution limits." Separately, in a direct 2022 statement she said she would focus on "supporting farmers in conserving their land, rather than imposing strict mandates on them," and her 2026 platform reaffirms that government should work "with farmers and business owners, not against them," favoring investments over unfunded mandates. This directly contradicts the response's framing of her as the stricter-oversight, mandate-favoring candidate; her actual documented position is closer to the voluntary/incentive-based approach the response attributes only to Miller-Meeks.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has criticized Miller-Meeks's past votes against measures targeting energy price inflation
description: Bohannan's documented criticisms of Miller-Meeks center on tariff votes, Medicaid cuts, and corporate donor influence on grocery/gas pricing generally, framed as opposing anti-price-gouging legislation (e.g., the Consumer Fuel Price Gouging Prevention Act) rather than a specifically framed attack on 'votes against measures targeting energy price inflation' as a distinct category. This is a loose characterization that blends real but distinct criticisms rather than a clean, verified claim.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan supports crackdowns on corporate consolidation within the agricultural and food retail sectors
description: Bohannan's documented platform includes cracking down on price gouging and anti-competitive practices, including anti-competitive seed/fertilizer/processing pricing and increasing competition in meat and grain processing, which is broadly consistent with opposing corporate consolidation. However, no direct statement specifically naming 'corporate consolidation' as a distinct targeted policy area was found in her platform materials; this is a plausible but unhedged inference rather than a directly sourced position, though closely aligned with her documented positions on anti-competitive pricing.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's approach includes investing in renewable energy to bring down everyday utility costs for families, as part of her grocery-price plan
description: Bohannan's campaign platform does discuss expanding clean energy and cracking down on utility monopolies to lower electricity bills, but this is presented separately from her grocery/price-gouging plank, which centers on cracking down on corporate price gouging at the grocery store and gas pump. Framing renewable energy investment as part of her grocery-price-lowering strategy conflates two distinct planks of her platform.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's approach includes clawing back unused federal relief funds to stabilize the national debt and economic environment, as part of her plan to lower grocery costs
description: No record exists of Bohannan proposing to claw back unused federal relief funds as part of her economic or grocery-price platform. Her documented affordability platform centers on ending tariffs, capping insulin costs, cracking down on price gouging, and preventing investor purchases of homes/farmland — not federal relief fund clawbacks, which is a distinct, unsupported claim not found in her campaign materials or reported statements.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supports policies that penalize sanctuary cities and require strict cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE to transfer individuals with criminal records to federal custody for deportation
description: No record exists in Miller-Meeks's documented platform or voting record of a specific stated position penalizing sanctuary cities or requiring strict local-ICE cooperation for custody transfers. Her confirmed immigration record centers on the Laken Riley Act, Secure the Border Act, SAVE Act, and general enforcement funding support, but this specific sanctuary-city/local-cooperation mechanism is not documented as her stated position, making this an unverified and likely embellished addition presented without hedging as her platform.

inaccurate_statement: Christina Bohannan bases her public safety strategy on building community trust, investing in local law enforcement resources, and enacting common-sense gun safety measures to prevent violence.
description: Bohannan's official campaign platform contains no dedicated public safety section describing a strategy built around community trust and investment in local law enforcement resources; that language does not appear on her campaign site or in her public statements. Her actual documented public-safety-adjacent record is narrower and more contested, centered mainly on her 2021 vote against Iowa's 'Back the Blue' bill over qualified-immunity and civil-liberties concerns, plus a separate, real position supporting expanded background checks and red-flag laws. Framing this inferred narrative as her stated 'strategy' overstates what she has actually said on the topic.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks advocates for robust funding for police departments
description: Miller-Meeks has secured specific local law-enforcement-related funding items (e.g., the Oskaloosa SAFECity Initiative) and generally emphasizes 'backing the blue,' but her official House 'Economy'/issue pages do not present a broad, itemized 'robust funding for police departments' platform akin to a comprehensive national policing budget commitment. This is a generalized characterization that overstates a more narrowly documented record, though it isn't a fabrication of her general pro-law-enforcement stance.

inaccurate_statement: She advocates for a robust federal Farm Bill that strongly protects crop insurance programs and expands investments in rural infrastructure.
description: Miller-Meeks has a documented record on farm income stabilization centered on voting for the Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026 and introducing the Lowering Input Costs for American Farmers Act (cutting fertilizer tariffs), plus emphasizing crop insurance as part of a 'farm safety net.' However, there is no confirmed record of her specifically advocating for expanded 'investments in rural infrastructure' as part of her Farm Bill platform; her documented infrastructure delivery record (roads, bridges) is a separate, distinct platform item not tied to the Farm Bill itself. This bundles a real position (crop insurance protection) with an unverified addition (rural infrastructure investment within the Farm Bill specifically), which is a narrow mischaracterization rather than a fabrication of her overall farm-income stance.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks favors aggressive trade policies and supports structural efforts to secure better export deals for American producers, aiming to shield Iowa farmers from unfair international competition, framed as strong trade enforcement/aggressive tariff enforcement to protect domestic markets.
description: Miller-Meeks's actual record on tariffs is more complicated than straightforward 'aggressive tariff enforcement to protect domestic markets.' She voted three times to block House consideration of ending Trump's tariff emergency declarations and voted against ending the Canada tariff emergency, while independent reporting has tied her broader tariff support to higher gas/fertilizer prices and depressed crop commodity prices — a tension with her own farmer-focused messaging. Framing her tariff stance simply as protective trade enforcement without any of this nuance overstates the case as settled fact rather than a contested characterization.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is a former nurse
description: Miller-Meeks's documented credentials are a BSN (nursing degree), M.S. in Education, and an M.D., followed by a career running a private ophthalmology practice as a physician. There is no record of her having worked as a nurse in a clinical role prior to becoming a physician; she is consistently described as a physician/ophthalmologist, not as someone who practiced nursing as a distinct former career before medical school.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks earned an endorsement from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.
description: The dossier for Miller-Meeks explicitly notes that Chamber of Commerce engagement (roundtables, meetings) is confirmed, but no formal Iowa Chamber of Commerce PAC endorsement was found in the original research pass, and any claim of formal endorsement should be treated as unconfirmed at that time. However, a later live-search sweep found that the U.S. Chamber of Commerce did endorse Miller-Meeks on August 28, 2026, specifically citing her work for Iowa businesses and pro-growth tax policies. Given this later confirmation supersedes the earlier caution, this endorsement claim is actually accurate, not inaccurate — reclassifying to confirmed_accurate is warranted, but since the automated categorization required a decision, note that this endorsement is real per the most recent findings.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is formally endorsed by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce
description: The U.S. Chamber of Commerce endorsed Miller-Meeks on August 28, 2026, so this is actually confirmed accurate rather than inaccurate.

inaccurate_statement: The U.S. Chamber of Commerce endorsement of Miller-Meeks was specifically for 'supporting pro-growth tax policies and engaging local business leaders'
description: The U.S. Chamber of Commerce did endorse Miller-Meeks on August 28, 2026, and its stated rationale did cite her work for Iowa businesses, pro-growth tax policies, and engagement with small-business leaders, so this framing is essentially accurate and not flagged as an error beyond what is already credited above.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks routinely highlights domestic manufacturing 'through initiatives like her Made in America Manufacturing tour' as a small-business support mechanism specifically
description: Miller-Meeks did complete a 'Made in America Manufacturing Tour,' but this is documented as a broader manufacturing/jobs-focused activity; her most concretely documented small-business-specific policy is support for making the Small Business Deduction permanent via OBBBA and Chamber/NFIB engagement, not the manufacturing tour itself. Presenting the tour as her small-business mechanism blurs two related but distinct parts of her record.

inaccurate_statement: Christina Bohannan's core message on data center growth focuses broadly on working-class affordability and protecting family farms, aligning with statewide Democratic initiatives calling for heavier regulation of industrial utilities
description: There is no record of Christina Bohannan taking any position on data center development. Multiple research passes, including direct review of her campaign's full platform page and social media, found this to be a confirmed, notable silence on a topic her own district is actively litigating (the Clinton QTS data-center controversy). Presenting a specific stance on data centers as her position, rather than disclosing that she has not addressed the topic, is a fabrication that could mislead a reader about her actual record on this specific issue.

inaccurate_statement: Mariannette Miller-Meeks's core message on data center growth emphasizes energy independence and grid reliability, maintaining that local consumer rates must be protected from sudden industry spikes
description: Miller-Meeks has made general, statewide remarks about data centers, including concern about water usage and electricity rates increasing and the need for transparency and community involvement, so this is not wholly fabricated. However, no statement specifically addressing the in-district Clinton, IA QTS data-center project was found despite dedicated searching, and framing this as a fully developed 'core message' on the topic overstates the specificity and completeness of her actual public record, which is general/statewide rather than a defined policy position.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan is aligned with the platform pushing back against unchecked data center development
description: Christina Bohannan has no documented public statement on data center development despite dedicated searches of her campaign site, social media, and news coverage, including specific coverage of the Clinton, Iowa data-center controversy inside her district. This is a confirmed, genuine gap in her record, not a position she has taken. Presenting her as actively pushing back against unchecked data center development directly contradicts the confirmed absence of any such stated position and would materially mislead a reader about her platform.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's platform utilizes a platform that questions large-scale corporate developments over local resource conservation, mirroring the wider Democratic strategy to demand federal guardrails for AI infrastructure projects
description: No source shows Bohannan's campaign platform addressing data centers, AI infrastructure guardrails, or corporate development scrutiny in this context. Her official campaign priorities page (checked in full across multiple research passes) contains no mention of data centers. This is a fabricated policy position presented as her own stated stance.

inaccurate_statement: Opponents have framed Bohannan as a 'multimillionaire liberal' whose proposed policies would increase economic burdens, rather than lower taxes, for local Iowa families
description: No record exists of Bohannan being labeled specifically a 'multimillionaire liberal' by opponents. Attack coverage has referred to her as a 'radical progressive' (Miller-Meeks's own characterization) and has scrutinized her stock holdings and home ownership, but the specific 'multimillionaire liberal' framing does not match documented attack lines against her.

inaccurate_statement: Critics have accused Bohannan of 'evaluating early American history through frames that emphasize the preservation of slavery'
description: No record exists of this specific characterization or attack line against Bohannan. Her documented controversies include the 2021 'backwater' quote about a transgender athletes bill and a separate 'backwards state' comment about DEI training restrictions, plus scrutiny of her DEI committee work promoting donations to bail funds. There is no documented basis for this specific claim about her framing early American history around slavery preservation; it appears to be an invented elaboration not grounded in any known controversy.

inaccurate_statement: A formal complaint was filed with the Office of Congressional Ethics alleging Miller-Meeks committed 'election misconduct and voter fraud'
description: A residency-related ethics complaint and a separate county-board residency challenge were real and documented, but no official body — the Scott County board, the Office of Congressional Ethics, or any court — has found that Miller-Meeks committed voter fraud or election misconduct. The Scott County board actually accepted and counted her 2024 ballot, and OCE did not pursue the complaint further. Characterizing the complaint's substance as an adjudicated or even squarely-alleged 'voter fraud' finding overstates what is actually a real but unresolved and disputed controversy.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks maintained her primary residence in Ottumwa while registering to vote using a Davenport (Scott County) address, and this Davenport address is the one at issue in the ethics complaint
description: The documented registration timeline shows she first registered at a state senator's home in LeClaire (Scott County) in October 2022, then registered at a Davenport apartment in 2024 (voting there that November) — and the residency challenge/ethics complaint in fall 2024 concerned that period. She later re-registered in December 2025 at her Ottumwa home, which is outside IA-01. The response conflates and compresses this timeline, describing the Davenport address as being used concurrently with a claimed Ottumwa 'primary residence' at the time of the complaint, when the actual chronology involves sequential registration changes across different addresses and years.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's office points to her being out across the district's 20 counties as evidence of accessibility.
description: Miller-Meeks completed a 20-county in-person tour, but the dossier describes this as a broader factual point rather than something specifically framed by her office as a defense against town-hall criticism; this detail is closely aligned with the documented record (a 20-county tour did occur), so any discrepancy here is negligible and largely accurate in substance.

inaccurate_statement: Christina Bohannan centers her campaign platform on working across the aisle and reducing partisan bickering.
description: Bohannan's official 2026 campaign platform centers on lowering costs, health care, ethics reform, education, family farms, and reproductive freedom, framed largely through sharp partisan contrasts with her opponent's voting record and corporate donations. 'Extreme partisanship' is mentioned only briefly as one of several problems alongside 'the corrupting influence of money and special interests,' and only one bipartisan bill from her state legislative record is cited. Her messaging is dominated by economic populism and pointed attacks on her opponent's record rather than a defining 'working across the aisle' theme.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has voted to override certain presidential vetoes as an example of bipartisan independence.
description: There is no record in the available material of Miller-Meeks voting to override a presidential veto during her time in Congress (2023–present, under Democratic and then Republican presidents). No such veto-override vote is documented in her legislative record, and this appears to be an invented or unsupported specific example of bipartisanship attributed to her.

inaccurate_statement: EMILY's List endorsed her nomination to help flip the House [attributed to Miller-Meeks]
description: EMILY's List is a Democratic organization that supports pro-choice Democratic women; it has endorsed Christina Bohannan (first endorsed in 2022, renewed for 2026), not Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a Republican. The response's structure attributes this endorsement to Miller-Meeks, which reverses the actual endorsement and misleads readers about which candidate has this support.

inaccurate_statement: Reproductive Freedom for All, Everytown for Gun Safety, and the League of Conservation Voters endorsed her [attributed to Miller-Meeks]
description: Reproductive Freedom for All, Everytown for Gun Safety Action Fund, and LCV Action Fund are all progressive/Democratic-aligned advocacy organizations that have endorsed Christina Bohannan, not Mariannette Miller-Meeks. Miller-Meeks is pro-life and has a Republican voting record on guns and environmental regulation, making endorsements from these groups implausible and contrary to the documented record, which shows these groups backing Bohannan instead.

inaccurate_statement: EMILY's List endorsed Bohannan as a key 'red-to-blue' candidate
description: The 'Red to Blue' program is run by the DCCC, not EMILY's List. EMILY's List has its own separate, longstanding endorsement of Bohannan (since 2022) unrelated to the DCCC's Red to Blue program, so attributing 'red-to-blue' status to EMILY's List conflates two distinct organizations' endorsements.

inaccurate_statement: New Democrat Coalition Action Fund named Bohannan to their initial 2026 midterm endorsement slate
description: No record exists of a New Democrat Coalition Action Fund endorsement of Christina Bohannan. This is a specific, named organizational endorsement not found in the available research, though it is a narrow, peripheral detail that does not change the overall accurate picture that Bohannan has received numerous real endorsements.

inaccurate_statement: Donald Trump endorsed Miller-Meeks, highlighting her background as a medical doctor and U.S. Army veteran
description: Trump's endorsement of Miller-Meeks (a 'Complete and Total Endorsement' issued in November 2025) is well documented, but no source ties his endorsement statement to specifically highlighting her medical or military background as the stated rationale. This specific framing detail appears to be an embellishment not grounded in the actual endorsement announcement.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan raised approximately $4.5 million specifically from individual contributors.
description: According to FEC data for the filing period ending June 30, 2026, Bohannan's individual contributions totaled $5,648,339.98, not approximately $4.5 million — the actual figure is over $1 million higher than stated.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's campaign has heavily emphasized grassroots and individual small-dollar contributions from supporters looking to flip the district.
description: FEC-based reporting on Bohannan's donor breakdown found that large individual contributions, not small-dollar donations, made up the largest share of her individual fundraising, which cuts against a characterization emphasizing small-dollar/grassroots giving as her primary funding driver.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks raised millions through individual donors, alongside support from political action committees and party committees.
description: Per FEC filings for the period ending June 30, 2026, Miller-Meeks's individual contributions totaled $2,945,343.16, which is less than her PAC/committee contributions of $2,416,206.95 combined with transfers from other authorized committees of $1,686,037.07 — while individuals are still her largest single category, the framing obscures that PAC money made up a substantially larger share of her fundraising than is typical for a campaign primarily described as individual-donor-driven, and this doesn't undermine the overall accurate point that she does raise from a mix of individuals, PACs, and committees.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has brought in approximately $4.5 million from individual contributors
description: Per FEC data for the filing period ending June 30, 2026, Christina Bohannan's total individual contributions were $5,648,339.98, not approximately $4.5 million.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has raised roughly $2.5 million directly from individual donors
description: Per FEC data for the filing period ending June 30, 2026, Miller-Meeks's individual contributions totaled $2,945,343.16, closer to $2.9 million than $2.5 million, though this is a relatively narrow numerical discrepancy.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan focuses on expanding Medicaid while opposing cuts to healthcare programs.
description: Bohannan's documented healthcare platform centers on a Medicare buy-in at any age, expanding Medicare to vision/dental/hearing, capping insulin costs, and reversing Medicaid cuts (i.e., opposing cuts to existing Medicaid, not proposing to expand it as a distinct policy). There is no record of her proposing to actually expand Medicaid eligibility or benefits as a named platform item; her documented position is reversing Medicaid cuts to prevent rural hospital closures, which is a narrower claim than 'expanding Medicaid.'

inaccurate_statement: Both candidates face each other after extremely close past results
description: Only the 2024 matchup between Bohannan and Miller-Meeks was extremely close, decided by just 799 votes after a recount. Their 2022 matchup was not close at all — Miller-Meeks won comfortably by about 7 points (53%-47%). Describing the 'past results' collectively as 'extremely close' mischaracterizes the 2022 race.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is seeking her fourth term
description: Miller-Meeks is the sitting incumbent seeking a third consecutive term representing Iowa's 1st Congressional District specifically (having won the seat in 2022 and 2024, after winning the old, differently-numbered IA-02 in 2020). Describing this as her 'fourth term' without clarifying that one of those terms was in a different, pre-redistricting district could be read as a term-count of the current seat, which would be inaccurate — she would be starting her third term representing IA-01 if she wins in 2026, though it would be her fourth term in the U.S. House overall.

inaccurate_statement: Both candidates face each other after extremely close past results
description: Only the 2024 matchup between Bohannan and Miller-Meeks was extremely close, decided by just 799 votes after a recount. Their 2022 matchup was not close at all — Miller-Meeks won comfortably by about 7 points (53%-47%). Describing the 'past results' collectively as 'extremely close' mischaracterizes the 2022 race.

inaccurate_statement: Critics point to her votes against measures like the Consumer Fuel Price Gouging Prevention Act
description: No record in the available material confirms a Miller-Meeks vote against a 'Consumer Fuel Price Gouging Prevention Act,' though she has been criticized for opposing similar corporate-accountability/price-gouging measures in general terms. This specific bill and vote could not be verified against her documented voting record.

inaccurate_statement: Critics contend that her support for major Republican tax packages, such as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, disproportionately benefits the top 1% of earners and large corporations while threatening reductions in social safety programs
description: This is presented as a specific critics' claim about distributional impact on 'the top 1% of earners' specifically. The dossier documents that OBBBA contains Medicaid work-requirement provisions and cuts that critics say hurt low-income Iowans, and that KFF estimates ~110,000 more Iowans uninsured by 2034, but does not document a specific '1%' distributional claim being made by her critics in this race. This specific framing is not clearly grounded in the documented criticism and should be treated with caution, though the general thrust that critics call the bill corporate/wealthy-favoring is otherwise supported.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks was fined $500 by the House Ethics Committee for violating federal House floor mask mandates
description: She was fined $500 by the House Sergeant at Arms for going maskless on the House floor, and the House Ethics Committee later published/documented this fine rather than being the body that levied it. This is a narrow procedural distinction that doesn't change the core fact that she was fined and did violate the mask mandate.

inaccurate_statement: Multiple complaints were filed with the House Committee on Ethics alleging she violated Iowa voting laws over her residency
description: The residency/voting complaint was filed with the federal Office of Congressional Ethics (OCE), and a separate residency challenge was filed with the Scott County board of supervisors — not the House Committee on Ethics directly. The Scott County board accepted and counted her ballot, and no official body found she broke the law.

inaccurate_statement: The 2020 financial disclosure complaint claimed she failed to report at least $25,000 from her prior salary as an Iowa State Senator, in addition to the $35,000 in pension/Great River Health Systems income
description: The dossier's documented complaint describes roughly $34,646-$35,000 in total unreported/misstated income encompassing her state pension, Great River Health Systems payments, and her state senate salary combined — not an additional separate $25,000 salary figure on top of the $35,000. The response appears to double-count or misstate the breakdown of the alleged unreported income.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's legal team faced pushback for objecting to a federal House review of her own election while she simultaneously signed onto generic Republican letters calling for a broader investigation into 2020 election irregularities, and her name was later removed from that letter
description: Contemporaneous reporting indicates Miller-Meeks's campaign stated she never signed or agreed to be included on the letter urging investigation of 2020 election irregularities; her name was reportedly added in error by a colleague's staff and then removed, rather than her having signed it and then had it retracted.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks amended her financial disclosure to officially disclose between $880,000 and $2.6 million in previously unlisted retirement assets and salaries
description: The documented ethics complaint concerned roughly $34,000-$80,000 in omitted income and assets (state pension, state senate salary, Great River Health Systems income, and retirement account assets), not a figure in the hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. No source in the available record supports an $880,000 to $2.6 million disclosed amount.

inaccurate_statement: The hoax veterans'-benefits story Miller-Meeks shared forced a regional VA hospital to issue an emergency alert clarifying that benefits were safe
description: While it is well documented that Miller-Meeks shared this satirical story and it caused concern among veterans, no source confirms that a regional VA hospital issued an emergency alert in response; this appears to be an embellishment added to an otherwise accurate underlying story.

inaccurate_statement: The complaint about her voter registration/residency was filed with the Office of Congressional Ethics regarding Scott County while her Ottumwa home is outside her district
description: The documented residency controversy involves Miller-Meeks registering at a LeClaire address in October 2022, then a Davenport apartment in 2024 (both in Scott County, within IA-01), while continuing to claim an Ottumwa property-tax homestead credit. A Bettendorf resident (not the OCE itself) filed both a residency challenge with the Scott County board and a separate OCE complaint in fall 2024. The Scott County board accepted and counted her 2024 ballot, and the OCE did not pursue the complaint further. The response's framing generally aligns with this but omits that no official body found wrongdoing, and conflates some details of the challenge process, though the core facts (Ottumwa residence outside the district, a complaint filed, dismissal by her campaign as frivolous) are substantively accurate.

inaccurate_statement: At a separate public forum, Miller-Meeks denied ever voting in favor of Donald Trump's tariff policies, and attendees booed her after being shown her voting record
description: No record exists of this specific incident in which Miller-Meeks denied voting for tariff policies at a public forum and was then confronted with her voting record, leading to booing. The documented town-hall controversy involves her Keosauqua town hall over healthcare, Medicaid, and federal spending, and separate voting-record facts show she voted multiple times to block ending tariff emergencies. No source describes this specific tariff-denial-and-booing incident, so it is unverifiable as described and inconsistent with the documented town-hall record.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's campaign mistakenly paid her son, Jonathan Miller-Meeks, $3,500 from her campaign account for "consulting," and the money was returned 22 days later with an amended FEC report
description: No record in available material corroborates this specific claim about a $3,500 payment to a son named Jonathan Miller-Meeks for consulting, a 22-day return period, or an amended FEC filing describing this specific error. While the dossier does note general scrutiny over campaign expenditures including payments to family members for consulting work, this specific dollar figure, family member name, and timeline could not be verified and appear to be a fabricated or invented detail layered onto a real but more general concern.

inaccurate_statement: Political opponents criticize her for voting against certain budget amendments meant to protect Medicaid funding.
description: Miller-Meeks's documented Medicaid-related vote of significance is her yes vote on the 2025 reconciliation bill (OBBBA), which contained Medicaid work-requirement provisions and cuts, not a vote against a specific budget amendment framed as 'protecting Medicaid funding.' The response's vague framing of 'certain budget amendments' does not match the specific, well-documented vote record, making this an imprecise characterization rather than a clearly sourced claim.

inaccurate_statement: Research groups warn that if these financial credits expire, monthly insurance bills could double or increase significantly for thousands of families in Iowa and across the nation.
description: KFF has estimated that the combined expiration of enhanced ACA subsidies and Medicaid cuts could result in roughly 110,000 more uninsured Iowans, and health policy organizations have warned premiums could rise substantially or roughly double for many marketplace enrollees if subsidies expire — this is a real, nonpartisan estimate, so the claim is broadly consistent with available reporting. It is included here only to note that Miller-Meeks's office has publicly disputed the causal framing tying local provider/cost problems specifically to her votes, a nuance the response omits, though this alone is not enough to make the statement inaccurate.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan supports expanding Medicare to cover home health costs for family caregivers
description: Bohannan's documented Medicare expansion proposal centers on a Medicare buy-in at any age plus adding dental, hearing, and vision coverage; her platform materials do not establish home health costs for family caregivers as part of this plan, and other research found this specific benefit was not part of her described Medicare platform.

inaccurate_statement: Medicare Expansion: Expand Medicare coverage to include vision, dental, hearing care, and home health costs for family caregivers.
description: Bohannan's documented Medicare expansion proposal centers on adding dental, hearing, and vision coverage alongside a Medicare buy-in option at any age. Home health costs for family caregivers is a separate proposal she has made regarding caregiver support, but it is not consistently documented as part of her core 'Medicare expansion' plank in the same way vision, dental, and hearing coverage are, and combining them without distinction slightly overstates the specificity of her core, most-cited Medicare platform.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's healthcare platform includes expanding Medicare to add coverage for dental, vision, hearing, and home health care
description: Bohannan's documented Medicare expansion proposal adds dental, hearing, and vision coverage along with a Medicare buy-in option, but does not include home health care as part of this specific plan. Multiple sources confirm her stated Medicare expansion covers dental, hearing, and vision only, not home health services.

inaccurate_statement: She served as a private [in the military]
description: There is no record in her biography of her serving as an enlisted private; she joined the Army Medical Department and her documented military roles are nursing and medical officer positions, not a description of starting as a private specifically noted anywhere in her biography.

inaccurate_statement: State Health Director: Appointed by Iowa Governor Terry Branstad as the Director of the Iowa Department of Public Health, serving from 2010 to 2014
description: Miller-Meeks served as Iowa Department of Public Health Director from 2010 to 2013, not through 2014 — she resigned in 2013 to run for Congress.

inaccurate_statement: Served as president of the Iowa Academy of Ophthalmology and president of the medical staff at Ottumwa Regional Health Center
description: Miller-Meeks's documented leadership roles are as the first female president of the Iowa Medical Society and the first woman in 20 years on the University of Iowa ophthalmology faculty; there is no record of her serving as president of the Iowa Academy of Ophthalmology or president of the medical staff at Ottumwa Regional Health Center.

inaccurate_statement: Assumed office in January 2021 representing Iowa's 1st Congressional District
description: Miller-Meeks was first elected to Congress in November 2020 and took office in January 2021 representing Iowa's 2nd Congressional District under the pre-2022 redistricting map, not the 1st District; she began representing the 1st District only in January 2023 after redistricting.

inaccurate_statement: Enlisted in the U.S. Army at age 18
description: No record supports the specific claim that she enlisted at age 18; her documented Army service ran from 1974 to 1982 (Army Medical Department, retired Lieutenant Colonel), followed by Army Reserve service from 1983 to 2000, but no source specifies her enlistment age.

inaccurate_statement: Introduced bills like the Supporting Children's Mental Health Care Access Act to expand behavioral health resources
description: No evidence in the available record ties Miller-Meeks to a bill titled the 'Supporting Children's Mental Health Care Access Act.' Her documented children's mental health/AI-safety work includes the Conversational AI Services Act and other named bills, but this specific title does not appear in her sponsored or co-sponsored legislation record.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan criticized Miller-Meeks for relying heavily on out-of-state and corporate donations, contrasting it with her own grassroots support coming from hardworking Iowa families.
description: While it is accurate that Bohannan's fundraising draws a somewhat higher share from within Iowa compared to Miller-Meeks, and that Miller-Meeks accepts corporate PAC money while Bohannan does not, there is no confirmed direct Bohannan quote or statement specifically framing this as an attack contrasting 'out-of-state and corporate donations' with 'hardworking Iowa families' grassroots support. This narrative is plausible given both candidates' documented fundraising patterns, but the specific framing and attribution as a direct Bohannan criticism could not be verified against her documented statements.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan opposed carbon capture pipeline projects that rely on eminent domain to take private land from Iowa landowners, whereas she criticized Miller-Meeks' stance on the projects.
description: Bohannan's opposition to eminent domain for carbon capture pipelines is documented and accurate. However, Miller-Meeks's own position on these pipelines is that she has expressed support for carbon capture projects to aid the ethanol industry while also opposing the use of eminent domain for them -- meaning the two candidates' stated positions on eminent domain specifically are not clearly opposed to the degree the claim implies. Framing this as a clear-cut criticism of Miller-Meeks's 'stance on the projects' overstates the documented contrast between the two candidates' actual positions.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan criticizes Miller-Meeks for voting against the bipartisan infrastructure law while noting Miller-Meeks has taken credit for parts of it
description: This is broadly accurate: Bohannan has criticized Miller-Meeks for voting against the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law and pointed out that Miller-Meeks has touted funding from bills she opposed. This is well-documented in both dossiers, so it is not an error; it is included here only because it overlaps with the accurate list, and is otherwise fine as stated.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan points out that Miller-Meeks voted against the PACT Act (burn pit legislation for veterans)
description: Neither dossier documents any Bohannan criticism of Miller-Meeks specifically regarding a vote against the PACT Act. The Bohannan dossier's catalog of her criticisms of Miller-Meeks does not mention veterans' burn pit legislation, and Miller-Meeks's own dossier records no vote against the PACT Act; it instead notes her criticism of Miller-Meeks for opposing burn pit reform legislation as a separate, unconfirmed thread found only in third-party sweep notes ('Bohannan criticized Miller-Meeks for opposing burn pit reform legislation intended to provide healthcare to toxic-exposed veterans' appears in the Miller-Meeks live-search sweep as accurate, but there it refers to a different, unspecified burn pit bill, not confirmed to be the PACT Act specifically). Given the lack of clear substantiation tying this specific claim (PACT Act vote) to a documented Bohannan attack line, this is a minor, likely overstated/conflated claim.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks defeated Bohannan in closely contested races (plural) for Iowa's 1st Congressional District
description: Only one of the two prior Miller-Meeks vs. Bohannan races was closely contested. The 2022 race was a comfortable Miller-Meeks win by about 7 points (53%-47%), not close; only the 2024 race was genuinely razor-thin, decided by 799 votes after a recount. Describing both races as 'closely contested' misstates the 2022 result.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has directed federal funds toward local water and wastewater system capacity enhancements to manage heavy rain overflows
description: Miller-Meeks's confirmed water infrastructure funding is specific and itemized (the $3 million Davenport Water Pollution Control Plant project, plus earlier Mediapolis wastewater funding), not a broadly stated 'regional grants' program framed around managing heavy rain overflows generally. Presenting this as a distinct, named policy category beyond the specific documented projects overstates and generalizes what is actually a narrower, itemized funding record.

inaccurate_statement: She worked to restore critical state and federal funding for the Iowa Cancer Registry to accurately track and understand the state's cancer trends.
description: No evidence supports this claim. The Iowa Cancer Registry's funding is a state-level matter, and recent threats to its funding have come from federal budget cuts to the CDC generally, not from any documented effort by Miller-Meeks to restore funding to it specifically. Her documented cancer-related legislative record consists of federal bills on screening and early detection (the EARLY Act reauthorization, Medicare coverage for multi-cancer early detection tests), not action tied to the Iowa Cancer Registry's funding.

inaccurate_statement: She has held discussions with National Institutes of Health (NIH) leadership to advocate for continued federal research funding into the root causes and treatments of cancer.
description: No documented evidence supports a specific claim that Miller-Meeks held discussions with NIH leadership on this topic; this appears to be an unverified or invented detail rather than a sourced fact about her record.

inaccurate_statement: Championed provisions to establish Medicare coverage for MCED blood tests starting in 2029
description: Multiple sources, including her own congressional press release and independent coverage, confirm that the Medicare coverage for FDA-approved multi-cancer early-detection tests established under legislation she co-sponsored begins in 2028, not 2029.

inaccurate_statement: Worked to restore critical funding for the Iowa Cancer Registry so researchers can accurately track cancer rates and identify local trends
description: No evidence supports this claim. The Iowa Cancer Registry's funding is a state and federal (CDC) matter, and no press releases, news coverage, or legislative record ties Miller-Meeks to any effort to restore or protect its funding specifically. Her documented cancer-related record centers on other measures, such as the multi-cancer early-detection Medicare coverage bill and the EARLY Act reauthorization, not the Registry's funding or data infrastructure.

inaccurate_statement: Consulted with National Institutes of Health (NIH) leadership to ensure ongoing federal support and funding for medical research into cancer causes and treatments
description: No source substantiates that Miller-Meeks held discussions or consultations with NIH leadership specifically about cancer research funding. Her documented cancer-related legislative record involves sponsoring screening and early-detection bills (the multi-cancer early-detection Medicare coverage act, the EARLY Act reauthorization) rather than any confirmed direct engagement with NIH leadership on research funding.

inaccurate_statement: Medicare coverage for FDA-approved MCED screening tests starts in 2029.
description: Multiple sources, including Miller-Meeks's own press releases and the bill text, confirm Medicare coverage for FDA-approved multi-cancer early detection tests under the Nancy Gardner Sewell Medicare Multi-Cancer Early Detection Screening Coverage Act begins in 2028, not 2029.

inaccurate_statement: Secured $500,000 for the Oskaloosa SAFECity Initiative including school panic button systems under Alyssa's Law
description: Miller-Meeks did secure $500,000 in federal funding for Oskaloosa's SAFECity Initiative, which does include school safety panic buttons among other technologies. However, there is no evidence that this funding is specifically tied to or authorized under 'Alyssa's Law' — the federal ALYSSA Act was sponsored by Rep. Josh Gottheimer and has not passed, and Iowa has not enacted a state-level Alyssa's Law. Framing the panic-button funding as being 'under Alyssa's Law' misattributes the legal basis for this initiative.

inaccurate_statement: Co-sponsored the Defund Cities that Defund the Police Act to withhold federal grants from unsupportive municipalities
description: No record exists in the available material confirming that Miller-Meeks co-sponsored a bill called the 'Defund Cities that Defund the Police Act.' This specific legislative claim could not be substantiated, and her documented public-safety record centers on other measures (SAFECity funding, COPS program support, body cameras, Laken Riley Act, HALT Fentanyl Act) rather than this named bill.

inaccurate_statement: Directed funds toward school safety panic buttons and a Distributed Antenna System under Alyssa's Law to directly connect schools to law enforcement.
description: There is no federal 'Alyssa's Law' legislation that Miller-Meeks sponsored, cosponsored, or voted on; the actual federal ALYSSA Act was introduced by a different member of Congress and never became law, and Iowa has not enacted a state-level Alyssa's Law either. The school safety panic buttons Miller-Meeks helped fund were part of the broader Oskaloosa SAFECity Initiative appropriation, not tied to any law by that name.

inaccurate_statement: Supported funding under Alyssa's Law to install direct school panic buttons connecting facilities straight to law enforcement
description: The federal Alyssa's Law (ALYSSA Act) was sponsored by Rep. Josh Gottheimer, not Miller-Meeks, and Miller-Meeks is not a cosponsor of either version introduced in Congress; Iowa also has no state-level Alyssa's Law. Miller-Meeks did vote for a broader Oskaloosa public-safety appropriations package that included funding for school safety panic buttons among many other technologies, but this was not tied to or framed as 'Alyssa's Law' funding, making the specific attribution incorrect even though the underlying panic-button funding fact has some basis.

inaccurate_statement: She leads a bipartisan effort to require regular federal reporting on fertilizer pricing
description: The bipartisan Fertilizer Transparency Act, requiring regular federal reporting on fertilizer pricing, was introduced and led by Reps. Dusty Johnson (R-SD) and Brad Finstad (R-MN), with a Senate companion led by Sens. Thune and Klobuchar. Miller-Meeks is one of several cosponsors, not the lead of this effort.

inaccurate_statement: Supported the Cattle Contract Library Act to challenge anti-competitive practices by large corporations and protect small cattle farmers
description: There is no record indicating Miller-Meeks specifically sponsored or led the Cattle Contract Library Act; her documented antitrust-related agriculture legislation centers on the Meat Packing Special Investigator Act. While she may have supported this bill in some capacity, no specific sourcing ties her to it as a named backer, making this an unverified attribution rather than a confirmed fact.

inaccurate_statement: Co-led federal initiatives to defend the stepped-up basis tax provision, preventing farm families from being hit with capital gains taxes when inheriting land
description: Miller-Meeks does support and has publicly advocated for preserving the stepped-up basis tax rule, but available research found no evidence she 'co-led' a specific federal initiative on this provision as a discrete, named effort distinct from her broader tax/estate-tax advocacy; this appears to overstate the specificity of a real but more general position.

inaccurate_statement: The suspension of Moroccan phosphate fertilizer duties cuts farm expenses by an estimated $1.82 billion annually nationwide
description: No source in available research corroborates this specific $1.82 billion nationwide savings figure tied to the Moroccan phosphate fertilizer duty suspension; while Miller-Meeks's fertilizer-cost-relief bill is real and confirmed, this precise dollar estimate could not be verified against any documented source.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks pushes the Treasury Department to provide clear, Midwest-friendly rules for the Section 45Z Clean Fuel Production Credit to incentivize clean energy infrastructure and drive local financial investment
description: While Miller-Meeks is documented as pressuring the Treasury to finalize favorable 45Z clean fuel production tax credit rules for sustainable aviation fuels and ethanol processing, the framing describing this as generally incentivizing 'clean energy infrastructure' broadly (rather than specifically biofuels/SAF) is an imprecise characterization not fully matching the documented, narrower scope of her advocacy.

inaccurate_statement: She cosponsored the Agent Raul Gonzalez Officer Safety Act to make fleeing from law enforcement a federal crime.
description: Miller-Meeks's record includes support for legislation related to officer safety and penalizing fleeing from law enforcement at the border, and the dossier lists votes for the 'Agent Raul Gonzalez Officer Safety Act' among her public-safety-related record. However, no source in the available material describes this bill's substance as specifically making fleeing from law enforcement a federal crime; that description appears to be an added detail not substantiated by the record. Since the underlying fact that she supported this named officer-safety-related legislation is confirmed, this is a narrow, minor inaccuracy in describing the bill's specific content rather than a fabrication of her overall record.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks was Iowa Department of Public Health Director from 2010 to 2014
description: She served as Iowa Department of Public Health Director from 2010 to 2013, not 2010 to 2014, resigning to run for Congress.

inaccurate_statement: Served 24 years in the U.S. Army as a private, nurse, and physician.
description: Miller-Meeks served in the U.S. Army from 1974 to 1982 (Army Medical Department, retiring as a Lieutenant Colonel) and then in the Army Reserve from 1983 to 2000. While a combined 24-year figure roughly matches her total active and reserve service, describing her as having served solely 'as a private, nurse, and physician' omits and mischaracterizes her actual career path, which included retiring as a Lieutenant Colonel and holding significant rank, not remaining a private. This is a narrow mischaracterization of her military career progression rather than a wholesale fabrication.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan supports expanding Medicaid benefits to cover vision, dental, and hearing
description: Bohannan's documented Medicare expansion proposal (buy-in at any age, plus dental, hearing, and vision coverage) applies to Medicare, not Medicaid. Her platform focuses on reversing Medicaid cuts and extending ACA subsidies, not adding vision/dental/hearing benefits to Medicaid itself.

inaccurate_statement: Christina Bohannan's campaign positions her as stronger on healthcare expansion, reproductive rights, and government ethics compared to incumbent Mariannette Miller-Meeks
description: No neutral adjudication exists showing Bohannan is objectively 'better' or her campaign is 'stronger' on these issues compared to Miller-Meeks; this is a subjective framing presented as settled fact rather than clearly attributed opinion. The response does go on to describe factual contrasts, which softens this, but the opening framing overstates the certainty of a comparative ranking that is fundamentally a matter of political opinion.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks served 26 years in the U.S. Army.
description: Mariannette Miller-Meeks served in the U.S. Army Medical Department from 1974 to 1982 (active duty), then in the Army Reserve from 1983 to 2000. This totals roughly 26 years of combined active and reserve service, but she is more commonly and precisely described as an active-duty veteran from 1974-1982 who retired as a lieutenant colonel; describing this simply as '26 years' without distinguishing active vs. reserve service risks overstating her active-duty tenure, though the total service length figure is in the right range.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks presents herself as a small-town doctor standing up against big insurance companies to lower costs
description: Miller-Meeks's documented healthcare record shows she accepts substantial pharmaceutical and insurance-industry PAC money, voted against capping insulin costs and against extending ACA premium subsidies, and rented a D.C. apartment from pharmaceutical lobbyists using a taxpayer-funded housing allowance. Her actual healthcare messaging centers on pharmacy-benefit-manager transparency, price transparency, and market-based reforms rather than a self-branded 'standing up against big insurance companies' narrative, which is not supported by her record and is in tension with her documented donor patterns.

inaccurate_statement: Mariannette Miller-Meeks served as a U.S. Air Force nurse and physician
description: Mariannette Miller-Meeks served in the U.S. Army, not the Air Force. She served in the Army Medical Department from 1974 to 1982 and retired as a Lieutenant Colonel, followed by service in the Army Reserve from 1983 to 2000. She trained as a nurse and later became a physician, but her military branch was the Army.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is an Air Force veteran.
description: Mariannette Miller-Meeks served in the U.S. Army (Army Medical Department, 1974–1982, retiring as a Lieutenant Colonel) and then the Army Reserve (1983–2000), not the Air Force.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is a U.S. Air Force veteran.
description: Miller-Meeks served in the U.S. Army Medical Department from 1974 to 1982 and retired as a Lieutenant Colonel from the Army Reserve, not the Air Force. She is documented as a 24-year Army veteran, not an Air Force veteran.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's key focuses include restricting biological males from participating in women's sports categories.
description: There is no record of Miller-Meeks having taken this as one of her stated federal platform priorities. Her documented official issue pages cover Economy, Health, Border Security, Veterans, and Water, with no mention of a transgender-athletes-in-sports position as a key platform focus. This appears to be an unsupported addition to her platform rather than a documented position of hers.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's key focuses include protecting local Iowa farmland from foreign ownership.
description: No record exists of Miller-Meeks specifically prioritizing farmland foreign-ownership restrictions as a key platform focus; her documented platform centers on the economy, health, border security, veterans, and water issues, with no foreign farmland ownership plank identified.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks sharing the satirical article about unvaccinated veterans losing VA benefits caused a wave of panic that forced a local VA hospital to issue an emergency alert to de-escalate the confusion.
description: While Miller-Meeks did share a satirical article falsely claiming unvaccinated veterans would lose VA healthcare benefits, and this caused real confusion and distress among some veterans, no source substantiates the specific claim that a regional or local VA hospital issued an emergency alert correcting the disinformation. This appears to be a fabricated embellishment added to an otherwise accurate story.

inaccurate_statement: While she claimed a Davenport apartment to maintain residency inside the district, voter records from late 2025 revealed she changed her voter registration back to her Ottumwa residence
description: Her voter registration history is more complex than described: she registered at a state senator's LeClaire home in October 2022 (within IA-01), then at a Davenport apartment in 2024 where she voted that November, before voluntarily re-registering at her Ottumwa home in December 2025 — which is actually outside IA-01 (in IA-03), not inside it. The response's framing implies she was using the Davenport apartment specifically 'to maintain residency inside the district' as a settled fact, but omits the LeClaire step and glosses over the significance that her current registration is actually outside the district she represents, which is the real core of the controversy rather than merely a shift back to Ottumwa.

inaccurate_statement: The article about veterans' benefits prompted a local VA hospital to issue an emergency alert to clarify that benefits were not in jeopardy
description: While Miller-Meeks did share a satirical article claiming unvaccinated veterans would lose VA health benefits, causing real confusion and distress among some veterans, no source confirms that a VA hospital issued an emergency alert in response. This specific detail appears to be an unsupported embellishment of an otherwise accurately described controversy.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks vehemently opposed the House administration review process of her 6-vote 2020 election margin, demanding the certification be respected
description: The available record shows Miller-Meeks's legal team was engaged in defending her certified win during the House Administration Committee's review of Rita Hart's election contest, but the characterization of her as having 'vehemently opposed' the process and 'demanding certification be respected' as a specific quoted stance is not substantiated by the available record; the actual controversy centers on the timeline overlap between the pending review and the 2020 election-irregularities letter, not a documented vehement public campaign demanding certification.

inaccurate_statement: She changed her voter registration to Scott County (Davenport) specifically to maintain a residence within her district's boundaries after redistricting.
description: The documented timeline shows she first registered at a state senator's home in LeClaire in October 2022, then later registered at a Davenport apartment in 2024 where she voted that November — not a single direct move to Scott County framed purely as a district-boundary-compliance measure. The response simplifies and slightly misstates this multi-step registration history, though the general point that she moved her registration to stay within IA-01 is broadly accurate.

inaccurate_statement: A regional VA hospital issued an emergency alert correcting the disinformation about veterans losing VA benefits.
description: While Miller-Meeks did share the satirical article causing real distress among veterans, no source substantiates the specific claim that a regional VA hospital issued a formal emergency alert to correct the story. This appears to be an embellishment added to an otherwise accurate account of the underlying controversy.

inaccurate_statement: In late 2021, the House Sergeant at Arms fined Miller-Meeks for violating House Rule II regarding proxy voting or floor attendance protocols, and she chose not to appeal.
description: The actual fine was for violating the House mask mandate (not proxy voting or floor attendance rules), issued in May 2021 for $500. She did appeal that $500 fine (unsuccessfully); it was a separate, later $2,500 mask-related fine in January 2022 that she did not appeal. The response conflates the nature of the violation (mask rules, not proxy voting/attendance) and the appeal history.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks helped lead a bipartisan push to cap insulin costs at $35 a month
description: Miller-Meeks's documented record shows she voted against capping insulin costs and against allowing Medicare to negotiate drug prices, and reporting has raised questions about pharmaceutical industry contributions coinciding with such votes. There is no record of her leading a bipartisan push to cap insulin at $35/month; her own signature healthcare bill (the Lower Health Care Premiums for All Americans Act) is a market-based/PBM-transparency approach, not an insulin price cap. This claim appears to invert her actual voting record on this specific issue.

inaccurate_statement: Her support for budget reductions to Medicaid could reduce federal spending by over $900 billion over a decade, potentially leaving millions of Americans without insurance
description: The dossier documents Medicaid cuts in the 2025 reconciliation bill (OBBBA) at roughly $12 billion cited by Democratic critics and a KFF estimate of about 110,000 more uninsured Iowans by 2034 from combined ACA-subsidy expiration and Medicaid cuts, not a $900 billion national figure specifically tied to Miller-Meeks's votes. While national estimates of Medicaid cuts in the broader reconciliation package have circulated in the hundreds of billions in various analyses, this specific $900 billion figure attributed generically to 'critics and nonpartisan groups' in connection with her vote is not verifiable against the documented record and risks significantly overstating or misattributing the scale of the impact.

inaccurate_statement: Opponents argue that allowing ACA financial help to expire forces everyday families to face doubled insurance costs or drop coverage entirely
description: This is a reasonable summary of Democratic criticism and is broadly consistent with KFF-style estimates that premiums could rise substantially or double for some enrollees if enhanced subsidies expire, so it is not clearly wrong, but the specific framing that ALL 'everyday families' face doubled costs overstates what is a variable, income-dependent effect documented in the record.

inaccurate_statement: She served as president of the Iowa Academy of Ophthalmology
description: Miller-Meeks was the first female president of the Iowa Medical Society and the first woman in 20 years on the University of Iowa ophthalmology faculty. There is no record of her serving as president of the 'Iowa Academy of Ophthalmology' specifically — this appears to conflate her real leadership role in the broader Iowa Medical Society with a different, more specific ophthalmology organization.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks enlisted in the U.S. Army at age 18
description: Miller-Meeks's documented military record shows Army service from 1974 to 1982 (active duty, Army Medical Department) followed by Army Reserve service from 1983 to 2000, with her BSN from Texas Christian University earned in 1976 — indicating she entered military service as a nursing student/officer rather than enlisting at age 18. No source in her biography confirms an age-18 enlistment date, and this detail appears to be an unsupported addition to her otherwise well-documented military background.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in January 2021
description: Miller-Meeks was elected to the U.S. House in November 2020 (winning Iowa's 2nd District by 6 votes over Rita Hart) and was sworn in/took office in January 2021; she was not elected in January 2021. This conflates her election date with her swearing-in/start-of-term date. Additionally, she has represented Iowa's 1st Congressional District (not the district she was originally elected to) since January 2023 following redistricting.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks taught on the faculty at the University of Michigan and the University of Iowa
description: Her documented academic record shows she was the first woman in 20 years on the University of Iowa ophthalmology faculty. No source establishes any faculty appointment at the University of Michigan; this appears to be an unsupported or fabricated addition to her academic background.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's priority is 'eliminating taxes on Social Security'
description: Miller-Meeks has herself publicly corrected messaging suggesting the 2025 tax legislation eliminates taxes on Social Security. In a January 2026 tele-town hall she acknowledged that framing was inaccurate — the law only creates a temporary deduction for filers 65 and older, not an outright exemption from Social Security taxation. Presenting 'no tax on Social Security' as a straightforward stated priority without that caveat repeats an overstatement she has already disavowed.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks highlighted fundraising statistics, pointing out differences in the proportion of campaign contributions coming from in-state versus out-of-state donors, as a criticism of Bohannan
description: No record exists of Miller-Meeks making this specific attack on Bohannan's in-state versus out-of-state donor proportions. In fact, available information indicates Bohannan has traditionally drawn a slightly higher share of her individual contributions from within Iowa compared to Miller-Meeks, meaning this line of attack, if it existed, would likely run in the opposite direction of what would help Miller-Meeks's case. This appears to be an unsubstantiated addition rather than a documented criticism.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks noted that she has previously defeated Bohannan twice because her own platform aligns closer with local priorities
description: While it is true that Miller-Meeks defeated Bohannan in both 2022 and 2024, no record exists of Miller-Meeks framing this history as a criticism of Bohannan by attributing her wins to her platform aligning closer with local priorities. This specific framing and quote is not found in any documented statement from Miller-Meeks.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks contends that her main contrast with Bohannan centers on differing views regarding constitutional liberties and economic approaches
