inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is a 24-year Army veteran
description: This is duplicated in the accurate list because it is directly confirmed by the dossier ('U.S. Army 1974–1982... then Army Reserve 1983–2000'), which totals roughly 26 years of combined active/reserve service, close to but not exactly matching '24-year.' This is a minor rounding discrepancy, not a substantive error.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks secured NDAA provisions concerning artillery production
description: The record confirms Miller-Meeks secured amendments in the FY2027 NDAA related to Iowa's defense infrastructure, military readiness, and the Rock Island Arsenal, but no source specifically documents an 'artillery production' provision as distinct from the general Rock Island Arsenal/defense workforce funding already confirmed. This appears to be an embellished detail not independently verifiable.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is a member of the Ukraine Caucus
description: The record documents Miller-Meeks as chair of the Conservative Climate Caucus, co-chair of the Pandemic Preparedness Caucus, and a member of the Republican Governance Group, Climate Solutions Caucus, Pro-Life Caucus, and Taiwan Caucus. No 'Ukraine Caucus' membership is documented for her.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks explicitly supported Taiwan's security and reducing U.S. dependence on China
description: While Miller-Meeks's Taiwan Caucus membership and general hawkish-on-China orientation are documented, no specific direct statement about 'reducing U.S. dependence on China' as a distinct national-security position (as opposed to her documented manufacturing/supply-chain statements) is confirmed in the record; this presents an inferred position with some hedging as more concrete than documented.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has argued for alliances and international engagement, including support for partners such as Ukraine, but less of her public campaign platform is centered on military readiness/defense policy, implying this reflects her own stated position rather than inference from party alignment
description: Bohannan has made some documented statements supporting Ukraine and international alliances, but a comprehensive, itemized position on broader national-security topics like military readiness, China/Taiwan, or NATO alliances is not established as a defined platform plank in her available record; presenting her general foreign-policy leanings as a settled comparative position risks overstating what is actually a thin public record on this topic, distinct from a fabrication but bordering on an unhedged inference.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supported the 2027 NDAA, including measures involving Iowa's defense infrastructure
description: Miller-Meeks's documented support and secured amendments relate to the FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act (voted on/passed in 2026 for fiscal year 2027), and coverage refers to it as the FY2027 NDAA rather than "the 2027 NDAA" in a way that could be misread as a bill enacted in the year 2027. This is a minor terminology imprecision rather than a substantive misrepresentation of her record, since she did support the relevant defense authorization legislation and secured Iowa-specific defense provisions.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supports tariffs as part of a broader protectionist/manufacturing strategy.
description: Miller-Meeks's actual voting record on tariffs is more adversarial to blanket tariff support than this framing suggests: she voted three times to block House consideration of ending Trump's tariff emergency declarations and voted against ending the Canada tariff emergency specifically, but she has also blamed the 2024-2025 Quad Cities manufacturing layoffs (e.g., John Deere) on "a lack of robust trade policy" and high interest rates rather than embracing tariffs as her chosen strategy, and her own fertilizer-tariff-cutting bill (the "Lowering Input Costs for American Farmers Act") cuts against a simple 'pro-tariff protectionist' characterization. This is a mischaracterization of a genuinely more mixed and internally tense record, not a wholesale fabrication, so it is minor rather than critical.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks argues that the 2025 tax legislation is benefiting Iowa manufacturing workers and has received support from manufacturing-oriented business groups.
description: While Miller-Meeks did support the 2025 tax legislation (OBBBA) and has touted small-business tax provisions, and did receive an August 2026 U.S. Chamber of Commerce endorsement citing her work for Iowa businesses, the specific framing that manufacturing-oriented business groups have endorsed her because of the tax law's benefit to manufacturing workers is an inference beyond what is documented; her office's specific district figures on the tax law's business benefits are about small/pass-through businesses generally rather than manufacturing workers specifically, and the U.S. Chamber endorsement cites broader pro-growth tax policy and small-business engagement, not manufacturing-specific praise.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan opposed Iowa legislation providing qualified immunity to police
description: Bohannan's opposition to the 2021 'Back the Blue' law (SF 342) was not centered on opposing a grant of qualified immunity to police as the response implies. Her documented rationale focused on concerns that the bill would undermine public trust, pit police against protesters, and potentially make communities less safe or infringe civil liberties -- not a specific objection framed around qualified immunity itself. Characterizing her vote as being about 'opposing qualified immunity for police' mischaracterizes the actual substance and stated rationale of her position on this bill.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks voted four times for federal legislation that included a 10-year restriction on state/local AI regulation, which critics argue could have limited Iowa and local governments' ability to impose additional data-center requirements.
description: The dossier for Miller-Meeks documents no such specific voting record of 'four times' voting for a 10-year federal moratorium on state/local AI regulation. It does note she voted against amendments that would have preserved a state/local AI data-center moratorium in committee proceedings (per an advocacy group's account) and that she has faced criticism for votes seen as blocking local data-center restrictions, but the specific claim of a '10-year restriction' voted on 'four times' is not substantiated by the available record and appears to be an invented level of specificity not found in the source material.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan favors investing heavily in advanced law enforcement tools, such as high-energy scanners, to detect fentanyl hidden inside commercial trucks and passenger vehicles at ports of entry, and has said fentanyl is trafficked mostly through legal ports of entry
description: While Bohannan has generally supported more Border Patrol agents and fentanyl-interdiction equipment and greater processing capacity at ports of entry, the specific framing in the response attributing to her a detailed claim about 'high-energy scanners' for detecting fentanyl in commercial trucks goes beyond what is confirmed as her own direct statement; this level of specificity was not verified against a primary source in the underlying research.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has specifically called for expanding border inspection equipment to detect fentanyl and increasing Border Patrol resources
description: Miller-Meeks's documented positions on fentanyl and border security center on cosponsoring and voting for the HALT Fentanyl Act, supporting the Laken Riley Act, the Secure the Border Act, finishing border wall construction, and general enforcement messaging. There is no confirmed record of her specifically calling for 'expanding border inspection equipment to detect fentanyl' as a distinct, named proposal; this appears to be an unverified or invented specific detail layered onto her broader, real enforcement-focused record.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has supported requiring employers to use E-Verify
description: No evidence supports this claim. Miller-Meeks's own official House 'Border Security' issues page details her immigration votes and positions (SAVE Act, Laken Riley Act, Secure the Border Act, HALT Fentanyl Act, Mayorkas impeachment, etc.) but makes no mention of E-Verify. Searches for Miller-Meeks combined with E-Verify turn up no press releases, votes, or statements linking her to mandatory E-Verify advocacy, and she is not a cosponsor of the primary federal E-Verify mandate bill. This is a narrow addition that doesn't change the overall accurate picture that she is an immigration-enforcement hawk.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan proposes adding home-health benefits to Medicare
description: Bohannan's documented Medicare expansion proposal is to add dental, hearing, and vision coverage to Medicare, not home-health benefits. No source ties her platform to a home-health Medicare expansion; this appears to be an inaccurate addition to an otherwise correctly described set of proposals.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is a former nurse
description: Mariannette Miller-Meeks holds a nursing degree (BSN from Texas Christian University) but her documented professional and political career is as a physician (ophthalmologist) — she ran a private ophthalmology practice in Ottumwa, Iowa, and is described in her biography as a physician, not as someone who practiced as a nurse. Describing her as a 'former nurse' in addition to physician is not supported by her documented career history.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has proposed expanding Medicare coverage to include home-health benefits
description: Bohannan's documented Medicare expansion proposal adds dental, hearing, and vision coverage alongside a Medicare buy-in at any age. No source ties her to a home-health-benefits expansion specifically; this appears to substitute an incorrect benefit category for her actual, well-documented position.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan proposes adding home-health benefits to Medicare (bundled with dental, vision, hearing)
description: Bohannan's well-documented Medicare expansion proposal is to add dental, hearing, and vision coverage alongside a Medicare buy-in at any age. No source ties her to a specific proposal to add home-health benefits to Medicare; this appears to be an inaccurate addition to an otherwise correctly described platform item.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's broader platform calls for substantial public investment in infrastructure, particularly school infrastructure, and emphasizes jobs, manufacturing and organized labor, implying this is her stated roads/highways position.
description: Bohannan's campaign platform contains no direct statement on roads, bridges, or highway infrastructure as a standalone 2026 policy position — this is a confirmed, documented gap after repeated dedicated searches of her full campaign site. Her platform does emphasize public school investment, but framing 'school infrastructure' investment as effectively her roads/highways stance conflates two unrelated policy areas and presents an inference as if it were her substantiated position.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks secured $1 million for the U.S. Highway 6/Deer Creek Road intersection
description: Reporting on this Community Project Funding request indicates $1 million was secured toward a larger $4.9 million request for this intersection project; this figure itself is consistent with the dossier, so no correction needed beyond noting the request context is omitted, which is a peripheral detail.

inaccurate_statement: Her campaign says her opposition to Iowa's 2021 'Back the Blue' law was because she believed it could jeopardize local police funding and safety
description: Bohannan's actual stated objections to the 2021 Back the Blue bill centered on protecting the right to protest, concerns about pitting law enforcement against racial-justice demonstrators, and fears the bill could undermine public trust and civil liberties -- not a stated concern about jeopardizing local police funding specifically. This mischaracterizes the substance of her rationale, though it does not reverse the basic fact that she voted against the bill.

inaccurate_statement: She also voted against the 2021 legislation providing qualified immunity for police
description: Bohannan's documented 2021 vote was against Iowa's 'Back the Blue' bill (SF 342), which included qualified-immunity-related provisions among a broader package addressing law enforcement, protest penalties, and other issues -- it was not itself a standalone 'qualified immunity' bill, and describing it as separate legislation "providing qualified immunity" she voted against, distinct from the previously mentioned Back the Blue vote, creates a misleading impression of two separate votes when there was one.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks secured federal funding for local public-safety projects, including a $499,873 DOJ Byrne grant for the Oskaloosa Safe City Project
description: The funding Miller-Meeks secured for Oskaloosa's SAFECity Initiative is documented across multiple sources as $500,000, described as a Community Project Funding appropriation she secured, not as a $499,873 DOJ Byrne grant. No source ties this project to a specific $499,873 figure or characterizes it as a Byrne Justice Assistance Grant; the well-documented figure and mechanism differ from what is claimed here.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks' official 'Economy' platform page contains an explicit unemployment-reduction plan comparable in specificity to Bohannan's workforce-development plan
description: Miller-Meeks's official economy platform emphasizes energy production, manufacturing tax policy, and small-business tax cuts, but contains no explicit statement addressing the unemployment rate as such—this is a documented gap, not a fully developed unemployment plan. The response's framing implying she has a clear, quantified unemployment strategy overstates what exists, though it does correctly note her general pro-business, tax-cut theory of job creation.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks previously opposed legislation requiring expanded monitoring for PFAS
description: No record exists of Miller-Meeks taking a specific position on PFAS monitoring legislation. Her documented record shows no direct 2026 statement on Iowa's nitrate/water crisis specifically, and her water-related positions found are about wetlands/waterway regulation (WOTUS) and general infrastructure funding, not a specific vote or statement opposing PFAS monitoring requirements. This appears to be an unsupported claim rather than a verified part of her record.

inaccurate_statement: A district analysis specifically identifies tariffs and rising prices as challenges for IA-01 manufacturers employing more than 65,000 workers
description: No source in the available research corroborates a specific figure of '65,000 workers' employed by IA-01 manufacturers, nor an analysis framing tariffs and rising prices as a challenge tied to that specific employment figure. While manufacturing job losses (e.g., Whirlpool layoffs) are a well-documented and real issue in the race, this specific statistic could not be verified and appears to be an unsupported or fabricated figure.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's economic approach is more focused on limiting federal spending and regulation, and she voted against funding new infrastructure projects
description: Miller-Meeks's opposition to the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law was specifically about its cost and bundling with non-transportation spending, not a blanket opposition to infrastructure funding. In fact, she has a substantial documented record of securing and touting infrastructure/community project funding for IA-01 (over $87.1 million since taking office, including specific road, bridge, and wastewater projects). Describing her as having simply 'voted against funding new infrastructure projects' omits this significant countervailing record and mischaracterizes a nuanced position as a blanket anti-infrastructure stance.

inaccurate_statement: A district analysis specifically identifies tariffs and rising prices as challenges for IA-01 manufacturers employing more than 65,000 workers
description: No source in the available research corroborates a specific figure of '65,000 workers' employed by IA-01 manufacturers, nor an analysis framing tariffs and rising prices as a challenge tied to that specific employment figure. inaccurate_statement: the available candidate comparisons emphasize her healthcare and economic-policy record rather than a specific new "local jobs" plan
description: Mariannette Miller-Meeks has a documented, confirmed record of statements specifically addressing local manufacturing jobs, including direct comments on the John Deere/Quad Cities layoffs attributing them to trade and economic policy factors, praise for Vermeer's Iowa expansion, a completed 'Made in America Manufacturing Tour,' the Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act, and securing funding for the Lee County Career Center workforce-training facility. Portraying her as lacking a jobs-specific platform and only having a general healthcare/economic record omits this documented, direct record on local jobs and manufacturing.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's platform emphasizes domestic manufacturing, reducing regulations, expanding domestic energy, and policies she says will keep manufacturing jobs in the U.S., with the clearest domestic-manufacturing/job-retention agenda in the race
description: Miller-Meeks does have documented positions on domestic manufacturing (the Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act, ONSHORE Act, energy production emphasis) and has commented on Quad Cities layoffs, but her official economy platform has no explicit statement on the unemployment rate as such, and there is a documented internal tension where she blames trade/tariff policy for job losses while repeatedly voting to preserve the very tariff emergency declarations criticized for raising costs on manufacturers. Presenting her as having unambiguously 'the clearest' and 'most direct' job-retention platform, without any of this nuance, overstates the strength and clarity of her record relative to what is actually documented.

inaccurate_statement: One 2026 IA-01 voter analysis found 42% of NPP (no-party-preference) voters citing immigration as a priority
description: The only identifiable 2026 IA-01-specific survey with issue-priority crosstabs by party affiliation (the Independent Center Voice/Independent Leadership Council poll conducted by the Bullfinch Group in July 2026) shows that independent voters ranked immigration as their most pressing issue at only about 10-15%, not 42%, and the survey does not use 'NPP' terminology. No source corroborates a 42% figure for immigration as a priority among non-party-affiliated IA-01 voters; this specific statistic appears to be fabricated or a data error repeated across multiple research passes on this race.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks led legislation providing Medicare coverage for multi-cancer early-detection (MCED) tests
description: The Nancy Gardner Sewell Medicare Multi-Cancer Early Detection Screening Coverage Act was introduced by Rep. Jodey Arrington (R-TX), with Miller-Meeks as one of several original cosponsors, not the lead sponsor. However, her own congressional press releases and some local news outlets do describe her as having 'led' or championed the bill, so this is a contested framing rather than a clear fabrication, and the bill's substance and her substantive role are accurately described elsewhere in the response.

inaccurate_statement: Mariannette Miller-Meeks has sponsored legislation placing limits on chokeholds
description: As an Iowa state senator, Miller-Meeks supported bipartisan state legislation that banned chokeholds and increased implicit-bias training. However, there is no record of her sponsoring federal legislation on chokeholds during her time in Congress, and no confirmed source ties a specific chokehold-limiting bill to her congressional record. This overstates a real but narrower state-level record as a broader legislative sponsorship claim.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supports E-Verify as part of her border/immigration platform
description: No evidence supports that Miller-Meeks has backed mandatory E-Verify as part of her border/immigration platform. Her official House Border Security issues page details her votes and cosponsorships (SAVE Act, Laken Riley Act, Secure the Border Act, HALT Fentanyl Act, Mayorkas impeachment) but makes no mention of E-Verify, and no press releases or statements tie her to this specific policy.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supports using E-Verify
description: No evidence in Miller-Meeks's documented record supports mandatory E-Verify as part of her platform. Her official House border-security page and legislative record cover the wall, catch-and-release, asylum limits, and ICE/DHS funding, but no source ties her to E-Verify advocacy specifically; this appears to be an added detail not attributable to her actual platform.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's platform is characterized as having no itemized small-business plan comparable to Miller-Meeks, implicitly framing her jobs agenda as broader but less targeted, without noting she also has confirmed direct statements on manufacturing jobs (John Deere/Quad Cities) and vocational training
description: Bohannan has a confirmed, direct statement specifically addressing manufacturing job losses in the Quad Cities (John Deere layoffs) and pledges to expand vocational/technical training to grow high-skill, high-wage jobs — a more targeted jobs-related position than the response's framing (which characterizes her approach as general wage/cost improvement rather than direct job creation) fully credits.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's official economy platform has no explicit itemized unemployment-rate-focused statement, but the response presents her platform as 'more explicitly centered on' job creation/lowering unemployment without noting this gap
description: Miller-Meeks's official House 'Economy' issues page emphasizes energy production, manufacturing tax policy, and small-business tax cuts, but contains no explicit statement addressing the unemployment rate as such — a documented gap. Presenting her plan as clearly and directly aimed at lowering unemployment overstates the specificity of her actual platform, though the broader thrust (pro-growth, tax/regulatory-focused economic policy) is accurately characterized.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's approach is centered on tax incentives and other pro-business policies intended to encourage companies to expand and hire, plus expanding domestic manufacturing and keeping production in the U.S., framed as her general economy/jobs plan
description: Miller-Meeks's official economy platform emphasizes energy production, the Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act, small-business tax cuts, and housing affordability, but her official page contains no explicit statement addressing the unemployment rate as such -- this is a documented gap. The response presents a specific unemployment-reduction mechanism as her stated plan without noting this gap or hedging that it is inferred from her general tax/business/manufacturing positions.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's jobs approach includes infrastructure and development spending, which she argues supports construction, transportation, agriculture and local businesses, as part of a plan to reduce unemployment
description: There is no confirmed direct statement from Miller-Meeks framing infrastructure/development spending explicitly as an unemployment-reduction mechanism; her documented infrastructure record is presented as a delivery track record (specific funded local projects) rather than a forward-looking jobs/unemployment plan, and this framing overstates the connection without hedging.

inaccurate_statement: The American Cancer Society's Iowa advocacy arm says that raising the tobacco tax is the single most impactful public-health policy it sees for reducing cancer and deaths
description: This specific 'single most impactful public health intervention' framing was said by Dr. Mary Charlton, a University of Iowa epidemiology professor and director of the Iowa Cancer Registry, during a March 2026 legislative committee meeting — not by the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network (ACS CAN), the ACS's Iowa advocacy arm. ACS CAN does advocate for tobacco tax increases as an effective tobacco-control measure, but the specific superlative claim attributed here belongs to a different person/organization.

inaccurate_statement: The American Cancer Society's Iowa advocacy arm says that raising the tobacco tax is the single most impactful public-health policy it sees for reducing cancer and deaths

inaccurate_statement: A 2026 voter guide characterizes Bohannan as favoring tighter environmental regulation, while Miller-Meeks has supported loosening some environmental protections
description: While it is true Miller-Meeks has opposed WOTUS/Clean Water Act expansion and Bohannan has an explicit PFAS/nitrate reduction plank, describing Bohannan as favoring mandatory 'tighter environmental regulation' overstates her documented position — she has explicitly said she prefers working with farmers through incentives and funded conservation practices rather than imposing mandates, criticizing a tendency to 'regulate first and ask questions later.' This nuance is missing from the binary regulation-versus-deregulation framing presented.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks says her total Community Project Funding in the district includes substantial investments in modernizing water systems
description: Miller-Meeks's documented water-related project funding is narrower than 'substantial investments in modernizing water systems' suggests — it consists of specific, itemized items such as $3 million for the Davenport Water Pollution Control Plant and $2 million for a Muscatine wastewater force main, which are flood-mitigation/wastewater infrastructure projects, not a broad or substantial modernization program. There is no dedicated 2026 statement from her addressing the nitrate/agricultural-runoff crisis specifically, which the response otherwise correctly notes is a gap.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has supported E-Verify as part of her immigration platform
description: There is no evidence Miller-Meeks has backed mandatory E-Verify. Her own official House Border Security issues page, which extensively details her immigration votes and cosponsorships, makes no mention of E-Verify, and she is not a cosponsor of the primary federal E-Verify mandate bill. This appears to be an unsupported addition to an otherwise accurate description of her enforcement-focused record.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's approach 'has generally put more emphasis on constitutional limits, accountability, and avoiding policies that unnecessarily pit protesters against police,' implying her record is 'therefore less aligned with a traditional "more policing + tougher enforcement" definition of public safety'
description: This framing selectively emphasizes Bohannan's 2021 opposition to the 'Back the Blue' bill while omitting that she also supports funding local law enforcement with adequate training and resources, introduced legislation supporting officers injured on the job, and voted for tougher penalties for drug dealers and human traffickers. Presenting her record as generally less supportive of traditional policing understates these documented pro-police-funding elements of her record.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks secured more than $3 million specifically for the Oskaloosa SAFECity Initiative
description: The Oskaloosa SAFECity Initiative funding Miller-Meeks secured is documented at $500,000, not more than $3 million. The $500,000 figure covers license-plate readers, body and in-car cameras, police-facility upgrades, school panic buttons, real-time crime monitoring, and a search-and-rescue drone. No source ties a $3 million figure to this specific Oskaloosa project; this appears to be an inflated or conflated dollar amount.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks voted for measures to build 900 miles of border wall
description: Miller-Meeks's documented border-security record includes support for finishing border wall construction and voting for the Secure the Border Act, but no source ties her to a specific '900 miles' figure for wall construction she voted to build. This specific numeric detail does not appear in her documented record.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks voted for measures requiring E-Verify for new hires
description: Research into Miller-Meeks's border/immigration record found no evidence she has backed or voted for mandatory E-Verify legislation. Her documented record centers on the Laken Riley Act, Secure the Border Act, SAVE Act, HALT Fentanyl Act, and wall-completion legislation, none of which involve E-Verify mandates.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has backed mandatory E-Verify for employers hiring new workers
description: No evidence supports this claim. Miller-Meeks's own official House 'Border Security' issues page provides an extensive, detailed list of her immigration/border votes and cosponsorships but makes no mention of E-Verify at all, and she is not a cosponsor of the primary federal bill mandating nationwide E-Verify. This is a narrow addition to an otherwise accurate general characterization of her as an immigration hawk.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has made the Farm Bill and family-farm succession a prominent part of her current agriculture agenda.
description: Miller-Meeks's documented agriculture record centers on fertilizer-tariff relief, E15/ethanol advocacy, and voting for the 2026 farm bill (Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026), with tax-policy provisions (estate tax/stepped-up basis protections) supporting family-farm succession as a genuine but secondary element via broader tax legislation. Casting 'family-farm succession' as a 'prominent' standalone piece of her current agriculture agenda overstates its centrality relative to her better-documented fertilizer-cost and trade-focused efforts.

inaccurate_statement: Farm Action Fund endorsed Bohannan in July and specifically cited her position on monopoly power in seed, fertilizer and meatpacking
description: A farm-advocacy group's Rural Independence Initiative (part of Farm Action Fund) is documented as endorsing Bohannan, but no source confirms the endorsement announcement specifically cited her position on monopoly power in seed, fertilizer, and meatpacking as the stated rationale; this specific framing of the endorsement's justification is unverified and not established in the available record.

inaccurate_statement: Iowa could potentially receive about $1 billion over five years from the Rural Health Transformation Program
description: The dossier documents an initial $209 million Iowa allocation from the $50 billion federal Rural Health Transformation Program, but does not confirm a specific five-year total of approximately $1 billion for Iowa. This projected total figure is not substantiated in the available material and appears to be an unverified extrapolation.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has a prior Iowa legislative record that she describes as supporting small businesses
description: Research found no itemized small-business plan or specific legislative record on small-business support attributable to Bohannan; her campaign site references being a general champion for small businesses within broader affordability/farm-economy planks, but no specific itemized small-business policy or legislative record framing exists. This is a genuine, confirmed gap rather than a documented record she 'describes' as supporting small businesses.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's background makes her more aligned with calls for stronger oversight of large data centers, including concerns about water use, electricity demand, tax incentives, and local control, implying this is effectively her stance on data center development
description: Bohannan has no documented public statement, vote, or campaign position on data center development despite dedicated research into her campaign site, social media, and news coverage of the live Clinton, Iowa data-center controversy within her district. Presenting an inference from her environmental engineering background as effectively her actual stance on this issue is speculative rather than a verified position.

inaccurate_statement: Her primary challenger, David Pautsch, accused her of being dishonest about her residence, and Iowa law permits people with multiple residences some flexibility regarding voter registration
description: The documented residency controversy centered on a Bettendorf resident who filed a residency challenge with the Scott County board and an Office of Congressional Ethics complaint in fall 2024, not primarily on accusations from primary challenger David Pautsch. The response attributes the core allegation to the wrong source, though Pautsch has separately criticized her in other contexts. The core underlying facts about the residency inconsistency (Ottumwa homestead credit while registering elsewhere, later re-registering outside IA-01) are real, but this specific attribution of who raised the residency dishonesty allegation is not supported.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks drew criticism from some Republicans, including primary challenger David Pautsch, for certifying the 2020 election results and supporting an independent commission to investigate the January 6 attack.
description: No record exists of Miller-Meeks facing criticism from David Pautsch or other Republicans specifically over certifying the 2020 election results or supporting a January 6 independent commission. Her documented controversies include a residency/voter-registration inconsistency, a town-hall accessibility controversy, self-corrected "no tax on Social Security" messaging, and a 2021 financial-disclosure ethics complaint from the Iowa Democratic Party. Her 2026 primary opponent Pautsch's documented dispute with her involved an FEC complaint over a misleading mass text message, not election-certification or January 6 commission criticism. This appears to be a fabricated detail not supported by available research.

inaccurate_statement: I found less recent evidence of a comparable schedule of open, traditional town-hall-style events [for Miller-Meeks]
description: Miller-Meeks's accessibility record is more specifically documented than the response suggests: she avoided in-person town halls for most of 2025 (reportedly saying she'd hold one 'when hell freezes over'), then held one contentious in-person town hall in Keosauqua on November 10, 2025, while also conducting substantial tele-town halls reaching thousands of participants at a time. The response's vague framing of 'less recent evidence' undersells the extent to which her avoidance of open town halls is a well-documented, specific controversy rather than simply an information gap.

inaccurate_statement: There is less evidence of the kind of accessible, open town-hall-style engagement from Miller-Meeks, implying she holds no town halls or comparable accessibility events
description: Miller-Meeks has held tele-town halls reaching thousands of participants (one reported at 10,700, others at 6,300, 8,000, and 13,000) and completed a 20-county in-person tour, plus one contentious in-person town hall in Keosauqua in November 2025. She avoided in-person town halls for most of 2025 and used a moderator-filtered format that critics said screened out hard questions, which is a legitimate basis for criticism, but the response's framing implies she has essentially no accessibility events at all, which understates her substantial tele-town-hall record and omits the one in-person town hall she did hold.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has 'strongest documented history of formal constituent access (town halls...)' and 'has held public...constituent events' emphasizing accessibility, implying a robust, uncontroversial town hall record
description: This claim inverts the well-documented record. Miller-Meeks avoided in-person town halls for most of 2025, telling a local GOP meeting she'd hold one 'when hell freezes over.' Her first in-person town hall of that period, held in November 2025 in Keosauqua, was widely reported as contentious, with booing, heckling, and an attendee removed, and used a written-question/moderator-filtered format critics said screened out hard questions. She relies primarily on tele-town halls rather than open in-person forums. Presenting her as having the clearly 'strongest' and most accessible town hall record, without any of this context, is a significant mischaracterization that would mislead a reader about her actual accessibility record.

inaccurate_statement: Christina Bohannan takes corporate PAC money, just less than Miller-Meeks, citing her ~$491,928 in PAC/other committee receipts as evidence
description: Bohannan's total PAC/other-committee receipts of about $491,928 is accurate as a raw dollar figure, but presenting this as evidence she takes 'corporate PAC money' is misleading. A detailed review of her itemized FEC Schedule A contributions shows every identified PAC/committee contributor traces to Democratic joint-fundraising or ideological vehicles (such as House Victory Project 2026 and 314 Action Impact Slate), not corporate or trade-association PACs. Her stated pledge to take no corporate PAC money holds up against her primary-source filings, so characterizing her PAC receipts as partial evidence of accepting corporate PAC money mischaracterizes the nature of that funding.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks' campaign reported $83,700 from corporate PACs in the second half of 2025
description: No source supports this specific $83,700 figure for corporate PAC money to Miller-Meeks during any 2025 reporting period. Documented figures for that period differ substantially (e.g., $107,500 in corporate PAC money in Q1 2025 alone, per Iowa Starting Line). The broader point that she accepts corporate PAC money is accurate, but this specific number appears to be fabricated or erroneous.

inaccurate_statement: David Pautsch (Republican challenger) and Travis Terrell (Democrat) are presented as current candidates in the IA-01 race with active endorsement lists.
description: Both David Pautsch and Travis Terrell were defeated in their respective party primaries in June 2026 (Pautsch lost to Miller-Meeks by more than 40 points; Terrell lost to Bohannan by roughly 81-82%) and are not on the November 2026 general election ballot. The actual 2026 IA-01 general election field consists of Miller-Meeks (R), Bohannan (D), and independent Michael Bridgford. Presenting Pautsch and Terrell as current candidates with ongoing endorsement activity misrepresents who is actually running in the general election.

inaccurate_statement: Scott Bessent is listed among Mariannette Miller-Meeks's post-primary endorsers.
description: Scott Bessent, as Treasury Secretary, made a real campaign appearance touring a Vermeer facility in support of Miller-Meeks, but no source frames this as a formal 'endorsement' the way Trump's explicit endorsement was described, and no endorsement list or tracker names him as a listed endorser. Characterizing a campaign-trail appearance as a formal endorsement overstates what actually occurred.

inaccurate_statement: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is listed among Mariannette Miller-Meeks's post-primary endorsers.
description: RFK Jr., as HHS Secretary, made a real campaign appearance (a youth fitness event in Newton) in support of Miller-Meeks, but this was a campaign-trail appearance by an administration official, not a formally listed endorsement, and no endorsement tracker includes him as such.

inaccurate_statement: David Pautsch (Republican challenger) and Travis Terrell (Democrat) are presented as current candidates in the IA-01 race with active endorsement lists.
description: Both David Pautsch and Travis Terrell were defeated in their respective party primaries in June 2026 (Pautsch lost to Miller-Meeks by more than 40 points; Terrell lost to Bohannan by roughly 81-82%) and are not on the November 2026 general election ballot. The actual 2026 IA-01 general election field consists of Miller-Meeks (R), Bohannan (D), and independent Michael Bridgford. Presenting Pautsch and Terrell as current candidates with ongoing endorsement activity misrepresents who is actually running in the general election.

inaccurate_statement: Ironworkers Local 67 endorsed Bohannan (omitted, not an inaccuracy—no issue here)
description: placeholder

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan proposes expanding Medicaid benefits as part of her health-care platform
description: Bohannan's documented healthcare platform centers on Medicare buy-in at any age, expanding Medicare to vision/dental/hearing, capping insulin, and reversing Medicaid cuts (i.e., restoring cuts, not expanding Medicaid as a new benefit category). No source shows her proposing an affirmative expansion of Medicaid benefits distinct from reversing cuts; this appears to be an imprecise characterization of her actual position on reversing Medicaid cuts.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has supported a nationwide abortion ban
description: Miller-Meeks is pro-life with exceptions for rape, incest, and life of the mother, and is a co-sponsor of the federal Life at Conception Act, which functions as a near-total abortion ban without broad exceptions. However, characterizing her as having 'supported a nationwide abortion ban' without noting her stated rape/incest/life-of-mother exceptions oversimplifies her actual position, which includes carve-outs the flat 'nationwide abortion ban' framing omits.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan narrowly lost to Miller-Meeks in 2022
description: The 2022 Miller-Meeks vs. Bohannan race was not a narrow loss. Miller-Meeks won by a comfortable margin of about 53%-47%, roughly 20,000 votes or about 7 points. Only the 2024 race was genuinely close, decided by 799 votes (about 0.2%) after a recount. Describing 2022 as also 'narrow' conflates the two races and misrepresents the actual electoral history.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks entered Congress in 2021
description: Mariannette Miller-Meeks was first elected to Congress in the November 2020 election (representing the old IA-02 district, winning by 6 votes over Rita Hart), and was sworn in and took office in January 2021, so this is technically accurate in that she entered Congress in January 2021. On reflection this matches the record and is not an error.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has won the district twice, but both recent races were competitive.
description: Miller-Meeks's two wins over Bohannan were not both competitive. Her 2022 win was a comfortable roughly seven-point victory (53%-47%, about 20,000 votes), not a close race. Only her 2024 win, by 799 votes after a recount, was genuinely close. Characterizing both races as competitive misstates the 2022 result.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks also maintained an apartment in Davenport, and registered to vote in Scott County where Davenport is located, in the context of the 2024 residency controversy
description: The documented record shows Miller-Meeks registered to vote in October 2022 at a state senator's home in LeClaire (Scott County) and then registered/voted using a Davenport apartment in 2024 — the Davenport apartment is accurately placed in Scott County, but the response's framing simplifies a more complex registration history (LeClaire in 2022, then Davenport in 2024) into a single generic 'apartment in Davenport' without capturing that nuance. This is a narrow simplification rather than a substantive misstatement of the core facts, which are otherwise accurately conveyed.

inaccurate_statement: She registered to vote in Scott County (the Davenport/LeClaire area) after redistricting
description: The registration history is more specific and multi-step than described: she registered at a state senator's LeClaire home (Scott County) in October 2022, then registered at a Davenport apartment in 2024 and voted there that November. The response compresses this into a single, slightly imprecise description conflating LeClaire and Davenport as one 'Scott County' registration, though both are indeed in Scott County, so this is a narrow simplification rather than a substantive error.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan explicitly said at the time, 'I do support law enforcement,' per PolitiFact
description: No source confirms Bohannan used this exact phrasing in 2021 in response to the Back the Blue vote or the abolish-law-enforcement claim. Her documented, verifiable quote is the later, more specific statement 'I do not support abolishing the police. I never have, I never will.' Presenting an unverified alternate quote as a direct PolitiFact-sourced statement is an unsupported specific attribution, though it doesn't change the overall accurate conclusion that she supports law enforcement funding rather than abolition.

inaccurate_statement: A 2026 fact-check from 'IA Fact Check' reviewed the current 'plan to defund the police' allegation and concluded the underlying associations and criticisms were real but that calling it 'her plan' overstates the evidence
description: There is a real outlet sometimes referenced as reaching this kind of conclusion about the defund-the-police mischaracterization, and this general finding (overstatement of a real underlying record) matches the broader documented record. However, the specific outlet name, the 2026 date, and framing are not independently verifiable as stated, and this appears to be a loosely sourced or invented citation rather than a confirmed real fact-check article by that exact name and date.

inaccurate_statement: Critics have pointed to her support for immigrant-related causes, including a 2019 donation connected to the Prairielands Freedom Fund
description: The donation to the Prairielands Freedom Fund that Miller-Meeks referenced in 2021 attacks was a $60 donation, and available records tie this to the 2021 controversy period, not a 2019 donation. The response introduces a specific year (2019) for this donation that is not supported by the available record, which describes it as part of a 2021 political controversy.

inaccurate_statement: The 2021 Iowa House sex-offender-registry bill Bohannan voted against was called 'HF 489' and passed 84-12
description: The documented record identifies the relevant bill as SF 2363, which passed 90-3, not 'HF 489' passing 84-12. No source in the available material corroborates a bill named HF 489 with an 84-12 vote tally on this topic, so this specific bill number and vote count appear to be fabricated or garbled details layered onto an otherwise real underlying vote and controversy.

inaccurate_statement: The House Ethics Committee formally announced the fine in January 2022 and noted that she did not appeal it within the prescribed period
description: This conflates two separate fines. Miller-Meeks was fined $500 in May 2021 for not wearing a mask on the House floor, and she did appeal that fine (unsuccessfully, with the Ethics Committee rejecting her appeal). It was a separate, later $2,500 fine issued in January 2022 for a different mask violation that she did not appeal. The response attributes the 'did not appeal' detail to the wrong fine and wrong timeline.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks did not appeal the $500 House mask-rule fine
description: Miller-Meeks did in fact appeal the $500 fine for violating the House mask mandate, and the House Ethics Committee rejected her appeal, upholding the fine. It was a separate, later $2,500 fine from January 2022 that she did not appeal. The response conflates the two fines.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks received a contribution from Eli Lilly's corporate PAC on the same day she voted against an effort to cap insulin costs
description: This same-day donation timing claim has not been independently verified against dated FEC records and should be treated as unconfirmed rather than established fact, as the response presents it.

inaccurate_statement: The House Ethics Committee officially confirmed that Miller-Meeks did not appeal the $500 mask-rule fine.
description: Miller-Meeks did appeal the $500 fine imposed in May 2021 for not wearing a mask on the House floor, though the appeal was rejected. It was a separate, later $2,500 fine (issued in January 2022) that she did not appeal. The response conflates the two fines by attributing the 'did not appeal' detail to the $500 fine rather than the $2,500 one.

inaccurate_statement: Whether Bohannan's policies will hurt Iowa's farmers is contested political spin not independently resolvable, framed here as a definitive mixed assessment with confident specific claims
description: This topic is explicitly a contested partisan framing dispute rather than a matter with a single verifiable answer. The response presents a confident, detailed 'mixed assessment' analysis (winners and losers, specific mechanisms) as though it were settled analysis, when no independent nonpartisan source has actually quantified the net effect of either candidate's platform on Iowa agriculture. This overstates the certainty available on this question, though it does not misstate any of Bohannan's specific documented positions.

inaccurate_statement: Iowa Democrats at a 2025 farm-policy forum emphasized ending tariffs and strengthening support for small and midsize farms
description: No record exists of a specific 2025 Iowa Democratic farm-policy forum where this occurred. While Bohannan did speak at an Iowa Farmers Union candidate forum in July 2026, no such 2025 event or the specific framing described is corroborated, making this an unverified and likely fabricated detail layered onto her generally accurate tariff position.

inaccurate_statement: Iowa's own 2026 Farm Act is already law and contains substantial state-level support for farmers, including expanded agritourism, local food markets, beginning-farmer programs and agricultural tax provisions
description: No record of a specific piece of Iowa state legislation named the '2026 Farm Act' with these exact provisions could be verified. This appears to be an invented or unverifiable state-level legislative reference not tied to either candidate's own record, and is a peripheral detail rather than central to the response's analysis of Bohannan.

inaccurate_statement: Implies Miller-Meeks's tariff votes/positions have an uncertain or unestablished effect on consumer prices, requiring further review of specific legislation
description: Miller-Meeks has a documented voting record on tariffs: she voted three times to block House consideration of ending Trump's tariff emergency declarations and voted against ending the Canada tariff emergency specifically in February 2026. The nonpartisan Tax Foundation estimated these tariffs cost the average U.S. household about $1,000 in 2025 and an additional roughly $700 in 2026. The response treats this as an open, unresearched question rather than acknowledging that her specific tariff votes and their associated cost impact are already documented.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has taught constitutional/First Amendment-related issues and competition law at the University of Iowa College of Law
description: Her documented teaching subjects are torts, copyright, and conflict of laws, plus constitutional law per a separate confirmed research note; there is no confirmation she taught a dedicated 'First Amendment' or 'competition law' course specifically, though her legal scholarship area is described as constitutional and intellectual property law. This is a narrow embellishment on an otherwise accurate teaching-subjects list.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has taught at the University of Iowa College of Law for roughly two decades
description: She moved to Iowa in 2000 to become a University of Iowa College of Law professor, and given the 2026 timeframe, that would put her tenure at roughly 26 years, not 'roughly two decades.' This is a modest understatement of her length of service rather than a substantive misrepresentation of her career.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's platform includes expanding Medicare coverage for home-health care
description: Her documented Medicare expansion proposal is specifically to add dental, hearing, and vision coverage alongside a Medicare buy-in option; no source ties her platform to a home-health-care benefit expansion under Medicare specifically.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan says she wants to grow Iowa's economy through better-paying jobs, support unions and worker protections, and encourage economic growth while avoiding unnecessary regulation, framed as centering her platform on labor unions specifically to prevent offshoring
description: Bohannan's campaign does mention continuing to invest in organized labor and 'union protected man hours' as part of a broader cost-of-living plank, and she has separately spoken about opposing offshoring in the context of manufacturing layoffs, but this is a passing reference within a much broader affordability-focused platform rather than a central, unifying 'jobs, wages and organized labor' pillar as the response frames it. Presenting worker protections and union support as one of her handful of core top-line priorities overstates its prominence relative to her actual platform structure.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks was an assistant professor at the University of Michigan and later the University of Iowa
description: Miller-Meeks's documented academic record shows she was the first woman in 20 years on the University of Iowa ophthalmology faculty; there is no record of an assistant professorship at the University of Michigan. This appears to be an inserted or conflated detail not supported by her biography.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's Army service dates were 1976–1982 (with Army Reserve 1983-2000)
description: Her documented U.S. Army service was 1974–1982, not 1976–1982, before her Army Reserve service from 1983–2000. This is a narrow date discrepancy on an otherwise accurate description of her military career.

inaccurate_statement: She... worked as a physician, including academic appointments at the University of Michigan and University of Iowa
description: Her academic appointment was at the University of Iowa, where she was the first woman in 20 years on the ophthalmology faculty; there is no record of an academic appointment at the University of Michigan. This appears to be an added, unsupported detail alongside an otherwise accurate claim about her University of Iowa faculty role.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks served in the U.S. Army from 1976-1982
description: Miller-Meeks's U.S. Army service began in 1974, not 1976; she served in the Army 1974-1982 before moving to the Army Reserve from 1983-2000.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan supports expanding Iowa's clean-energy economy
description: There is no documented direct statement of Bohannan proposing a specific plan to expand Iowa's clean-energy economy as a named platform item; while she has criticized cuts to clean-energy projects and their effect on jobs and utility bills, presenting broad clean-energy-economy expansion as a stated platform pillar goes beyond what is confirmed in her documented positions.

inaccurate_statement: She lost that race [2022] and later ran again in 2024, losing by a very narrow margin
description: The response's framing implies the 2022 loss was also somewhat close by juxtaposing it with the 2024 'narrow margin' loss, but the two races differed dramatically: Miller-Meeks won the 2022 race comfortably by about 7 points (53%-47%, roughly 20,000 votes), while the 2024 race was the genuinely razor-thin one, decided by just 799 votes (about 0.2%) after a recount. The response does correctly note 2024 was narrow, but does not clarify 2022 was not close, which could leave a reader with an inaccurate impression of the first race's competitiveness.

inaccurate_statement: She also taught at the University of Michigan and University of Iowa.
description: Miller-Meeks was the first woman in 20 years on the University of Iowa ophthalmology faculty, but there is no record of her teaching at the University of Michigan. This appears to be a fabricated or erroneous addition to an otherwise accurate biographical detail.

inaccurate_statement: She taught at the University of Michigan and University of Iowa
description: Miller-Meeks was the first woman in 20 years on the University of Iowa ophthalmology faculty, but there is no record of her teaching at the University of Michigan. This appears to be a fabricated or erroneous addition to an otherwise accurate description of her academic background.

inaccurate_statement: She served in the U.S. Army and Army Reserve for 24 years, including as a nurse and physician
description: Miller-Meeks served in the U.S. Army from 1974 to 1982 (Army Medical Department, retiring as a Lieutenant Colonel) and then in the Army Reserve from 1983 to 2000, which totals roughly 26 years of combined service, not 24. She is also documented as a physician throughout her military career; there's no indication in her background that her earlier role was specifically as a 'nurse' before becoming a physician, though she did hold a BSN before earning her M.D. This is a minor discrepancy in the total years and role framing rather than a substantive misrepresentation of her military background.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has criticized Miller-Meeks over votes affecting public education funding, arguing that Miller-Meeks supported cuts to public schools while favoring other priorities
description: No documented statement or criticism from Bohannan specifically attacking Miller-Meeks over public education funding votes could be found. Bohannan's own platform emphasizes public school investment as a priority of hers, and her documented criticisms of Miller-Meeks center on health care, tariffs, abortion, and infrastructure votes rather than a specific attack on Miller-Meeks's education funding record. This appears to be an unsubstantiated addition rather than a well-documented line of attack.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has accused Miller-Meeks of subsequently "backtracking" or moderating her abortion position because it is politically unpopular, and portrays Miller-Meeks as trying to moderate her public position for electoral reasons
description: There is no documented instance in Bohannan's sourced criticisms of Miller-Meeks framing her opponent's position as a deliberate election-driven "backtrack" or moderation. Bohannan's documented criticisms focus on Miller-Meeks's actual votes and sponsorships (the Life at Conception Act, Iowa's abortion law, Medicaid cuts, tariffs) rather than an accusation of insincere political repositioning. This appears to be an unsupported characterization layered on top of otherwise accurate underlying criticisms, though it does not reverse the overall accurate picture that abortion is Bohannan's most prominent line of attack.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks previously accused Bohannan of wanting to 'abolish law enforcement,' citing Bohannan's support for certain criminal justice reform efforts and a donation connected to a bail reform group.
description: The underlying facts are accurate — Miller-Meeks did make an 'abolish law enforcement' claim about Bohannan in 2021, tied to a donation to a group involved in bail/immigration-detention advocacy, and PolitiFact rated this claim false. The response correctly reports this and its PolitiFact rating, so this is largely accurate; flagging only because the donation was specifically to the Prairielands Freedom Fund (an immigration-bond group), not a 'bail reform group' in the general sense described — a narrow characterization difference that doesn't change the overall accurate takeaway that the claim was rated false.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan pointed specifically to lung cancer as a major cause of cancer deaths in Iowa as part of her tobacco-cessation position.
description: Available reporting confirms Bohannan supports continued funding for smoking-cessation programs and opposes weakening tobacco regulation, but there is no record of her specifically citing lung cancer as a major cause of cancer deaths in Iowa in this context. This appears to be an added detail not substantiated by the available record.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's economic message includes helping local entrepreneurs and reducing barriers that make it harder for small businesses to grow and hire, framed as an itemized small-business plan
description: Bohannan's campaign site and public record contain only general framing of her as a supporter of small businesses within broader affordability and farm-economy planks; no itemized small-business tax, lending, or regulatory-barrier-reduction plan has been found despite dedicated research. Presenting this as a specific, itemized policy area overstates what is actually a general, unspecified position.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has supported reforms aimed at fairness and due process, including changes involving bail and sentencing
description: Bohannan's documented record centers on opposing the 2021 'Back the Blue' law (concerns about protest rights, qualified immunity, and civil liberties) and, as a University of Iowa DEI committee chair, circulating donation suggestions that included a bail fund. There is no documented record of her supporting broader bail or sentencing reform legislation as a distinct policy initiative; framing this as an established part of her platform overstates a much narrower and more contested record.

inaccurate_statement: Her approach has included focusing on issues that can contribute to crime, such as substance abuse, mental health challenges, and community conditions, rather than relying only on enforcement
description: There is no documented general public-safety/crime-prevention plan from Bohannan addressing substance abuse, mental health, or community conditions as crime-prevention mechanisms. Her campaign platform has no discrete public-safety plan at all beyond a gun-violence-prevention position found via a third-party advocacy group; presenting this specific framing as her stated approach without hedging overstates what is a confirmed, genuine gap in her platform.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan would protect existing gun-safety measures that she says were weakened by Iowa Republicans, including background-check requirements
description: There is no direct sourcing for a specific 2026 statement from Bohannan framing her gun position as 'protecting' background-check measures she says were 'weakened by Iowa Republicans.' The documented record shows she opposed a rollback of background-check requirements while in the Iowa legislature and supports expanding background checks and extreme-risk protection orders going forward, but the specific framing in this claim (protecting measures already weakened, attributed to Iowa Republicans) is not confirmed as her own stated position and presents an inferred formulation as if it were a direct claim.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's past promotion of organizations associated with criminal-justice reform is cited by Republican opponents as evidence she is soft on crime
description: This is a real but distorted attack line. Bohannan, as a University of Iowa DEI committee chair, promoted donations including to bail funds and organizations involved in criminal justice reform, and this has been used in attack coverage to suggest she supports defunding or abolishing police -- a characterization PolitiFact rated false. The response accurately notes this dispute exists, but framing it simply as 'promotion of organizations associated with criminal justice reform' without noting the specific bail-fund/DEI-committee context understates how attenuated and contextually stripped this attack line is documented to be.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's likely strategy is characterized as a conservation-and-infrastructure model addressing Iowa's water quality crisis broadly, without noting she has made no direct 2026 statement on the nitrate/cancer-linked water crisis specifically
description: Miller-Meeks has no confirmed direct 2026 statement addressing Iowa's nitrate/cancer-linked water crisis specifically, despite it being the district's most locally salient issue. Her documented water-related statements are general infrastructure/wastewater funding and Clean Water Act/WOTUS regulatory positions, not a stated plan responding to the nitrate crisis itself. Presenting a synthesized 'strategy' as her clear approach to 'Iowa's water quality crisis' without flagging this gap risks implying she has a specific stated position on the nitrate crisis when she does not.

inaccurate_statement: Critics of Miller-Meeks' approach argue that voluntary conservation and infrastructure investments may not be enough to reduce nutrient pollution at the scale needed
description: There is no direct 2026 statement from Miller-Meeks addressing the nitrate/cancer-linked water crisis specifically, and the dossier notes this is a genuine, confirmed gap in her record on the topic dominating 2026 IA-01 coverage. The response's framing implies she has a fully articulated water-quality plan being critiqued by opponents, when in fact her public record on this specific crisis is limited to general remarks and infrastructure funding not specifically targeted at nitrate cleanup.

inaccurate_statement: A bill Miller-Meeks championed providing Medicare coverage for multi-cancer early-detection tests was signed into law in May 2026
description: The Nancy Gardner Sewell Medicare Multi-Cancer Early Detection Screening Coverage Act, which Miller-Meeks championed, was signed into law on February 3, 2026, not May 2026.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks' strategy is largely 'find cancer earlier and make treatment/screening more accessible,' rather than a plan that addresses the underlying causes of Iowa's rising cancer rates
description: Miller-Meeks has, in fact, directly and publicly addressed the causes behind Iowa's cancer crisis on the record, citing factors such as obesity, tobacco use, genetic predisposition, and water quality, and has met with cancer survivors, researchers, and advocates to discuss the state's cancer burden. Framing her approach as exclusively centered on detection and access while implying she has not engaged with or spoken to the underlying causes of the crisis mischaracterizes her documented public statements.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks championed legislation that was signed into law in May 2026 to provide Medicare coverage for MCED tests
description: The Nancy Gardner Sewell Medicare Multi-Cancer Early Detection Screening Coverage Act, which Miller-Meeks co-sponsored, was signed into law on February 3, 2026, not May 2026. The substance of her support for the bill and its 2028 coverage start date are accurate; only the signing date is wrong.

inaccurate_statement: The Iowa Cancer Consortium says Iowa is projected to have about 21,700 new invasive cancer cases and 6,400 cancer deaths in 2026, and that Iowa has the second-highest cancer incidence rate in the country
description: These statistics come from the Iowa Cancer Registry (housed at the University of Iowa), not the Iowa Cancer Consortium, which is a separate though related nonprofit organization focused on the Iowa Cancer Plan rather than producing incidence/mortality data. The underlying figures themselves are accurate.

inaccurate_statement: I don't see an equally specific Miller-Meeks plan, as of August 2026, for substantially reducing the incidence of cancer by addressing Iowa's suspected environmental, occupational, behavioral, or agricultural risk factors
description: This conclusion is contradicted by documented reporting: multiple 2026 news reports (Iowa Public Radio, The Gazette) show Miller-Meeks directly and specifically addressing Iowa's cancer-rate crisis, including on-record comments about suspected causes (obesity, tobacco, genetic predisposition, and water quality) and her signing of the American Cancer Society's 2026 Cancer Promise. The claim that she has made no direct statement or engagement on this specific topic mischaracterizes her documented public engagement with exactly this question.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks championed legislation that was signed into law in May 2026 to establish Medicare coverage for FDA-approved multi-cancer early-detection (MCED) tests.
description: The Nancy Gardner Sewell Medicare Multi-Cancer Early Detection Screening Coverage Act, which Miller-Meeks championed, was signed into law on February 3, 2026, not May 2026. The substance of the claim — that she championed this legislation and that coverage begins in 2028 — is accurate; only the signing date is wrong.

inaccurate_statement: Her earlier position was notably skeptical of treating a massive wall as the entire solution; she pointed out that many unauthorized immigrants historically entered legally and then overstayed visas.
description: There is no record of Miller-Meeks making this specific argument. Her actual documented record shows the opposite emphasis: she has praised the border wall as having strengthened national security, criticized the Biden administration for halting wall construction, and supported legislation to let states finish wall construction. No source ties the visa-overstay argument to her personally.

inaccurate_statement: In a 2021 policy discussion, she argued that mass deportation would be extraordinarily expensive and disruptive while advocating enforcement focused on threats to public safety.
description: This specific cost-based argument against mass deportation traces to a Newsmax op-ed by a different author (Daniel Di Martino) that was merely republished on Miller-Meeks's House website listing her among several Republicans favoring legal immigration reform; the argument itself was not made by her personally in a policy discussion.

inaccurate_statement: In her earlier immigration proposals, Miller-Meeks argued that immigrants should be vetted for security risks while also making the legal immigration system more functional
description: This framing traces to a 2021 Newsmax op-ed by Daniel Di Martino that was republished on Miller-Meeks's House website; the op-ed merely lists her among Republicans favoring legal immigration reform but the specific vetting/legal-system argument was the author's own framing, not a personal proposal or statement she made herself.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has argued that expanding legitimate temporary work visas could reduce illegal migration by giving workers a legal alternative to unauthorized entry
description: This specific argument comes from the same 2021 Newsmax op-ed by Daniel Di Martino republished on her House website, not from Miller-Meeks's own statements or a proposal she personally authored.

inaccurate_statement: In a 2021 article she explicitly argued that a wall by itself would not solve the problem because many unauthorized immigrants initially enter legally and overstay visas
description: No source shows Miller-Meeks making this specific argument herself. This appears to derive from the same republished op-ed context and does not reflect her own statement. In fact, her actual documented record shows the opposite emphasis — she has praised the border wall, criticized halts to wall construction, and cosponsored legislation to finish wall construction, making this claim not just unattributed but in tension with her real, sourced position on the wall's value.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has campaigned explicitly on reducing Washington's partisan bickering and working across party lines as a meaningful part of her stated governing philosophy
description: Bohannan's actual campaign platform centers primarily on economic affordability, healthcare costs, and pointed attacks on Miller-Meeks's record, with 'extreme partisanship' mentioned only briefly as one of several problems alongside corporate/special-interest influence. Her messaging is dominated by economic populism and adversarial contrasts with her opponent rather than a defining 'working across the aisle, less bickering' theme, so presenting this as a central, meaningful part of her governing philosophy overstates its role in her actual platform.

inaccurate_statement: Her Stop Insider Trading Act passed the House in July 2026, framed as her own bill
description: A bipartisan congressional stock-trading ban did pass the House in July 2026 and Miller-Meeks strongly supported and cosponsored it, but the lead sponsor of the Stop Insider Trading Act (H.R.7008) is Rep. Bryan Steil, not Miller-Meeks. Calling it "her" Stop Insider Trading Act overstates her role from cosponsor/backer to author.

inaccurate_statement: Her campaign says she visited every county in the district four times during 2025 and completed two tours of all 20 counties before the 2026 primary
description: The documented record shows Miller-Meeks completed a 20-county in-person tour, but there is no confirmation of visiting every county four times in 2025 or completing two full 20-county tours before the primary. The dossier notes her accessibility record centers on tele-town halls (reaching thousands of participants) and one 20-county tour, not multiple full-district tours; this specific claim about frequency and count appears to be an embellishment not supported by the documented record.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan lost both the 2022 and 2024 races by narrow margins
description: The 2022 race between Bohannan and Miller-Meeks was not close — Miller-Meeks won comfortably, 53%-47%, about a 7-point margin (~20,000 votes). Only the 2024 race was genuinely narrow, decided by just 799 votes after a recount. Describing both losses as 'narrow' misrepresents the 2022 result.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan lost by about 23,000 votes in 2022
description: The 2022 Bohannan-Miller-Meeks race was decided by roughly 20,000 votes (53%-47%, about a 7-point margin), not approximately 23,000 votes.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan lost by about 23,000 votes in 2022
description: The 2022 Bohannan-Miller-Meeks race was decided by roughly 20,000 votes (53%-47%, about a 7-point margin), not approximately 23,000 votes.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan explicitly supports paid family leave / nationwide paid family leave as part of her platform
description: Bohannan's documented platform priorities (cost of living, health care, education, family farms, seniors, government ethics, and family economy) do not include a specific, itemized paid family leave proposal in the available record. While her broader platform emphasizes a 'family friendly economy' and caregiving supports such as Medicare coverage of home-health costs for caregivers, no direct statement establishing a specific paid family leave policy was found, so presenting this as a settled, itemized position without hedging overstates what is documented.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan supports incentives for cover crops to reduce agricultural chemical use and runoff, framed as her environmental approach to cancer prevention.
description: Bohannan does support increasing resources and incentives for farmers to boost buffer zones and reduce nitrate/PFAS pollution as part of her water-quality platform, and separately has discussed environmental/agricultural risk factors in the context of cancer in an August 2026 interview. However, her direct 2026 cancer-focused remarks centered on NIH funding, clinical trial access, and conservation-practice funding (cover crops) while explicitly declining to tie crop-insurance eligibility to farming practices — not a fully worked-out standalone 'cover crops to reduce agricultural chemical use' cancer-prevention platform as the response frames it. This is a reasonable but somewhat overstated synthesis of scattered real positions rather than a clean, itemized policy the way the response presents it.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has proposed an Iowa State University biochar research institute aimed partly at improving water filtration and purification.
description: No record exists in Miller-Meeks's documented legislative or policy history of a proposal for an Iowa State University biochar research institute focused on water filtration and purification. Her documented water-related positions concern Clean Water Act permitting reform, WOTUS/Navigable Waters Protection Rule advocacy, and general infrastructure/wastewater funding, none of which involve a biochar research institute. This appears to be a fabricated or invented detail not attributable to her actual record.

inaccurate_statement: The strongest documented 'bipartisan' profile in the current IA-01 race appears to be Miller-Meeks's.
description: This framing is presented as a settled comparative conclusion, but bipartisanship rankings among the three candidates are not neutrally adjudicated facts. While Miller-Meeks does have a three-term voting record with some bipartisan co-sponsorships (Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act, Alternatives to the PAIN Act, EARLY Act Reauthorization) that can be checked against Congress.gov, her record is also mixed with documented town-hall avoidance and party-line votes on major legislation (OBBBA), and Bohannan's more limited state legislative record includes bipartisan elder-abuse/human-trafficking work. Presenting one candidate as definitively having 'the strongest' bipartisan profile in the race overstates what is actually a contested, mixed picture on both sides.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan lost to Miller-Meeks by about 23,000 votes in 2022
description: The 2022 Iowa 1st District race between Miller-Meeks and Bohannan was won by Miller-Meeks 53%-47%, a margin documented as approximately 20,000 votes, not 23,000 votes. This is a specific figure that doesn't match the well-documented margin, though it doesn't change the broader accurate point that 2022 was a comfortable, non-competitive win for Miller-Meeks compared to the razor-thin 2024 rematch.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has recently led bipartisan legislation to cap insulin costs at $35/month for people with private insurance
description: Miller-Meeks's own voting record shows she voted against capping insulin costs and opposed a Democratic-backed insulin price cap provision; her documented legislative work is the 'Lower Health Care Premiums for All Americans Act' (PBM transparency, association health plans) rather than a $35/month insulin cap bill she led. She has separately cited past votes to cap insulin at $35 in some contexts, but describing her as currently 'leading bipartisan legislation' specifically to cap insulin costs for private insurance is not supported and runs counter to her documented record of voting against an insulin price cap provision.
