inaccurate_statement: Bohannan lost by about 23,000 votes in 2022
description: Bohannan did lose the 2022 IA-01 race to Mariannette Miller-Meeks by a similar margin, but the commonly reported margin was approximately 21,000 votes (about 53%-47%, roughly a 6.5-point spread), not 23,000 votes. The core claim that she lost by a margin in the tens of thousands is correct, but the specific figure appears to overstate the margin by a couple thousand votes. This is a narrow numerical discrepancy that doesn't undermine the overall point that Bohannan narrowly lost in 2022.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan lost by about 23,000 votes in 2022
description: In the actual 2022 IA-01 election, Mariannette Miller-Meeks defeated Christina Bohannan by an extremely narrow margin of roughly 800 votes (about 0.3 percentage points), which triggered a recount and was widely reported as one of the closest U.S. House races in the country that cycle. The claim that Bohannan lost by about 23,000 votes is off by more than an order of magnitude and misrepresents what was in fact a nail-biter race. This is a significant factual error because it changes the reader's understanding of the competitiveness of the district and the closeness of the Miller-Meeks/Bohannan rivalry, which is a defining feature of this race (they also had an extremely close rematch in 2024, decided by under 800 votes).

inaccurate_statement: A House ethics complaint was also filed regarding her residency/voting
description: The residency-related ethics complaint against Miller-Meeks was filed with the federal Office of Congressional Ethics (OCE), not directly with the House Committee on Ethics. The OCE did not pursue the complaint further; there is no indication it was referred to or filed with the House Ethics Committee itself.

inaccurate_statement: In July 2025, Miller-Meeks changed her voter registration back to her Ottumwa address in Wapello County
description: Miller-Meeks voluntarily re-registered to vote at her Ottumwa home in December 2025, not July 2025. Additionally, her Ottumwa home is located in Iowa's 3rd Congressional District, not the district she represents (IA-01), a detail the response omits.

inaccurate_statement: In 2023–24, her voter registration was at an address in Scott County, which is outside the 1st Congressional District
description: This inverts the actual facts of the controversy. Scott County (where she registered in LeClaire and later Davenport) is inside Iowa's 1st Congressional District — that was precisely why she registered there after her longtime Ottumwa home in Wapello County was redistricted out of IA-01 following the 2020 census. It is the Ottumwa/Wapello County home that is outside IA-01 (it's in IA-03), not the Scott County address. This reverses the core geography at the heart of the residency controversy and would seriously mislead a reader about what the dispute was actually about.

inaccurate_statement: A complaint filed with the House Ethics Committee in September 2024 alleged that she actually resided in Wapello County and therefore had improperly registered and voted in Scott County
description: The residency-related ethics complaint was filed with the federal Office of Congressional Ethics (OCE), not directly with the House Ethics Committee. The House Ethics Committee would only become involved via a referral from the OCE, not through a direct complaint filing. A separate residency challenge (not an ethics complaint) was filed with the Scott County board of supervisors around the same period.

inaccurate_statement: She subsequently changed her voter registration back to her Ottumwa home in July 2025
description: Reporting indicates Miller-Meeks re-registered to vote at her Ottumwa home in December 2025, not July 2025. Additionally, this move placed her registration outside the district she represents, since Ottumwa/Wapello County is in IA-03, not IA-01 — a detail the response omits.

inaccurate_statement: Iowa's 'Back the Blue' legislation that Bohannan opposed was from 2020
description: The 'Back the Blue' bill (SF 342) that Bohannan voted against was 2021 legislation, not 2020. She was elected to the Iowa House in November 2020 and took office in January 2021, and the vote occurred during the 2021 legislative session.

inaccurate_statement: Iowa's 'Back the Blue' law is described as a 2020 law
description: The Back the Blue legislation Bohannan opposed was Iowa Senate File 342, passed and signed in 2021, not 2020. This is a minor date error within an otherwise accurate description of the underlying controversy.

inaccurate_statement: The Iowa GOP currently alleges that Bohannan donated to a group calling for 'a world without police'
description: Bohannan's real, documented donation controversy involves a $60 donation to the Prairielands Freedom Fund, a group that helped pay immigration bonds and supported ending immigrant detention — not a group described as calling for 'a world without police.' While she has separately promoted donations to organizations like the National Bail Out Fund and Minnesota Freedom Fund as a DEI committee chair, no source ties any Iowa GOP allegation to a group using the specific phrase 'a world without police.' This appears to be an invented or garbled version of the real, documented donation controversy, though the broader point that Republicans have attacked her over donations tied to criminal-justice-reform groups is accurate.

inaccurate_statement: The NRCC has attacked Bohannan over her opposition to Iowa's 2020 'Back the Blue' law.
description: Iowa's 'Back the Blue' legislation that Bohannan voted against and has been criticized for opposing was a 2021 bill (SF 342), not a 2020 law. This is a narrow date error that does not change the substance of the underlying controversy.

inaccurate_statement: In 2019, Bohannan donated $60 through a birthday fundraiser to the Prairielands Freedom Fund
description: The donation and its use as an attack line are real, but the documented year for this controversy in connection with Miller-Meeks's 2021 'abolish law enforcement' claim is associated with 2021-era reporting, not specifically dated to 2019 in the available record. This is a narrow dating discrepancy rather than a fabrication of the underlying donation or its political use.

inaccurate_statement: Fox News reported in 2025 that Bohannan bought a $1.55 million Iowa City mansion and also owns a waterfront condominium in Sarasota, Florida that has generated substantial rental income, and critics have connected her investments in individual technology stocks to her proposed congressional stock-trading ban
description: The documented version of this controversy involves Bohannan's financial disclosure showing stock holdings in Apple, Alphabet, and Meta (reported as up to $280,000) plus a separate $500,001-$1,000,000 Amana Mutual Funds Trust position, with Miller-Meeks countering that she owns no individual stocks while Bohannan owns hundreds of thousands worth -- this is a real, sourced controversy. However, no source in the available record corroborates a specific '$1.55 million Iowa City mansion' purchase or a 'Sarasota, Florida waterfront condominium' generating 'substantial rental income' as reported by Fox News in 2025; while Bohannan and her husband are noted elsewhere as owning a million-dollar-plus Iowa City home and a Florida rental condo, the specific $1.55 million figure and the Fox News 2025 sourcing for this exact framing could not be verified against the available material. The core 'wealth vs. working-class messaging' controversy and the stock-holdings hypocrisy critique are accurately characterized, so this is a narrow, unverified embellishment on real underlying facts rather than a wholesale invention.

inaccurate_statement: The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee specifically attacked her over what it called 'disinformation and quack science'
description: No record in available material substantiates this specific quoted phrase or that the DCCC made this particular attack against Miller-Meeks. While her sharing of a satirical article and COVID-related commentary did draw documented criticism and fact-checks from local media and medical professionals, this specific DCCC quote could not be verified.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's campaigns had raised about $22.6 million across seven elections through the 2026 cycle, while outside groups had spent roughly $19.6 million for or against her
description: These aggregate lifetime fundraising and outside-spending figures cannot be verified against the documented record, which instead provides per-cycle FEC figures (e.g., about $7.2 million raised for the 2025-2026 filing period) and per-cycle outside-spending totals that don't clearly sum to $19.6 million across her career. No source in the available material supports these specific cumulative totals, and given the pattern of similar fabricated aggregate financial statistics found elsewhere in this race, this figure should be treated as unverified rather than accepted at face value.

inaccurate_statement: Iowa Democrats alleged in 2021 that Miller-Meeks had failed to properly report more than $59,000 in income on her financial disclosure
description: The 2021 Office of Congressional Ethics complaint against Miller-Meeks alleged she failed to disclose income in amounts reported as approximately $34,646, $35,000, or $80,000 depending on the source, but no source ties the figure to $59,000. The underlying allegation (unreported state pension, state senate salary, and health-system income) is real, but the specific dollar amount cited does not match any documented figure.

inaccurate_statement: In July 2025, Miller-Meeks changed her voter registration back to her longtime home in Ottumwa, which is outside the current 1st Congressional District
description: Miller-Meeks voluntarily re-registered to vote at her Ottumwa home (which is outside IA-01) in December 2025, not July 2025. The underlying fact that she re-registered outside the district she represents is accurate, but the timing given is incorrect by about five months.

inaccurate_statement: Tariffs analyses cited by the Washington Post found U.S. importers and consumers bear roughly 95% of the costs of those tariffs, in the context of the House vote over Canada's tariffs
description: The dossier documents that the nonpartisan Tax Foundation estimated Trump-era tariffs cost the average U.S. household about $1,000 in 2025 and roughly an additional $700 in 2026, and that a Democratic-sourced $2,400/year figure was not independently verified. No source in the available material corroborates a specific claim that a Washington Post-cited analysis found consumers bear 95% of the cost of the Canada-specific tariffs Miller-Meeks voted on. This appears to be an unverified or invented statistic layered onto an otherwise real, documented voting record (she voted against ending the Canada tariff emergency).

inaccurate_statement: The 2025 Republican tax-and-spending law is projected to add about $3.4 trillion to federal deficits over a decade
description: This specific deficit figure is not addressed in the available material on this bill, which documents the bill's Medicaid work-requirement provisions, its passage by a 218-214 vote, and the $50B Rural Health Transformation Program, but does not confirm or deny a $3.4 trillion decade-long deficit projection. While this figure is commonly cited by outlets like the CBO, it cannot be verified against the source material provided here, so it is treated as an unresolved figure rather than confirmed.

inaccurate_statement: Reuters reported that the law was projected to increase the federal deficit by about $3.4 trillion over a decade and leave 10 million more people uninsured by 2034
description: The knowledge base cites a KFF (Kaiser Family Foundation) estimate that the combined ACA-subsidy expiration and Medicaid cuts would leave roughly 110,000 more Iowans uninsured by 2034, and does not corroborate a Reuters-sourced 10 million nationwide uninsured figure or a $3.4 trillion deficit increase specifically attributed to Reuters reporting on this bill. While CBO and other nonpartisan estimates for the broader reconciliation bill in this range have circulated publicly, the specific attribution to Reuters and the exact figures could not be verified against the available material, making this an unresolved sourcing/figure claim rather than a confirmed accurate statistic.

inaccurate_statement: She has supported legislation intended to protect Medicare payments
description: Miller-Meeks's documented Medicare-related record centers on reforms to Medicare Advantage prior authorization, physician payment restructuring, and multi-cancer early detection coverage, not a specific, itemized effort framed as 'protecting Medicare payments' in general. This is a vague characterization not clearly grounded in a specific, checkable position.

inaccurate_statement: The enhanced ACA subsidies have already expired, contributing to higher costs for some enrollees
description: According to the available record, Miller-Meeks voted against a January 2026 bipartisan bill that would have extended the enhanced ACA premium tax credits, and the dossier discusses these credits as an active point of dispute in the 2026 cycle rather than a subsidy that has definitively already lapsed with settled consequences as of this response's September 2026 timeframe. The framing that they 'have already expired' is stated as a flat fact without the nuance present in the record about ongoing legislative fights over extension.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan supports expanding paid family leave and child-care support
description: Bohannan's documented campaign platform covers lowering costs, health care, education, family farms, seniors/Social Security/Medicare, government ethics, and reproductive freedom, but no source shows a specific paid family leave or child-care expansion plank as part of her stated priorities. This appears to be an unsupported addition not grounded in her actual platform, though it is a narrow, generic policy claim consistent with typical Democratic platforms rather than one that fundamentally mischaracterizes her positions.

inaccurate_statement: She completed an ophthalmology residency at the University of Iowa
description: Available biographical sources describe Miller-Meeks becoming the first woman in 20 years on the University of Iowa ophthalmology faculty, but do not document that her ophthalmology residency itself was completed at the University of Iowa. This detail is not confirmed by the available record.

inaccurate_statement: She also served as an assistant professor at both the University of Michigan and the University of Iowa
description: There is no record of Miller-Meeks having any faculty appointment at the University of Michigan. Her documented academic role was at the University of Iowa, where she became the first woman in 20 years on the ophthalmology faculty. The University of Michigan affiliation does not appear in any available biographical material and appears to be fabricated.

inaccurate_statement: She completed an ophthalmology residency at the University of Iowa and practiced as an ophthalmologist and served as an assistant professor at both the University of Michigan and University of Iowa
description: Available records describe Miller-Meeks running a private ophthalmology practice in Ottumwa, Iowa, and being the first woman in 20 years on the University of Iowa ophthalmology faculty. No record confirms a residency specifically completed at the University of Iowa or a faculty appointment at the University of Michigan; this detail cannot be corroborated against the available biographical information and appears to add unsupported specifics to an otherwise accurate general description of her medical career.

inaccurate_statement: She enlisted at 18 and served 24 years in the U.S. Army
description: Miller-Meeks's documented military service was in the U.S. Army Medical Department from 1974 to 1982 (retiring as a Lieutenant Colonel), followed by Army Reserve service from 1983 to 2000. The commonly cited '24-year Army veteran' framing appears elsewhere and is treated as accurate in available research, but the claim that she 'enlisted at 18' is not supported by any source in the available material — she attended nursing school and joined as part of the Army Medical Department rather than enlisting as a teenager, and no source corroborates an enlistment age of 18. This is a narrow, unverified embellishment on an otherwise accurate general point about her military service.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is chair of the House Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee
description: Miller-Meeks sits on the House Energy and Commerce Committee's Health subcommittee and chairs the House Veterans' Affairs Subcommittee on Health, but she is not documented as chairing the Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee specifically. This conflates two different subcommittee roles.

inaccurate_statement: Guns: She has opposed efforts that would weaken Iowa's firearm restrictions, including protections affecting people convicted of felonies or domestic abuse.
description: Bohannan's documented gun-policy record is that she is a gun owner who grew up hunting, supports the Second Amendment, and supports commonsense reforms such as expanding background checks and extreme risk protection order laws. She opposed a 'strict scrutiny' gun-rights constitutional amendment and the gutting of background-check requirements. There is no record of a specific statement or vote from her specifically framed around opposing weakened restrictions on firearm access for people convicted of felonies or domestic abuse; this appears to be an invented specific detail rather than a documented position, though it is broadly consistent with her general pro-background-check stance.

inaccurate_statement: She also supports expanding Medicare benefits to dental/vision/hearing care
description: Bohannan's documented Medicare expansion proposal adds dental, hearing, and vision coverage as part of a Medicare buy-in at any age; this is her actual, well-sourced position, so this particular claim is accurate rather than inaccurate. No correction needed here.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan supports nationwide paid family leave and greater assistance for caregivers as part of her families platform
description: There is no confirmed record of Bohannan's campaign platform including a specific nationwide paid family leave proposal. Her documented family-related policy items include expanding Medicare to cover home-health costs for family caregivers, the Child Care Tax Credit, and Head Start expansion, but a distinct 'nationwide paid family leave' plank is not substantiated in the available material, making this an unsupported addition to an otherwise accurate list of family-policy items.

inaccurate_statement: She has led bipartisan efforts to cap insulin costs at $35/month for privately insured patients
description: Miller-Meeks's documented voting record shows the opposite: she voted against legislation that would have capped insulin prices for certain Medicare beneficiaries, and her record on capping insulin costs generally is one of opposition rather than a bipartisan effort she led to cap costs at $35/month for privately insured patients. No source documents her leading such a bipartisan insulin-cap effort for private insurance specifically.

inaccurate_statement: She has supported a $35/month insulin cap for people with private insurance
description: Miller-Meeks's documented insulin-cap vote was for a $35/month Medicare insulin cap (part of the Inflation Reduction Act provisions she voted for as one of a small number of House Republicans), not a cap specifically for people with private insurance. The response itself later correctly describes this as a 'Medicare insulin cap,' creating an internal inconsistency, and no record shows her supporting a private-insurance-specific insulin cap as a distinct policy.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has argued that Miller-Meeks subsequently tried to moderate or distance herself from that [Life at Conception Act] position
description: No source in the available record shows Bohannan making this specific claim that Miller-Meeks tried to moderate or distance herself from the Life at Conception Act. The documented Bohannan criticism is that Miller-Meeks has an extreme record and 'sold out Iowa women,' not that Miller-Meeks retreated from her position; separately, it is Miller-Meeks who is documented as trying to portray herself as more moderate on abortion generally, but this is not attributed to Bohannan's criticism specifically in available material.

inaccurate_statement: An Iowa fact-check rated the Republican framing of Bohannan's 'backwards Iowa' comments as 'materially misleading.'
description: Extensive search results document the 'backwards'/'backwater' comments controversy in detail—including Fox News, Iowa GOP, RedState, and other outlets covering Republican attacks on Bohannan over these remarks—but no Iowa fact-checking organization (PolitiFact Iowa, Des Moines Register, etc.) appears to have issued any 'materially misleading' rating of the Republican framing of these comments. This is a specific, checkable claim (a named fact-check verdict) that should surface in search if real, and it does not. No such fact-check could be found, suggesting this claim is fabricated.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has contrasted her own congressional experience with Bohannan's background as a University of Iowa law professor and former state legislator, suggesting Bohannan lacks the experience needed in Congress
description: No documented Miller-Meeks quote or campaign statement specifically frames Bohannan's professional background (law professor, one-term state legislator) as a lack-of-experience attack. The documented, sourced Miller-Meeks criticism of Bohannan centers on calling her a 'radical progressive' pursuing a 'radical agenda,' not an experience-based critique. This appears to be an invented characterization rather than a substantiated attack line.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's campaign characterized Bohannan's 2024 recount request as essentially a delay tactic, arguing the outcome was statistically irreversible
description: No source in the available record documents Miller-Meeks or her campaign describing the 2024 recount request as a 'delay tactic' or claiming the outcome was 'statistically irreversible.' While the recount and its 799-vote outcome are well documented, this specific characterization of Miller-Meeks's response to the recount request could not be verified and appears to be an invented detail.

inaccurate_statement: After Bohannan sought a recount in their extremely close 2024 race, Miller-Meeks called her an 'election denier' and characterized the recount as an effort to delay the result.
description: No record exists of Miller-Meeks calling Bohannan an 'election denier' over the 2024 recount. The 2024 race was decided by just 799 votes after a recount, and while this was a genuinely contested, closely-fought race, there is no documented instance of Miller-Meeks using the term 'election denier' against Bohannan or characterizing her request for a recount (a normal, legal procedure available in an extremely close race) as an improper delay tactic. This appears to invert the typical dynamic, since it is usually Democrats who label Republicans 'election deniers' over disputes about the 2020 election, and Bohannan's 2024 recount request was a standard legal process following a razor-thin margin, not a basis for such an attack documented anywhere in the record.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan does not currently appear to have a detailed, standalone water-quality plan, and her campaign's formal 2026 priorities page doesn't identify water quality as a separate major policy plank
description: Bohannan's campaign platform explicitly and directly addresses water quality as a named issue, stating that 'water pollution from nitrates, PFAS chemicals, and other contamination is increasingly widespread across the state' and pledging to reduce PFAS and increase buffer-zone incentives for farmers. This is documented as her strongest, most explicit platform item in this policy area, with a dedicated statement naming the crisis directly — not an omitted or absent plank. Describing it as lacking any standalone treatment on her priorities page mischaracterizes a genuinely documented, explicit position.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's water-quality approach includes protecting and strengthening public-health infrastructure, including continued funding for local health departments and radon testing
description: No source ties Bohannan to a specific position on local health department funding or radon testing as part of her water-quality or public-health platform. Her documented public-health-adjacent statements center on cancer research funding, rural hospital access, and Medicaid, not radon testing or local health department funding specifically.

inaccurate_statement: Iowa's 1st District has experienced declining union manufacturing employment, particularly in the Mississippi Valley, as district-specific context for Bohannan's jobs pitch
description: While there is documented manufacturing job loss in the district (e.g., Whirlpool layoffs in Amana and John Deere layoffs in the Quad Cities), no source ties this specifically to a decline in "union manufacturing employment" framed this way, nor is this characterization drawn from Bohannan's own campaign materials. This is a generalized framing not clearly grounded in the available record, though the broader point about manufacturing job losses in the district is genuine and documented.

inaccurate_statement: The district has experienced declines in union manufacturing employment
description: There is documented evidence of significant manufacturing layoffs in the district, notably at John Deere/Quad Cities facilities and the Whirlpool plant in Amana, which affected unionized workers. However, no source in the available material specifically frames this as a broader, sustained 'decline in union manufacturing employment' as a district-wide trend; the documented facts are specific plant layoffs rather than an aggregate union-employment decline statistic. This is a plausible but unverified generalization rather than a confirmed district-wide statistic.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has supported Iowa's Nutrient Reduction Strategy and has promoted increasing federal resources for conservation practices that reduce nitrogen and phosphorus runoff, with her office highlighting efforts to fund wetlands and other conservation structures
description: The dossier documents no direct 2026 statement from Miller-Meeks specifically addressing Iowa's nitrate/water-quality crisis; her only documented water-related positions are a 2022 call to drop the WOTUS rule expansion (a water-regulation stance, not a nitrate-cleanup one) and the Davenport wastewater/flood-mitigation funding, which is not agricultural-runoff-specific. No sourced statement ties her to promoting Iowa's Nutrient Reduction Strategy or increased federal conservation funding for nitrogen/phosphorus runoff specifically. This is presented as her demonstrated position without the hedging the record calls for, though it is broadly consistent with generic Iowa Republican messaging on the topic, so it is a minor rather than critical fabrication.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has generally aligned with the approach of protecting farmers from what she views as excessive federal regulation, framed as part of a coherent water-quality regulatory stance
description: This is broadly consistent with her documented general opposition to federal water regulatory overreach (e.g., the WOTUS/Navigable Waters Protection Rule resolution), but the dossier notes there is no direct 2026 statement from her addressing the nitrate/cancer-linked water crisis specifically — treating this general regulatory philosophy as her actual water-quality-crisis approach risks overstating a documented position into an inferred one, though the underlying general stance itself is accurate.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks says federal research funding should support more innovative, higher-risk research rather than concentrating research opportunities on the coasts, and wants clinical trials redesigned so rural patients can participate without repeatedly traveling long distances
description: No record exists of Miller-Meeks making this specific argument about redirecting federal research funding away from coastal concentration or about redesigning clinical trials to reduce travel burden for rural patients. Her documented cancer-related record centers on the multi-cancer early detection legislation, the EARLY Act reauthorization, and general statements about rural care access and Iowa's cancer research investment through the Rural Health Transformation Program, none of which include this specific research-funding-geography or clinical-trial-redesign framing.

inaccurate_statement: Environmental exposures associated with agricultural practices and water quality are not the centerpiece of the cancer proposals Miller-Meeks has publicly outlined, implying she has made no substantive statement addressing causes of Iowa's rising cancer rates
description: Miller-Meeks has in fact made direct, on-record statements specifically addressing Iowa's cancer-rate crisis, including discussing possible causes (obesity, tobacco, genetic predisposition, and water quality) in reported interviews, and she signed the American Cancer Society's cancer promise while meeting with survivors and researchers about the state's cancer burden. Framing her engagement as limited only to detection/access/research while implying she hasn't substantively addressed the causes side of the debate understates a documented record of her directly discussing causal factors, including water quality.

inaccurate_statement: Recent reporting puts Iowa's overall cancer rate around 506 cases per 100,000 people, versus about 442 nationally
description: No source in the available material corroborates these specific per-100,000 incidence figures (506 for Iowa vs. 442 nationally). The documented Iowa cancer statistics center on projected case counts (21,700 new cancers, 6,400 deaths in 2026) and Iowa having the nation's second-highest/fastest-rising cancer rate, not these particular rate-per-100,000 figures, so this specific numeric claim cannot be verified against known figures and appears to be an unverified or invented statistic layered onto an otherwise accurate general point about Iowa's elevated cancer incidence.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks led legislation signed into law in 2026 establishing Medicare coverage for MCED tests beginning in 2028 as her 'biggest concrete accomplishment' (implying sole/lead authorship)
description: Miller-Meeks was a substantive co-sponsor and champion of the Nancy Gardner Sewell Medicare Multi-Cancer Early Detection Screening Coverage Act, which was signed into law in February 2026 and establishes Medicare coverage for FDA-approved MCED tests beginning in 2028. However, the bill was introduced by Rep. Jodey Arrington, with Miller-Meeks as one of several original co-sponsors, not the lead author. Describing this as something she personally 'led' overstates her role relative to the actual lead sponsor, though her substantive involvement and public championing of the bill are real.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has supported the Empowering Law Enforcement to Fight Sex Trafficking Demand Act
description: No record exists in Miller-Meeks's documented legislative history of sponsoring, cosponsoring, or supporting a bill by this specific name. Her documented anti-trafficking-adjacent record includes votes and statements on border security, fentanyl interdiction (HALT Fentanyl Act), and general law-enforcement support, but this particular named piece of legislation does not appear anywhere in her verified record.

inaccurate_statement: In 2021, Miller-Meeks argued that expanding vetted temporary work visas could reduce incentives for unauthorized migration
description: This specific argument traces to a 2021 Newsmax op-ed by Daniel Di Martino that was republished on Miller-Meeks's House website, not to a statement she personally made. The op-ed merely lists her alongside other Republicans as favoring legal immigration reform; it does not attribute this specific visa-expansion argument to her as her own proposal.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supported employment verification and enforcement against unlawful hiring as part of her border/immigration approach
description: No press releases, votes, or public statements were found linking Miller-Meeks to advocacy for mandatory employment verification (e.g., E-Verify) or enforcement against unlawful hiring specifically, despite her border/immigration record being otherwise extensively documented on her own official House website.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has said there should be 'no more open borders'
description: No source in the available record attributes this specific phrase to Miller-Meeks. Her documented border-security statements and voting record (support for the Laken Riley Act, Secure the Border Act, SAVE Act, Mayorkas impeachment, wall construction legislation) are consistent with a border-hawk position, but this specific quoted phrasing could not be verified against any primary source.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks questioned Mayorkas specifically about the administration's use of Title 42 during a Homeland Security Committee hearing
description: Mariannette Miller-Meeks is not a member of the House Homeland Security Committee (her committee assignments have included Agriculture, Veterans' Affairs, and Budget), so she would not have questioned Secretary Mayorkas 'during a Homeland Security Committee hearing.' While it's plausible she has raised Title 42/border policy questions in other contexts (e.g., a different committee hearing or floor statement), the specific attribution of this exchange to a Homeland Security Committee hearing appears to be a factual error. Note: I was unable to complete a live web search in this session due to tool access errors, so this assessment relies on known committee assignments rather than a fresh, confirmed source check; the substantive point that she likely opposes/has criticized Title 42 policy may still be accurate even if this specific hearing detail is wrong.

inaccurate_statement: She supported FY2026 funding legislation that she says ends Biden-era catch-and-release programs, increases ICE funding, and includes increased resources for intercepting fentanyl at the border
description: The knowledge base documents Miller-Meeks's border/immigration voting record in detail, including the Laken Riley Act, the Secure the Border Act of 2023, the SAVE Act, the HALT Fentanyl Act, and various community project funding, but contains no record of a specific 'FY2026 funding legislation' package attributed to her that bundles catch-and-release termination, increased ICE funding, and fentanyl interdiction resources together. This specific bundled bill and its framing as her own distinct 2026 legislative accomplishment could not be verified against her documented record, though the general thrust that she supports these enforcement priorities individually is consistent with her overall record.

inaccurate_statement: Her campaign says she raised more than $2 million in the first quarter of 2026 without corporate PAC money
description: Bohannan's FEC filings for the period covering 2025-2026 show total receipts of over $7 million across the filing period, and her no-corporate-PAC-money pledge is documented and holds up, but no source ties a specific '$2 million in the first quarter of 2026' figure to her fundraising; this specific quarterly amount could not be verified against her campaign finance record and appears to be an invented figure layered onto an otherwise accurate underlying claim about her not taking corporate PAC money.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks led bipartisan efforts on a $35 insulin cap for privately insured patients
description: Miller-Meeks's documented record shows she voted against capping insulin costs and against a Democratic bill to cap insulin prices for Medicare beneficiaries, and there is no record of her leading a bipartisan effort on a $35 insulin cap for privately insured patients. Her own healthcare legislation (the Lower Health Care Premiums for All Americans Act) focuses on pharmacy benefit manager transparency and premium reduction, not an insulin price cap, and she has faced criticism for opposing insulin-cap legislation while accepting pharmaceutical industry contributions. This directly contradicts rather than merely fails to confirm the claim, since her voting record on insulin caps runs the opposite direction.

inaccurate_statement: She has secured provisions in the 2027 defense bill related to the Rock Island Arsenal
description: The claim references securing provisions in 'the 2027 defense bill,' but no FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act exists yet to have provisions secured in it — the most recent bills under consideration are for FY2025/FY2026. This claim appears to be a fabricated or anachronistic detail, as there is no legislative vehicle by this name for Miller-Meeks to have secured anything in. Without being able to run searches this turn, I could not find corroborating evidence, and the claim's premise (a 2027 bill already containing secured provisions) is inherently implausible given current legislative timelines, making it very likely fabricated or a significant date/attribution error.

inaccurate_statement: Her office says she secured $209 million for rural hospitals in Southeast Iowa in 2026
description: The $209 million figure refers to Iowa's initial statewide allocation from the federal Rural Health Transformation Program, deployed broadly to stabilize small-town clinics across Iowa (and including cancer research/prevention funding), not a sum specifically secured for hospitals in Southeast Iowa alone. The response narrows the scope of this statewide funding to a specific sub-region inaccurately.

inaccurate_statement: In 2022, she was one of only 12 House Republicans who voted for legislation establishing the $35 Medicare insulin cap; in 2026 she has continued pushing to extend similar protections to privately insured patients.
description: This directly contradicts her documented voting record. Available research shows Miller-Meeks voted against capping insulin costs, and reporting has noted she received a contribution from Eli Lilly's PAC on the same day she voted against legislation that would have capped insulin prices for certain Medicare beneficiaries. There is no support for the claim that she was among a small group of House Republicans voting for a $35 insulin cap in 2022, or that she has continued pushing to extend such protections to privately insured patients in 2026. Since the response presents this as one of the defining, signature aspects of what she is 'best known for,' this mischaracterization is significant enough to give readers a fundamentally wrong impression of her record on this issue.

inaccurate_statement: She served as director of the Iowa Department of Public Health from 2011 to 2014
description: Miller-Meeks served as director of the Iowa Department of Public Health from 2010 to 2013, not 2011 to 2014, per the biographical record.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has represented Iowa's 1st Congressional District since 2021.
description: Miller-Meeks was first elected to Congress in 2020 to the old Iowa 2nd Congressional District (pre-redistricting) and took office in January 2021. She has represented Iowa's 1st Congressional District only since January 2023, following redistricting. Describing her as having represented IA-01 'since 2021' conflates her time in the old IA-02 with her current district.

inaccurate_statement: In 2022 Miller-Meeks was among a small group of House Republicans who voted for legislation capping insulin costs for Medicare beneficiaries.
description: Miller-Meeks voted against capping insulin costs, not for it. This reverses her actual position on a notable and specific health-policy vote, materially misrepresenting her record on an issue central to the response's characterization of her as a bipartisan health-care dealmaker.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan supports expanding Medicare coverage for home health care for family caregivers
description: Bohannan's documented Medicare expansion proposal specifically adds dental, hearing, and vision coverage alongside a Medicare buy-in at any age. No source shows her campaign proposing to add home health care coverage for family caregivers as part of her Medicare platform; this substitutes an incorrect benefit category for her actual, well-documented position.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks voted for the PROTECT Taiwan Act and legislation addressing Iran as a state sponsor of terrorism
description: No record exists in Miller-Meeks's documented voting/legislative history of a 'PROTECT Taiwan Act' vote or specific legislation addressing Iran as a state sponsor of terrorism. Her documented record includes membership in the Taiwan Caucus and general support for countering Chinese influence and aid to Taiwan, and votes related to Iran conflict resolutions, but no source ties her to these two specifically named pieces of legislation. This is a narrow, specific claim that doesn't undermine the broader accurate point that she has a hawkish, pro-defense voting record, so it is minor rather than critical.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supports reducing administrative costs and increasing Medicare Advantage transparency
description: Miller-Meeks's documented healthcare-cost record centers on pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) transparency, price transparency legislation (the 'Prices on the Wall Act'), and her 'Lower Health Care Premiums for All Americans Act,' not a specifically named push for 'Medicare Advantage transparency' as a distinct cost-of-living mechanism. She has separately worked on Medicare Advantage prior-authorization reform, but framing this as her primary healthcare cost-reduction approach conflates several distinct initiatives into an imprecise composite that isn't clearly grounded in her stated platform.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's approach to water quality is more focused on infrastructure and investment than imposing new agricultural pollution controls, implying a clear, documented position on this tradeoff.
description: Miller-Meeks has no direct 2026 statement specifically addressing the nitrate/cancer-linked water crisis, and her documented water-related actions are limited to general infrastructure funding (like the Muscatine wastewater project) and a past call to roll back WOTUS regulation — a water-regulation position, not a nitrate-cleanup one. The response's framing implies a settled, deliberate policy contrast between infrastructure investment and agricultural pollution controls, when in fact this specific area is a confirmed gap in her record rather than a clearly articulated position.

inaccurate_statement: Mariannette Miller-Meeks is seeking a fourth term
description: Miller-Meeks is the sitting incumbent seeking a third consecutive term representing IA-01 (having first won the old IA-02 in 2020, then IA-01 in 2022 and 2024). In terms of overall House terms, this would be her fourth term in Congress overall, but framed in context as "seeking a fourth term" without clarifying the district change is a common but potentially confusing characterization; the dossier explicitly frames her as the sitting 3-term incumbent (her third term representing IA-01, fourth Congress overall). Since she is in fact serving her third term in the 119th Congress and running for what would be a fourth term in Congress overall, this claim is technically defensible depending on framing, but the more standard, dossier-confirmed framing is "third term" in the current district / fourth overall — flagging as a minor point of potential confusion rather than a clear reversal.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan explicitly supports nationwide paid family leave
description: There is no record of Christina Bohannan having a stated position specifically on nationwide paid family leave. Her documented platform focuses on lowering costs (tariffs, insulin, housing, price gouging), healthcare (Medicare buy-in, ACA subsidies, Medicaid), farm policy, and water quality, along with a Child Care Tax Credit expansion and Head Start slot expansion — but no source shows her taking an explicit position on a nationwide paid family leave program. Presenting this as one of her stated positions without hedging overstates what is actually documented.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks won by only about 50% in 2024, making IA-01 the narrowest Republican House win in Iowa that year
description: Miller-Meeks won the 2024 race by roughly 799 votes, about 0.2 percentage points, after a recount, not by "about 50%" as a margin figure — a candidate's vote share being near 50% is a different fact from her margin of victory being that large, and the phrasing here misleadingly presents her raw vote share as though it were her winning margin.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan is generally the more moderate candidate relative to her party
description: Available characterizations of Bohannan consistently describe her as progressive/liberal rather than moderate — a political ideology tracker labels her a 'Progressive Democrat,' and even her own pushback is that she isn't 'radical,' not that she is moderate. While she is deliberately campaigning with moderate economic messaging and rural outreach in 2026, presenting her as 'generally the more moderate candidate relative to her party' overstates and mischaracterizes her actual documented ideological positioning.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has generally been viewed as a relatively pragmatic/moderate Republican
description: This characterization is contested rather than a settled fact. While Miller-Meeks belongs to relatively moderate House GOP caucuses suggesting some fiscal centrism, she co-sponsored the Life at Conception Act and supported Iowa's restrictive abortion law, which critics and advocacy groups cite as evidence she is not moderate on social policy despite attempting to portray herself that way. Her 'moderate' branding is itself a disputed campaign narrative, not an independently verified characterization.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is generally the more moderate candidate overall on the left-right spectrum compared to Bohannan, including calling her 'the more conservative/moderate-right candidate' as though this itself establishes greater centrism
description: Characterizing Miller-Meeks as more moderate than Bohannan is a contested claim not well supported by the record. Miller-Meeks co-sponsored the Life at Conception Act and backed Iowa's restrictive abortion law, which critics and even neutral observers note undercuts her moderate branding, and her voting record includes votes for the 2025 reconciliation bill and against ACA subsidy extension. Meanwhile Bohannan has actively marketed herself as the pragmatic, common-sense candidate. Reporting frames the 'moderate' label for Miller-Meeks as contested political branding rather than settled fact, so presenting her as clearly more moderate without that caveat is a one-sided characterization, though it does not rise to a critical error since it is inherently a subjective framing question rather than a hard factual claim.

inaccurate_statement: Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks is currently the slight favorite
description: Recent 2026 polling (a July 2026 Bullfinch Group survey) actually showed Bohannan leading Miller-Meeks 40% to 35%, with independent Michael Bridgford at 11%, and nonpartisan forecasters like Cook Political Report continue to rate the race a pure toss-up rather than giving either candidate a lean or slight edge. Describing Miller-Meeks as 'currently the slight favorite' is not supported by the most recent available polling or forecaster ratings, which if anything have shown Bohannan with a modest polling lead while forecasters remain neutral.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has the incumbent advantage
description: While Miller-Meeks is the sitting incumbent, characterizing this as giving her a clear 'advantage' in this specific race is not well supported given that the two most recent matchups have been extremely close (a 799-vote margin in 2024) and the most recent 2026 polling found her trailing Bohannan, with nonpartisan forecasters rating the race a pure toss-up rather than leaning toward the incumbent.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan narrowly losing to Miller-Meeks in 2022 and 2024
description: The 2022 Miller-Meeks vs. Bohannan race was not close — Miller-Meeks won by about 7 points (53%-47%, roughly 20,000 votes). Only the 2024 race was narrow, decided by just 799 votes after a recount. Describing both 2022 and 2024 as narrow losses misrepresents the actual history of this matchup and could mislead readers about how competitive the district has been over time.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks previously served in the Iowa House
description: Mariannette Miller-Meeks's documented legislative career consists of one term in the Iowa Senate (District 41, 2019–2021). There is no record of her having served in the Iowa House of Representatives. This appears to be a factual error, though it is a narrow detail that doesn't change the overall accurate point that she has a longer government/elected-office record than Bohannan.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks served in the Iowa House before Congress
description: Mariannette Miller-Meeks served in the Iowa Senate (District 41, 2019–2021) before Congress, but there is no record of her having served in the Iowa House of Representatives. This appears to be an added, unsupported detail alongside her genuine Iowa Senate service.

inaccurate_statement: In 2024, Iowa's violent-crime rate was 243 per 100,000 and property crime was 1,297 per 100,000, and preliminary data show Iowa violent crime down about 4% and property crime down about 12% through March 2026
description: While Iowa's violent-crime rate of roughly 243 per 100,000 is consistent with figures referenced elsewhere as being well below the national average, no source in the available material corroborates the specific property-crime figure of 1,297 per 100,000 or the claimed 2026 preliminary year-over-year changes (down 4% violent crime, down 12% property crime). Available information instead references an 8% year-over-year increase in statewide property crime, which is inconsistent with a claimed 12% decrease. This is a narrow statistical detail rather than a claim central to either candidate's record.

inaccurate_statement: In 2024, Iowa's violent-crime rate was 243 per 100,000 and property crime was 1,297 per 100,000, and preliminary data show Iowa violent crime down about 4% and property crime down about 12% through March 2026

Available information instead references an 8% year-over-year increase in statewide property crime, which is inconsistent with a claimed 12% decrease. This is a narrow statistical detail rather than a claim central to either candidate's record.

inaccurate_statement: A 2026 analysis of IA-01 polling found that 42% of non-party-affiliated voters identified immigration as a priority
description: The only identifiable 2026 IA-01-specific survey with party-ID crosstabs on issue priorities (an Independent Center Voice/Bullfinch Group poll) shows immigration was ranked as the top pressing issue by only about 10-15% of independent/non-party-affiliated voters, not 42%. No survey or analysis matching this 42% figure for non-party-affiliated IA-01 voters could be found; this appears to be a fabricated or invented statistic that has recurred across multiple unrelated race analyses.

description: No evidence supports this claim. Miller-Meeks's own official House 'Border Security' issues page, which extensively details her immigration votes and cosponsorships, makes no mention of E-Verify, and she is not a cosponsor of the primary federal mandatory E-Verify legislation. This appears to be an unsupported addition to an otherwise accurate description of her enforcement-focused record.

inaccurate_statement: One 2026 survey of IA-01 voters found 42% of non-party-affiliated voters identified immigration as a priority issue
description: The only identifiable 2026 IA-01-specific survey with party-ID crosstabs on issue priorities (the Independent Center Voice/Bullfinch Group poll, July 2026) shows immigration was cited by only about 10-15% of independent/non-party-affiliated voters as their top issue, not 42%. No survey matching this 42% figure could be found for IA-01 non-party-affiliated voters on immigration; this appears to be a fabricated or garbled statistic not attributable to any real analysis of the race.

description: The only identifiable 2026 IA-01-specific survey with party-ID crosstabs on issue priorities (the Independent Center Voice/Bullfinch Group poll, July 2026) shows immigration was cited by only about 10-15% of independent/non-party-affiliated voters as their top issue, not 42%. No survey matching this 42% figure could be found for IA-01 non-party-affiliated voters on immigration; this appears to be a fabricated or garbled statistic not attributable to any real analysis of the race.

inaccurate_statement: One recent independent voter survey found that 42% of non-party-affiliated voters in the district identified immigration as a priority.
description: The actual 'Independent Center Voice' IA-01 district survey shows immigration was cited as a top pressing issue by only about 10-15% of voters (depending on subgroup), not 42%, and no crosstab in that survey specifically breaks out non-party-affiliated voters at 42% on immigration. This specific statistic does not appear in any identifiable poll or analysis of the district and appears to be a fabricated or garbled figure, though it does not change the broader accurate point that immigration is a real issue in the race.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supports mandatory E-Verify for employers hiring new workers.
description: No evidence supports that Miller-Meeks has backed mandatory E-Verify as part of her border/immigration platform. Her own official House 'Border Security' issues page and other detailed sourcing on her immigration votes and cosponsorships (SAVE Act, Laken Riley Act, Secure the Border Act, HALT Fentanyl Act, Mayorkas impeachment) make no mention of E-Verify, and no press release, vote, or statement ties her to advocating for it.

inaccurate_statement: One recent independent voter survey found that 42% of non-party-affiliated voters in the district identified immigration as a priority.

This specific statistic does not appear in any identifiable poll or analysis of the district and appears to be a fabricated or garbled figure, though it does not change the broader accurate point that immigration is a real issue in the race.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan supports restoring Medicaid funding and expanding benefits such as dental, vision, and hearing coverage
description: Bohannan's documented Medicare expansion proposal adds dental, hearing, and vision coverage as part of a Medicare buy-in plan, and separately she pledges to reverse Medicaid cuts to prevent rural hospital closures — but 'expanding benefits such as dental, vision, and hearing coverage' is specifically tied to her Medicare buy-in proposal, not a Medicaid benefits-expansion plan. The response conflates her Medicare dental/vision/hearing expansion with Medicaid, misattributing which program these specific benefit expansions apply to.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's healthcare agenda includes a $35 insulin cap for people with private insurance
description: There is no record of Miller-Meeks proposing or supporting a $35 insulin cap for people with private insurance. Her documented voting record shows she voted against capping insulin costs and against allowing Medicare to negotiate drug prices. The $35/month insulin cap is Christina Bohannan's stated proposal, not Miller-Meeks's. This appears to be a misattribution of the opponent's policy to Miller-Meeks, which could materially mislead a reader comparing the two candidates' actual insulin-cost positions.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks voted for the FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act
description: Miller-Meeks's documented 2026 defense-authorization vote was for the FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act (passed in July 2026), not a 'FY2026' NDAA. This is a narrow fiscal-year labeling error; the broader point that she voted for and secured provisions in that year's defense authorization bill is accurate.

inaccurate_statement: The League of Conservation Voters gives Miller-Meeks a 10% lifetime environmental score (6% for 2024)
description: This specific LCV scorecard figure for Miller-Meeks could not be verified against the available research, which found no quantitative LCV score for her in this research pass. While it is plausible given her voting record and general Republican alignment on environmental issues, the specific percentages cited are unconfirmed and should not be treated as a settled fact without further verification.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks' manufacturing approach is more closely tied to the Republican strategy of tariffs and reshoring, implying she has been a consistent proponent of the tariffs driving these outcomes without noting her documented internal tension on trade policy.
description: Miller-Meeks's record on tariffs and trade is more complicated than a simple embrace of 'tariffs and reshoring.' She has publicly framed tariffs as a negotiating tactic while also introducing legislation to cut fertilizer tariffs/duties, and she voted three times to block House consideration of ending Trump's tariff emergency declarations, including one specifically involving Canada, Iowa's largest trading partner. Independent reporting has tied her broader tariff support to higher input costs and depressed crop prices for farmers, a tension the response glosses over by presenting her position as a clean embrace of tariff-driven reshoring rather than a genuinely mixed and internally tense record.

inaccurate_statement: At a House Energy & Commerce hearing, Miller-Meeks described data centers as a driver of rising electricity demand and argued the solution is to build infrastructure faster and reform permitting, rather than restrict data-center growth.
description: No record exists of a specific House Energy & Commerce hearing statement from Miller-Meeks framing data centers this way. Her documented public comments on data centers are general remarks made outside a hearing context, stating that people are 'rightly concerned about water usage and electricity rates going up' and that data-center development 'needs to be done transparently' with 'community involvement' — a more balanced, transparency-focused framing than the response's characterization of her as simply pushing to build faster and reform permitting to enable unrestricted data-center growth. No dedicated statement addressing the in-district Clinton, IA data-center project was found despite research, and her actual general remarks reflect more nuance than the response conveys.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's platform emphasizes utility oversight, clean energy, and reducing energy costs, implying this is her stance relevant to data centers
description: Bohannan has no confirmed direct statement on data center development despite this being a live, high-salience issue in her district (the Clinton, IA QTS data-center controversy). While she does have general platform planks on utility monopolies and clean energy costs, presenting these as effectively her position on data centers implies a specific stance she has not actually taken, which is a documented, confirmed gap in her record.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has explicitly discussed data centers as a major driver of rising electricity demand and argues for faster permitting and infrastructure expansion to accommodate that demand
description: Miller-Meeks's actual documented public comments on data centers are notably cautious, not pro-expansion: she said 'People are rightly concerned about water usage and electricity rates going up... it needs to be done transparently. You need to have community involvement.' There is no record of her arguing for 'faster permitting' or framing data centers as something to accommodate via expansion; if anything, her quoted remarks emphasize public concern about water usage and rate increases and the need for transparency and community input, which is nearly the opposite framing from what the response attributes to her. This mischaracterization is central to the response's core recommendation and would materially mislead a reader shopping specifically on this issue.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks sponsored/co-sponsored legislation targeting opioid trafficking, described broadly alongside the HALT Fentanyl Act
description: The dossier confirms Miller-Meeks is a cosponsor of the HALT Fentanyl Act, which was signed into law, but it does not document a specific additional bill she sponsored or co-sponsored that is separately described as 'targeting opioid trafficking' beyond this. This is a vague, potentially overstated bundling rather than a clear fabrication, but the specific framing of multiple distinct measures isn't fully supported.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks voted for the 'Stop Chinese Fentanyl Act'
description: No record exists in Miller-Meeks's documented legislative history of a vote for or sponsorship of a bill by this specific name. Her confirmed fentanyl-related legislative record includes the HALT Fentanyl Act (cosponsor, signed into law) and cosponsorship of the Cooper Davis and Devin Norring Act (targeting online fentanyl sales) and the Securing the Border for Public Health Act, but no bill titled 'Stop Chinese Fentanyl Act' appears in her record. This is a narrow, specific bill-title claim that isn't corroborated, though it doesn't contradict her broader, well-documented record of supporting fentanyl-interdiction legislation.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is currently pushing a $35/month insulin cap for people with private insurance.
description: Miller-Meeks's documented insulin-related record is a vote against capping insulin prices for certain Medicare beneficiaries, and her signature health bill (the Lower Health Care Premiums for All Americans Act) focuses on PBM transparency, association health plans, and cost-sharing reduction payments, not a specific $35/month private-insurance insulin cap. No source shows her currently sponsoring or pushing a $35-per-month insulin price cap for privately insured people; that specific figure and mechanism is Bohannan's stated proposal (a $35/month insulin cap for all Americans), not Miller-Meeks's.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan proposes housing and childcare policies intended to make it easier for people to work.
description: Bohannan's campaign platform does include housing affordability proposals (increasing housing supply, restricting investor purchases of homes) as part of her cost-of-living agenda, but no documented childcare-specific policy plank tied explicitly to employment/workforce participation was found in her platform materials; presenting a childcare policy as part of her jobs-enabling agenda goes beyond what is confirmed in her stated positions.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has previously supported conservative immigration reform that combined stronger border security with legal immigration, work-visa modernization and a pathway to legal status for some unauthorized immigrants who meet conditions such as paying taxes and maintaining good conduct.
description: Miller-Meeks has genuinely supported legal-immigration measures like protections for Documented Dreamers and visa-backlog fixes, but her signature Dreamers legislation covers children of legal, long-term visa holders, not unauthorized immigrants. No specific Miller-Meeks proposal offers a pathway to legal status for unauthorized immigrants conditioned on paying taxes and maintaining a clean record; this appears to blend her real legal-immigration record with a broader, unsupported characterization.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan proposes policies to increase jobs and wages and strengthen organized labor as part of her cost-of-living plan
description: While Bohannan does mention continuing investment in organized labor and union-protected work hours as one bullet point within her broader affordability platform, this is a minor, passing reference rather than a distinctly emphasized wages/labor plank as implied by the framing here, which could overstate the centrality of union strengthening to her cost-of-living pitch.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is currently pushing a bipartisan bill to cap private-insurance insulin costs at $35/month
description: Miller-Meeks's documented healthcare legislation centers on the Lower Health Care Premiums for All Americans Act (PBM transparency, association health plans, premium reduction) rather than a specific insulin price cap bill; the available record shows she voted against capping insulin costs in a separate context, and no source confirms she is currently pushing a $35/month private-insurance insulin cap bill. This conflates her general PBM/price-transparency work with a specific insulin-cap proposal not documented as hers.

inaccurate_statement: She also secured $1 million to resurface Iowa Route G13
description: Miller-Meeks secured $1 million for Keokuk County Route G13, but this is described in the source material as a general county road funding item, not specifically tied to the same FY2026 southeast Iowa Community Project Funding cluster the response otherwise correctly cites; more importantly, the response conflates this with the $1 million project 'for the U.S. 6/Deer Creek Road intersection,' which is a separate, distinct project also totaling $1 million. Listing both as if they are two separate confirmed $1 million allocations without clearly distinguishing them risks double-counting, though both projects themselves are independently documented as real Miller-Meeks-secured funding.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's record includes sponsoring legislation to encourage body-camera use, improve training, and reduce chokeholds
description: There is no documented federal bill sponsored by Miller-Meeks specifically addressing police training or use-of-force reform such as chokehold bans. Her documented support for banning chokeholds and increasing implicit-bias training came from bipartisan legislation she supported as an Iowa state senator, not from congressional legislation she sponsored. Federally, she has supported (not authored) measures encouraging body-camera use and training, but claiming she 'sponsored' legislation covering body cameras, training, and chokehold reduction overstates and conflates her actual record.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan wants to invest in Iowa's clean-energy economy and increase federal resources and incentives for farmers and small businesses, as part of an 'industrial-policy and worker-oriented' unemployment plan
description: Bohannan's documented platform does emphasize farm-income support, clean energy for lower utility bills, and general small-business advocacy, but there is no confirmed itemized small-business or unemployment-reduction plan in her platform; framing this collection of general planks as a coherent 'industrial-policy' unemployment strategy overstates the specificity of her actual documented positions.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan emphasizes protecting unions and workers' bargaining power, arguing that good-paying jobs—not merely any jobs—should be the goal
description: Bohannan's platform mentions continuing investment in organized labor and 'union protected man hours' only briefly within a broader cost-of-living section, not as a central, defined pillar about bargaining power as described here; this overstates how prominent or developed this position is in her platform.

inaccurate_statement: A nonpartisan voter guide characterizes Miller-Meeks's economic position as favoring less government investment and regulation
description: No specific 'nonpartisan voter guide' characterizing Miller-Meeks's position in these exact terms is documented; while broadly consistent with her general pro-deregulation stance, this specific sourced characterization cannot be verified and functions as an unconfirmed citation.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's approach to reducing unemployment focuses on raising wages and lowering household costs, while expanding affordable housing, strengthening organized labor, and creating jobs through investment
description: Bohannan's official campaign platform centers on lowering costs (ending tariffs, capping insulin, price gouging), health care, farm policy, and water quality, with organized labor and wage increases mentioned only briefly as a passing item within her cost-of-living section rather than as a defined unemployment-reduction strategy. Her documented jobs-related statements emphasize opposing tariffs, vocational/technical training investment, and supporting manufacturing workers (e.g., John Deere layoffs), not a distinct platform centered on 'strengthening organized labor' and 'affordable housing' as unemployment-reduction mechanisms. This framing overstates and reorganizes her actual, more diffuse positions into a specific unemployment plan that isn't clearly documented as such.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks argues that urban runoff, not only agricultural runoff, contributes to the water quality problem.
description: No record exists of Miller-Meeks making a specific statement distinguishing urban runoff from agricultural runoff as a contributor to Iowa's water quality problems. Her documented water-related statements focus on working with farmers, the Iowa DNR, and agricultural officials on voluntary conservation, opposing WOTUS expansion, and securing wastewater infrastructure funding in Davenport and Muscatine — none of which include this specific urban-runoff framing. This appears to be an invented detail not attributable to her, though it is a narrow addition within a broader accurate point that she frames water quality around agricultural conservation.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has advocated regenerative agriculture and cover crops and proposed studying biochar for soil and water purification.
description: No record exists of Miller-Meeks proposing a study of biochar for soil and water purification, or advocating regenerative agriculture specifically by that term. Her documented water/agriculture-related positions emphasize voluntary, incentive-based conservation (cover crops, buffers, wetlands) coordinated with the Iowa DNR and agricultural officials, and she has no confirmed 2026 statement addressing the nitrate/cancer-linked water crisis specifically — this is a documented gap in her record. The specific 'biochar' proposal appears fabricated and not grounded in any known statement or bill from her.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has recently led a bipartisan effort to cap private-insurance insulin costs at $35/month
description: This inverts Miller-Meeks's documented record. She voted against capping insulin costs and voted no on a January 2026 bipartisan bill extending enhanced ACA premium tax credits, arguing against related subsidy/cost-control measures. There is no record of her leading a bipartisan effort to cap private-insurance insulin at $35/month; her actual healthcare cost approach centers on pharmacy benefit manager transparency and her own 'Lower Health Care Premiums for All Americans Act,' not an insulin price cap. This is a significant reversal of her real position on a key affordability issue central to the response's healthcare comparison.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's platform calls for investing in clean energy as part of her jobs plan
description: Bohannan's documented platform includes opposing cuts to clean-energy projects and framing them as job-preserving, and she has criticized Miller-Meeks's energy vote as damaging to Iowa's renewable sector, but there is no confirmed itemized 'invest in clean energy' jobs plank distinct from her general affordability/utility-bill messaging. This is a loose characterization rather than a clearly documented, itemized position, though it is broadly consistent with her overall record.

inaccurate_statement: Independent Center Voice reports 42% of no-party voters in IA-01 cite immigration as a priority
description: The actual Independent Center Voice IA-01 district survey found immigration was cited as the top pressing issue by only about 10-15% of independent/no-party voters, not 42%. No 42% figure appears anywhere in that survey's data tied to immigration among non-party-affiliated voters. This specific statistic does not match the real data from the cited source, though the broader point that immigration is a salient issue in the race has some support.

inaccurate_statement: Recent Iowa reporting suggests cancer has even overtaken cost of living in some statewide polling
description: No polling or reporting was found showing that cancer concerns have overtaken cost of living as a top issue in Iowa statewide polling. Available polling and coverage consistently show affordability/cost of living as the dominant issue, with cancer and water quality as a serious but secondary concern. This specific comparative claim does not appear to be substantiated by any identifiable source.

inaccurate_statement: Independent Center Voice reports 42% of no-party voters in IA-01 cite immigration as a priority
description: The actual Independent Center Voice IA-01 district survey found immigration was cited as the top pressing issue by only about 10-15% of independent/no-party voters, not 42%. No 42% figure appears anywhere in that survey's data tied to immigration among non-party-affiliated voters. This specific statistic does not match the real data from the cited source, though the broader point that immigration is a salient issue in the race has some support.
