description: Huizenga voted twice for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which CBO projected would result in roughly $900 billion in Medicaid reductions nationally over 10 years and which the Michigan Hospital Association projects will cost Michigan hospitals $6 billion in Medicaid payments over the next decade. Huizenga has defended these changes as reducing 'waste' rather than framing his position as preserving Medicaid funding for hospitals; describing his platform as focused on preserving Medicaid for hospitals mischaracterizes a record associated with substantial Medicaid cuts.

inaccurate_statement: Huizenga co-owns Huizenga Ready-Mix, a family gravel business in Zeeland
description: Bill Huizenga co-owns Huizenga Gravel Inc., located in Jenison, Michigan, not a business called 'Huizenga Ready-Mix' located in Zeeland. The business name and location cited are both incorrect, though the general fact that he has a family gravel-business background is accurate.

inaccurate_statement: A 2019 House Ethics Committee-related review recommended a fuller investigation into allegations involving Huizenga's campaign spending
description: The relevant House Ethics Committee matter (H. Rept. 118-541) was ordered printed and closed in June 2024, originating from a 2018 complaint, not a 2019 review recommending further investigation. There was also a separate 2019 FEC complaint that deadlocked 2-2 and was closed 4-0 with no violation finding, and a 2019 Office of Congressional Ethics referral is mentioned in the record, but the response's description of a '2019 House Ethics Committee-related review' recommending 'a fuller investigation' does not match the documented timeline, which shows the actual Ethics Committee review concluded in 2024 with no sanctions after finding 'no clear pattern of misspending.' The response also omits that this matter was fully closed with no sanctions, which risks leaving the impression of an ongoing or escalating investigation.

inaccurate_statement: In 2024, the House Ethics Committee concluded that Huizenga's campaign had inadequate recordkeeping that violated the House Code of Official Conduct.
description: The House Ethics Committee's 2024 report found 'no clear pattern of misspending,' concluded Huizenga 'generally acted within the bounds of the law,' attributed issues to 'a lack of knowledge or confusion about the applicable requirements,' recommended updated guidance, and closed the matter with no sanctions. It did not issue a formal finding that he violated the House Code of Official Conduct — the report's tone was explanatory/corrective rather than a violation determination, a materially softer conclusion than the response implies.

inaccurate_statement: Sean McCann is running in MI-04, but there is no comparable public documentation showing a consistent town-hall schedule for him
description: McCann has a documented history of town halls, community conversations, coffees, and open office hours as a state legislator, and other sources describe him as having the strongest documented record among MI-04 candidates for holding town halls and staying accessible to voters, including participation in an in-person town hall event in Saugatuck in August 2026 with other members of Congress. The response's claim that no comparable documentation exists for McCann understates his actual accessibility record.

inaccurate_statement: Sean McCann's town-hall/accessibility evidence is documented via sources that actually describe Diop Harris's events, not McCann's own
description: The response explicitly concedes its cited sources for McCann's accessibility claim actually document Harris's activity, not McCann's, undermining its own attempt to credit McCann. Separately, McCann does have a real, though only partially documented, record of accessibility (state legislative activity, town halls with other officials, and social media engagement) that the response fails to surface accurately.

inaccurate_statement: Rep. Jason Crow (D-CO) endorsed McCann
description: No evidence supports this endorsement. Sean McCann's own campaign endorsements page lists Whitmer, Benson, Schauer, Scholten, LiUNA Local 355, and other named supporters, but does not include Jason Crow, and no independent news coverage of McCann's endorsements mentions him.

inaccurate_statement: Jocelyn Benson is described as 'Michigan secretary of state Elissa Slotkin' — conflating the two officials' titles
description: Jocelyn Benson is Michigan's Secretary of State; Elissa Slotkin is a U.S. Senator from Michigan. The response's jumbled phrasing misattributes Benson's title to Slotkin's name in a way that garbles who holds which office.

inaccurate_statement: Hillary Scholten is described as 'U.S. senator from Michigan'
description: Hillary Scholten is a U.S. Representative (MI-03), not a U.S. Senator.

inaccurate_statement: Suzan DelBene is described as 'U.S. representative from Michigan'
description: Suzan DelBene is a U.S. Representative from Washington state, not Michigan.

inaccurate_statement: Mark Schauer is described as 'U.S. representative from Washington'
description: Mark Schauer is a former U.S. Representative from Michigan, not from Washington state.

inaccurate_statement: Sean McCann has garnered support from more than 50 local elected officials and community leaders
description: A direct review of McCann's own campaign endorsements page identified roughly 20 named local officials in Kalamazoo County/city government supporting him, not more than 50.

inaccurate_statement: Huizenga's PAC backing includes major contributors such as American Bankers Association PAC and Mortgage Bankers Association PAC
description: No record exists confirming American Bankers Association PAC or Mortgage Bankers Association PAC as specific contributors to Huizenga's campaign. The available financial data covers DTE Energy, CMS Energy, and general PAC/committee totals, plus industries like securities/investment, insurance, real estate, and commercial banking among individual donors, but does not document these two specific named PAC contributors.

inaccurate_statement: McCann's platform emphasizes expanding health-care subsidies
description: McCann's documented health-care platform centers on extending existing ACA tax credits and protecting/expanding Medicaid access, not on a broader 'expanding subsidies' framing; a distinct 'public option' or subsidy-expansion mechanism beyond the ACA tax credits is not confirmed as part of his stated platform.

inaccurate_statement: Huizenga's approach includes lowering utility costs through expanded domestic energy production
description: Huizenga has claimed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Palisades nuclear repowering provisions save Michiganders money on energy costs, but a partisan advocacy group's analysis disputes this, claiming the law's clean-energy tax credit rollback raises household bills over time; this is a genuinely disputed claim between two non-neutral sources rather than a settled fact, so presenting it as a clean, established fact is an overstatement.

inaccurate_statement: Huizenga favors greater state/small-business involvement in health care alongside HSAs
description: Huizenga's 2026 campaign site and official health-care materials do not articulate a specific HSA-based or 'state/small-business involvement' health-care plan; his campaign site is notably silent on healthcare, ACA, Medicaid, and prescription drugs, and his official House health-care page still uses dated 2017-era ACA-repeal language rather than a specific HSA/market-based mechanism.

inaccurate_statement: McCann has pushed tenant-protection legislation that would require landlords to correct serious health and safety hazards quickly, including potentially imposing penalties on landlords who fail to make repairs
description: The tenant-protection legislation described (mandating faster landlord repairs, penalties for noncompliance) matches Michigan's 'Tenant Empowerment Package,' which was introduced and championed by state Sen. Sarah Anthony, not Sean McCann. There is no record of McCann personally sponsoring, promoting, or advocating for this specific legislative package; his housing-related messaging is limited to general affordability language and past 'slumlord' crackdown comments from his time as a city commissioner.

inaccurate_statement: In 2026, McCann argued against Cleveland's continued use of Flock Safety license-plate readers, saying mass surveillance does not necessarily produce greater public safety and raises privacy concerns
description: No record exists of Sean McCann, a Michigan state senator running for Michigan's 4th Congressional District, commenting on Cleveland's use of license-plate reader technology — a matter entirely outside his jurisdiction in a different state. This appears to be an invented example with no basis in his documented public statements, and presenting it as one of his primary public-safety positions would materially mislead a reader about the actual content of his platform.

inaccurate_statement: McCann has stronger worker and tenant protections; has promoted a "Tenant Empowerment Package"
description: The Tenant Empowerment Package (mandating faster landlord repairs, rent deduction for repairs, tenant unions, and advance notice of rent increases) was introduced and championed by Michigan state Sen. Sarah Anthony, not Sean McCann. No evidence shows McCann personally promoted or championed this specific package; there is no record of him sponsoring or advocating for it.

inaccurate_statement: Huizenga backed efforts to preserve manufacturing jobs at Sun Chemical's Muskegon facility
description: No record exists of Huizenga supporting a Sun Chemical Muskegon facility jobs effort. Muskegon is also not part of Michigan's 4th Congressional District (it falls within MI-02/MI-03), so this example is both unsupported and geographically misplaced as an illustration of Huizenga's in-district manufacturing advocacy.

inaccurate_statement: J.C. Huizenga, one of the investors who acquired Howard Miller, is Bill Huizenga's son
description: No confirmed family relationship between J.C. Huizenga (chairman of Huizenga Group, which acquired the Howard Miller brand) and Rep. Bill Huizenga has been established. They share a surname but are documented as unrelated in available research, and Bill Huizenga's children are not identified as J.C. Huizenga. Asserting J.C. Huizenga is Bill Huizenga's son fabricates a father-son relationship and materially misleads readers into believing the congressman's own family financially benefited from the closure and relaunch of the plant his tariff support is being blamed for.

inaccurate_statement: Huizenga had taken the opposite position in 2018, warning that broad tariffs could cause West Michigan workers to lose their jobs
description: Available research found no substantive 2018 statement from Huizenga arguing that tariffs would cost West Michigan workers their jobs. The only related item found was a mild, non-substantive 2018 hearing comment expressing skepticism about recapturing a bygone manufacturing era, not an argument about tariffs raising costs or causing job losses. Huizenga's documented record shows him consistently defending and voting to continue tariffs rather than historically opposing them on cost grounds, so characterizing him as having taken the 'opposite position' in 2018 overstates and mischaracterizes the historical record.

inaccurate_statement: A July 2026 report, based on FEC records, says McCann received at least $57,600 since 2011 from the DTE Energy PAC and CMS Energy Corporation Employees for Better Government
description: The $57,600 figure comes entirely from Michigan state campaign-finance disclosures covering McCann's state Senate campaigns (2011–2023), not from federal FEC records. A direct FEC Schedule A search of his congressional committee found zero federal receipts from either PAC. Attributing this figure to 'FEC records' misrepresents the jurisdiction of the money at the core of the very question being asked, making the response's central factual premise inaccurate.

inaccurate_statement: The Guardian reported that Consumers Energy made a $2,000 contribution to McCann and another $1,500 contribution in 2025, while McCann was a Senate energy-committee vice chair and co-author of legislation concerning carbon sequestration, and that his office said the checks weren't received until November, explaining a reporting delay
description: No evidence exists of any Guardian report describing contribution-date/disclosure-date discrepancies for Michigan utility PAC donations or connecting such a story to McCann; this appears to be a fabricated report and fabricated details (including describing McCann as committee 'vice chair,' when he in fact chaired the Senate Energy and Environment Committee, and an invented carbon-sequestration co-authorship claim). The broader idea that McCann has received utility PAC money is accurate, but this specific sourced narrative is not documented anywhere.

inaccurate_statement: A 2026 investigation by The Guardian found that Consumers Energy's PAC made a $2,000 contribution to McCann, in addition to a $1,500 contribution recorded in June 2025, with McCann's office saying the checks were not actually received until November
description: No Guardian investigation of this kind exists. There is no record of any such report, and no corroborating source for a $2,000 or $1,500 Consumers Energy PAC contribution, or an explanation from McCann's office about delayed check receipt in November. The one confirmed, dated PAC contribution on record is a $2,500 DTE Energy PAC contribution to McCann's state Senate campaign in April 2021 — a different company, amount, and date than described here. This appears to be an invented source and invented factual details presented as the primary evidence for the claim being asked about.

inaccurate_statement: His 2026 congressional campaign had raised about $1.59 million by March 31, 2026, so the reported energy-industry contributions were a relatively small portion of his overall fundraising
description: The roughly $57,600 in energy-PAC money referenced is documented entirely in McCann's state legislative campaign committees (2011–2023); a direct check of his federal congressional committee's FEC Schedule A receipts found zero dollars from DTE or CMS Energy PACs. Framing the energy contributions as 'a small portion' of his 2026 congressional fundraising total incorrectly implies they are part of the same fundraising pool, when in fact none of that money went to his federal campaign at all.

inaccurate_statement: An older campaign document from his state Senate career also described maintaining funding for police and fire departments as a priority.
description: No such distinct 'older campaign document' from McCann's state Senate career describing police/fire funding as a priority is documented; the actual sourced statement on this topic comes from his current congressional campaign's issues page, which references his voting record 'In the Michigan Legislature' within the same current campaign material, not a separate older document.

inaccurate_statement: Republican opponents have accused McCann of having an anti-police record, pointing to his vote against funding school resource officers
description: No record exists of McCann voting against funding for school resource officers, nor of Republican opponents making this specific accusation. No such claim, vote, or attack line is documented; this appears to be an invented specific allegation.

inaccurate_statement: Republican opponents have accused McCann of...endorsements from organizations that have supported defunding law enforcement
description: There is no documented record of McCann receiving endorsements from organizations that have supported defunding law enforcement, nor of this specific attack line being used against him. His documented endorsers (unions, Giffords, DCCC, elected officials) do not fit this description, and no news coverage or opposition research alleging this was found.

inaccurate_statement: McCann's record may include votes for reallocating or limiting certain police-related funding
description: No evidence supports McCann having voted to reallocate or limit police funding; his direct, on-record position and voting history (fully funding police/fire, gun-violence-prevention measures) point the opposite direction, and no specific vote of this kind is documented.

inaccurate_statement: Political opponents have characterized McCann as aligned with Democrats who support 'open borders'
description: A dedicated search specifically for a Huizenga or NRCC 'open borders' or 'sanctuary'/'amnesty' attack targeting McCann found none — this is a confirmed absence of such an attack line against McCann, not merely an unfound one. The NRCC's national 'open borders' messaging this cycle targets other candidates in other races, not McCann.

inaccurate_statement: The Daily Beast reported spending including a luxury restaurant in Puerto Rico
description: The documented ethics-scrutinized travel spending includes Aspen, Montana snowmobiling, Florida golf/dining, and a Scotland castle trip (a separate official-travel matter) — there is no record of a Puerto Rico restaurant expenditure in the available material.

inaccurate_statement: The House Ethics Committee concluded in June 2024 that Huizenga's campaign had inadequate recordkeeping that violated House rules.
description: The Ethics Committee's actual findings were more equivocal than a clear rule-violation finding: it found 'no clear pattern of misspending,' concluded Huizenga 'generally acted within the bounds of the law,' and attributed some issues to 'a lack of knowledge or confusion about the applicable requirements' rather than a definitive violation of House rules. It recommended updated guidance rather than declaring a rules violation.

inaccurate_statement: The House Ethics Committee did find that his campaign violated House rules concerning recordkeeping
description: The House Ethics Committee's 2024 report did not make an affirmative finding that Huizenga's campaign violated House rules on recordkeeping. It found 'no clear pattern of misspending,' concluded Huizenga 'generally acted within the bounds of the law,' and only noted that some spending 'fell within unclear areas' of the regulations and that the campaign 'should have exercised more care' — it recommended updated guidance rather than declaring a rule violation, and closed the matter with no sanctions. Characterizing this as an affirmative finding of a rules violation overstates what the committee actually concluded.

inaccurate_statement: Most substantiated controversy: his campaign had House-rule violations involving recordkeeping and campaign-finance compliance
description: This restates the same overstatement noted above — the House Ethics Committee's 2024 closure found no clear pattern of misspending and imposed no sanctions, describing issues only as falling in 'unclear areas' of regulation rather than as a formal violation finding.

inaccurate_statement: McCann sponsored a proposed 'Tenant Empowerment Package' that would have required landlords to address serious hazards quickly
description: The Tenant Empowerment Package was introduced and championed by Michigan state Sen. Sarah Anthony (D-Lansing), not Sean McCann. No evidence shows McCann personally sponsored, authored, or was the public face of this legislation, though as a Senate Democrat he may have voted for it.

inaccurate_statement: In April 2022, an alleged sexual assault occurred at a political event associated with McCann, with former labor leader Jonathan Byrd subsequently charged with fourth-degree criminal sexual conduct, and Republicans raised questions about how Democratic officials handled the matter
description: No record exists of any such incident, criminal case, or named individual connected to a McCann political event. Dedicated research into McCann's controversies found no criminal charge, ethics-board finding, or election-authority sanction against him, and no such episode appears anywhere in the record of his conduct or controversies. This appears to be an entirely fabricated scandal that would seriously mislead readers about McCann's history.

inaccurate_statement: The Guardian reported that Consumers Energy made a $2,000 contribution to McCann around the time he was involved in carbon-sequestration legislation, with a timing/disclosure discrepancy noted by the Guardian.
description: No evidence exists that The Guardian published reporting on contribution-date/disclosure-date discrepancies for utility PAC donations to Sean McCann, or on a specific $2,000 Consumers Energy contribution tied to carbon-sequestration legislation. This appears to be a fabricated source attribution and invented detail; real reporting on McCann's utility-industry money has come from other outlets (e.g., Fox News, NRCC materials) discussing state-level PAC donations, not a Guardian investigation into contribution-date discrepancies.

inaccurate_statement: Huizenga has publicly said Medicaid should continue supporting people who need it, including mothers, children, and people with disabilities, and in 2025 he specifically said Medicaid should be protected.
description: Huizenga's documented position on Medicaid is more complicated than a straightforward protection pledge. He voted for the 2025 budget resolution and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which the CBO projected would produce roughly $900 billion in Medicaid reductions nationally and new work-reporting requirements, and his stated defense of these votes was that the cuts eliminate 'waste' while preserving Medicaid for those he considers genuinely in need — a defense of cuts, not an unqualified pledge to protect the program as the response implies. There is no record of a direct statement from him simply saying 'Medicaid should be protected' without that cuts-eliminate-waste framing.

inaccurate_statement: McCann's actual voting record is more informative than campaign statements (implying he has a relevant congressional voting record)
description: McCann is a non-incumbent challenger with no federal congressional voting record; his only voting record is at the Michigan state legislative level. Presenting 'his actual voting record' as available/informative context for this federal race without clarifying it is a state-level record only is misleading about what evidence actually exists for his federal candidacy.

inaccurate_statement: He worked on the staff of Rep. Peter Hoekstra from 1996–2002
description: Huizenga served as Director of Public Policy for then-Rep. Pete Hoekstra from 1997 to 2003, not 1996 to 2002.

inaccurate_statement: He served in the Michigan House of Representatives from 2003–2009.
description: Huizenga served in the Michigan House of Representatives from 2003 to 2008, not through 2009.

inaccurate_statement: He served as a staff member for U.S. Rep. Pete Hoekstra from 1996 to 2002
description: Huizenga served as Director of Public Policy for then-Rep. Pete Hoekstra from 1997 to 2003, not 1996 to 2002.

inaccurate_statement: McCann's campaign pairs lowering costs with getting federal spending and the national debt under control
description: No record exists of McCann's campaign platform framing deficit or national-debt reduction as a paired priority alongside affordability. His documented platform emphasizes tariff-driven cost increases, healthcare, and jobs, with no stated fiscal-responsibility/national-debt plank of this kind.

inaccurate_statement: McCann has highlighted democratic institutions and making government more responsive to constituents as a priority
description: While McCann's platform does include support for independent redistricting as an election/democracy-reform plank, no source shows him framing 'strengthening democracy' broadly or 'constituent responsiveness' as a top self-stated priority in the way described; this appears to be an invented or overstated characterization not tied to a specific documented statement.

inaccurate_statement: McCann's platform includes protecting Medicare (in addition to Medicaid)
description: McCann's documented health-care platform emphasizes protecting/expanding Medicaid, extending ACA tax credits, and lowering prescription drug costs; while a 10-point plan later confirmed a general pledge to 'protect Medicare,' this was scored as unsupported at the time it was checked against his campaign issues page alone, so it is treated cautiously here as a minor, narrow point rather than a fundamental mischaracterization.

inaccurate_statement: McCann wants to pursue stronger ethics rules to prevent politicians from personally benefiting from public office
description: No source describes an ethics-reform plank framed this way as part of McCann's stated platform on government reform; his documented reform position is limited to voting-rights protection and independent redistricting. This is a narrow, unverified addition rather than a claim that changes the overall picture of his platform.

inaccurate_statement: McCann has supported stronger protections for renters and penalties for negligent landlords, proposing a 'Tenant Empowerment Package' that would require landlords to address serious hazards quickly and allow rent withholding through escrow in certain circumstances
description: The 'Tenant Empowerment Package' (requiring faster landlord repairs, rent-deduction/escrow provisions, tenant unions, and advance notice of rent increases) was introduced and championed by Michigan state Sen. Sarah Anthony, not Sean McCann. No evidence shows McCann sponsored, championed, or publicly advocated for this specific package; it does not appear in his campaign materials or legislative sponsorship record.

inaccurate_statement: Current position: U.S. Representative for Michigan's 4th Congressional District, serving since 2011.
description: Bill Huizenga has represented Michigan's 4th Congressional District only since January 2023, following redistricting. From 2011 to 2023 he represented Michigan's 2nd Congressional District, not the 4th. He has been continuously in the U.S. House since 2011, but attributing 'serving since 2011' to his 4th District tenure specifically is inaccurate, even though the response does separately note he previously represented the 2nd District.

inaccurate_statement: The National Republican Congressional Committee has similarly called McCann 'Tax Man McCann,' accusing him of raising costs and 'lining his own pockets.'
description: The phrase about 'lining his own pockets' is documented as language McCann's own campaign used to criticize Huizenga ('he's working hard to line his own pockets while we fall further behind'), not language the NRCC used to attack McCann. Attributing this phrase to the NRCC as a criticism of McCann reverses who said it about whom.

inaccurate_statement: Huizenga's campaign characterizes McCann as someone who would 'rubber-stamp' Democratic leaders' agenda, rather than acting independently for Southwest Michigan.
description: The 'rubber stamp' characterization is documented the other way around: McCann's campaign has called Huizenga a 'rubber stamp' who is 'lockstep with Donald Trump.' No record exists of Huizenga's campaign using this framing against McCann, making this an apparent reversal of an actual attack line.

inaccurate_statement: In August, McCann specifically pointed to Huizenga opposing a congressional insider-trading ban
description: McCann's campaign did make this attack, but as of the most recent relevant vote (July 2026, H.R. 7008, the Stop Insider Trading Act), Huizenga actually voted YES in favor of a congressional stock-trading ban. His only 'no' vote on this type of measure was in 2019 (H.R. 2534). Presenting this as a current, unqualified fact about Huizenga's position is inaccurate unless attributed specifically to the 2019 vote.

inaccurate_statement: McCann alleges Huizenga is 'one of 13 House Republicans who voted against legislation banning members of Congress from trading individual stocks'
description: The 2019 vote on the Insider Trading Prohibition Act had 13 total 'no' votes, but only 12 were Republicans (the 13th was independent Justin Amash) — not 13 Republicans. More importantly, this is presented without any date qualifier, making it look like Huizenga's current position, when in fact on the actual 2026 congressional stock-trading ban (the Stop Insider Trading Act, H.R. 7008), Huizenga voted YES along with all voting Republicans. Presenting the 2019 vote unqualified as if it reflects Huizenga's current stance on a stock-trading ban is misleading.

inaccurate_statement: Huizenga has supported legislation that would restrict new spending measures that are projected to increase inflation
description: No specific legislation matching this description is documented in Huizenga's record. His documented fiscal position is a general argument that federal spending fuels inflation and that spending should be cut, but no specific bill restricting inflationary spending measures is identified in his record; he has in fact voted for large spending bills like the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that increased deficits, which cuts against this framing as literally described.

inaccurate_statement: Huizenga's approach includes lowering Medicare drug costs through reforms, with the broader Republican approach now including Medicare drug-price negotiations, and CMS currently negotiating another 15 drugs with prices taking effect in 2028
description: Huizenga voted against the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, which created Medicare's statutory drug-price negotiation authority, and his recent public statements emphasize negotiated agreements with individual pharmaceutical companies (e.g., praising the Pfizer/TrumpRx deal) rather than expanding or embracing that Medicare negotiation program. Presenting Medicare drug-price negotiation as part of Huizenga's own approach, without noting he opposed the law that created it, mischaracterizes his actual position.

inaccurate_statement: His campaign's current issues page does not spell out a detailed prescription-drug plan — such as specific proposals for Medicare negotiation, importation, or drug-price caps
description: McCann published a detailed 10-point affordability plan (via his official LocalCandidates.org position page) that explicitly proposes expanding Medicare's ability to negotiate drug prices and capping insulin costs at $35/month for everyone — specific prescription-drug-cost mechanisms that this response claims are absent from his platform.

inaccurate_statement: McCann would invest in energy infrastructure and support unions and workers as part of his jobs platform
description: McCann's campaign issues page does not contain a specific plank pledging to support unions and workers as a distinct jobs-platform element; his documented jobs messaging centers on manufacturing, tariff-driven closures, and attracting new businesses, without a specific union-support pledge found in his platform materials.

inaccurate_statement: McCann's platform includes investing in career and technical education to help residents train for skilled jobs
description: McCann's official campaign issues page does not mention career and technical education or workforce training as part of his jobs platform; this specific mechanism was not found in his documented platform materials.

inaccurate_statement: McCann supports small businesses and local economic development rather than relying solely on large employers
description: While McCann has a state-level record on small-business budget provisions, no federal-campaign statement framing this as 'rather than relying solely on large employers' was found in his platform materials; this specific framing appears to be an embellishment not directly supported by his campaign's stated positions.

inaccurate_statement: McCann has also supported extending Maple Hill Drive in Kalamazoo and other local transportation projects
description: The Maple Hill Drive extension is a local/county-level road project handled by the Road Commission of Kalamazoo County and other local entities; no source shows McCann has spoken about, advocated for, or otherwise supported this specific project beyond the state budget request figure noted separately. Treating this as evidence of ongoing support for 'local transportation projects' generally overstates what is documented.

inaccurate_statement: He is a Kalamazoo native
description: Sean McCann was born and raised in Detroit, Michigan, not Kalamazoo, per independent reporting from ICT News and Native News Online. He does reside in the Kalamazoo area and built much of his career there, but describing him as a 'Kalamazoo native' misstates his birthplace and upbringing.

inaccurate_statement: He served in the Michigan House of Representatives from 2003–2009
description: Huizenga served in the Michigan House of Representatives from 2003 to 2008, not 2003 to 2009.

inaccurate_statement: McCann's plan explicitly proposes expanding Medicare (in addition to protecting it)
description: McCann's campaign platform emphasizes protecting Medicaid expansion, extending ACA tax credits, and lowering prescription drug costs; it does not contain a specific pledge to expand Medicare coverage. Framing 'expanding' Medicare as one of his explicit platform goals overstates his documented position, which is better characterized as protecting Social Security and Medicare rather than expanding them.

inaccurate_statement: Sean McCann operated a small business
description: No source in the available material confirms that Sean McCann personally operated a small business; his documented career includes nonprofit executive-director roles (Vine Neighborhood Association, Kalamazoo Friends of Recreation) and Red Cross fundraising work, not business ownership. This specific claim appears to be unsupported by his documented biography.

inaccurate_statement: McCann's supporters point to his state-level legislative record such as helping craft balanced budgets
description: No record exists in McCann's documented state legislative record specifically crediting him with 'helping craft balanced budgets' as a distinct achievement; his documented record centers on Medicaid expansion, tax relief for working families, ending the retirement tax, clean energy legislation, and committee work on Appropriations, Energy & Technology, and Natural Resources. This appears to be an unsupported addition rather than a documented accomplishment.

inaccurate_statement: There is no evidence or widespread public record indicating that Bill Huizenga's congressional policies caused factory closures in West Michigan
description: This overstates the absence of evidence. The Howard Miller clockmaker plant in Zeeland (legitimately in MI-04) closed with over 130 jobs lost, and the company itself cited tariffs—a policy Huizenga has publicly and consistently defended and voted to continue—as one of several contributing causes, alongside inflation, rising interest rates, and industry decline. While it's accurate that no single Huizenga vote was shown to be the sole or primary cause of any closure, and no source ties the closure solely or primarily to him personally, the response's blanket claim of 'no evidence or widespread public record' omits this real, independently-confirmed, multi-causal example connecting tariff policy (which Huizenga supported) to an in-district factory closure.

inaccurate_statement: Discussions regarding industrial and energy infrastructure in Huizenga's district have centered on the J.H. Campbell coal-fired power plant, which faced a delayed closure due to federal grid-reliability orders, but this dealt with power generation and utility transitions rather than manufacturing plant closures
description: The response implies there is no significant manufacturing-plant-closure story tied to tariff policy in the district, but a real, independently confirmed closure exists: the Howard Miller clockmaker plant in Zeeland (in-district, ~100 years old) shut down with 130+ jobs lost, with the company itself citing tariffs as one of several causal factors alongside inflation, interest rates, and industry decline. The response omits this real, documented manufacturing closure and instead frames the district's industrial policy discussion as solely about the J.H. Campbell power plant, which is a different type of facility (energy generation, not manufacturing) and was kept open rather than closed.

inaccurate_statement: Implies McCann bankrolled his (congressional) campaign with energy-company support while pushing Michigan's 'Green New Deal', without clarifying the donations are from his state legislative campaigns, not his federal committee, and that 'Green New Deal' is not the bill's actual name nor was McCann its sponsor
description: The ~$57,600 (or 'tens of thousands') in DTE/CMS Energy PAC money is documented in McCann's state campaign committees, not his federal congressional committee — a direct FEC Schedule A search found zero federal energy-PAC receipts to his congressional committee. Additionally, there is no Michigan law officially named 'Green New Deal'; the actual legislation (Senate Bill 271 of 2023, branded 'Clean Energy Future' by its sponsors) was sponsored by Sen. Erika Geiss, not McCann, who chaired the committee that advanced it and voted yes on final passage but was not its sponsor or author. The response's framing, by failing to make these distinctions, repeats the core inaccuracy of the underlying attack line it is fact-checking.

inaccurate_statement: McCann's leadership PAC has collected money from corporate utility PACs like DTE Energy and CMS Energy
description: No record exists of Sean McCann operating a leadership PAC. The documented DTE/CMS Energy PAC contributions (roughly $57,600+) were made directly to his state campaign committees over his legislative career, not to any separate leadership PAC structure, which appears to be an invented detail (possibly conflated with his opponent, who does have such a structure).

inaccurate_statement: Huizenga faced FEC complaints filed by political opponents over allegations that his campaign failed to properly disclose tens of thousands of dollars in expense reimbursements made to his wife, his brother, and other family members
description: The documented FEC matter (Matter Under Review #7534) named James R. inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie argues that heavy regulatory red tape delays critical improvements on local corridors like Interstate 78 and Route 22, and focuses on redirecting funding to projects like Route 222 and Route 22

Characterizing his position as favoring highway planning that accommodates expanding commercial/logistics development misrepresents his actual, more restrictive stance on this issue.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie's approach centers on opposing commuter taxes and tolls, combatting inflationary spending, and streamlining regulations rather than infrastructure investment.

He also supports restoring passenger rail service to the Lehigh Valley with connections to NYC and Philadelphia. There is no documented statement of him opposing tolls or framing his infrastructure approach primarily around spending cuts and deregulation; his actual record shows active pursuit of federal infrastructure funding, not resistance to it.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie and his allies consistently oppose proposals that place additional financial burdens directly onto drivers, such as new highway tolls or bridge-user fees.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks plans to hold the EPA accountable to enforce stricter federal standards on pollution, sewage sludge, and industrial runoff associated with booming development

His documented immigration-related record centers on Homeland Security committee work, interior enforcement rhetoric, and support for the border wall and deportation of criminals, not a named state package with E-Verify, uncompensated healthcare reporting, and driver's-license invalidation provisions.
