description: This sweeping characterization, especially the claim of moderation on social policy, is not supported by Mackenzie's documented record. As a state legislator and congressman he voted for abortion restrictions, opposed treating abortion as a constitutional right, backed a state constitutional amendment stating abortion isn't a right, opposed LGBTQ nondiscrimination protections (the Fairness Act), and has stated marriage is between one man and one woman with 'no government' having authority to alter that definition — all solidly conservative, not moderate, positions. On labor/economic issues he has a very low AFL-CIO score, opposed a $15 minimum wage, opposed prevailing-wage protections, and supports right-to-work measures. While he has taken some bipartisan actions (e.g., signing a discharge petition on ACA subsidies, cosponsoring housing and PBM bills), presenting him as 'clearly' the more moderate candidate 'especially on social policy' inverts the actual, well-documented direction of his record on that specific dimension, which is materially misleading on the exact question being asked.

inaccurate_statement: Bob Brooks is a former president of the Pennsylvania Professional Fire Fighters Association
description: Bob Brooks was elected president of the Pennsylvania Professional Fire Fighters Association (PPFFA) in December 2021 and multiple contemporaneous sources (IAFF, City & State PA, Ballotpedia, PPFFA's own website, campaign materials) describe him as the current/sitting president of the PPFFA throughout his 2026 congressional campaign, not a 'former' president. For example, Ballotpedia states: 'In 2021, he was elected president of the Pennsylvania Professional Fire Fighters Association,' and City & State PA refers to him in April 2026 as 'The president of the Pennsylvania Professional Fire Fighters Association.' The claim's designation of him as a 'former president' misstates his status; the core fact of having led/leading the PPFFA is accurate, but the 'former' framing is a factual error about his current status. This is a narrow, minor error rather than one that changes the overall picture of his background.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks is currently the slight favorite, but PA-07 remains very much up for grabs
description: The claim refers to a candidate named 'Brooks' as the favorite in PA-07, but this is factually wrong. Ryan Mackenzie's actual 2024 opponent in PA-07 was Democratic incumbent Susan Wild, whom Mackenzie defeated in November 2024. Mackenzie has been the sitting U.S. Representative for PA-07 since January 2025. There is no candidate named 'Brooks' associated with this race in available search results. This claim appears to either fabricate a candidate name or conflate this race with an entirely different one, and it misrepresents the current status of the race (which Mackenzie already won, rather than an ongoing contest that is 'up for grabs' with a different frontrunner). This is a critical error because it fundamentally misstates who Mackenzie's opponent was/is and the current state of the race.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie is a former 12-year Pennsylvania state representative
description: Ryan Mackenzie served in the Pennsylvania House of Representatives from 2012 to 2024, which is 11 years (six terms), not 12 years. This is a minor numerical discrepancy that doesn't change the overall picture of his experience as a multi-term state legislator before winning his current congressional seat.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie served 12 years in the Pennsylvania House of Representatives (2012–2024)
description: Ryan Mackenzie's Pennsylvania House service is documented as 11 years and 6 terms (2012–2024), not 12 years. This is a minor discrepancy in a supporting detail and does not change the overall conclusion that he has significantly more elected-office experience than Bob Brooks.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie sponsored the Back the Blue Act
description: Ryan Mackenzie is a cosponsor of the federal Back the Blue Act of 2025 (H.R. 4310), not its sponsor — the bill's actual sponsor is a member of Congress from Nebraska. Describing Mackenzie as having 'sponsored' the bill overstates his role, though he has publicly backed and highlighted his support for it.

inaccurate_statement: Bethlehem and Easton had substantially lower violent-crime rates—175.0 and 176.0 respectively
description: No source could be found attributing this specific statistical claim (Bethlehem 175.0, Easton 176.0 violent crime rate) to Ryan Mackenzie. Searches for his statements, press releases, and campaign materials on crime in the Lehigh Valley turned up no such figures. Independent crime data sources (e.g., FBI-derived 2024 statistics compiled by AreaVibes) show materially different numbers—Bethlehem's violent crime rate is reported around 206 per 100,000, not 175.0—and no comparable figure for Easton matching 176.0 was found. Given the claim's high specificity (precise decimal figures for two named cities), a genuine statement or dataset would likely be discoverable if real. This appears to be a fabricated or invented statistic not grounded in any identifiable source or Mackenzie statement.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks favors better technology/faster visa processing.
description: No source ties Brooks to a position favoring 'better technology' or 'faster visa processing.' His official campaign platform page on immigration discusses securing the border, humane treatment of migrants, and pathways to citizenship, with no mention of 'visa' or 'technology' anywhere on the page. The closest related statement found, from a February 2026 podcast interview, has him saying enforcement should focus on serious criminals rather than everyday people, and that he supports streamlining the pathway to citizenship and adding more immigration judges to speed up long wait times — a proposal about court staffing for citizenship cases, not technology upgrades for visa processing. Since this is a specific, checkable policy claim that fails to surface any supporting evidence across his campaign site and multiple interviews, it appears fabricated or at minimum a significant mischaracterization of his actual immigration position.

inaccurate_statement: A recent survey had Brooks at 47% and Mackenzie at 43%.
description: Ryan Mackenzie ran in PA-07 against incumbent Democrat Susan Wild in the 2024 general election — there is no candidate named "Brooks" associated with this race. Search results confirm the actual matchup was Mackenzie vs. Wild, with polling (e.g., the Muhlenberg College/Morning Call poll) showing Wild leading Mackenzie 51% to 45%, not a 47%-43% Brooks-Mackenzie result. The claim references a candidate and poll figures that do not correspond to any verifiable survey in this race, making it a fabricated/misattributed claim that would materially mislead a reader about who Mackenzie's actual opponent and polling standing were.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie voted for $75 billion in additional ICE funding
description: Available records describe Mackenzie supporting roughly $150 billion in border/ICE budget investment, not a distinct $75 billion figure tied to a specific vote. The specific dollar amount cited does not match documented figures for his immigration-funding position.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie sponsored the Back the Blue Act
description: Mackenzie is a cosponsor of the federal Back the Blue Act of 2025 (H.R. 4310), not its sponsor — the bill was introduced by a Nebraska representative. Records also confirm there is no Pennsylvania state-level 'Back the Blue Act' that Mackenzie authored while in the state legislature; his actual state-level record on this topic involved creating the Keystone First Responder Award. Describing him as having 'sponsored' the Back the Blue Act overstates his role, which was as a cosponsor of a federal bill after joining Congress.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie sponsored the Back the Blue Act
description: Ryan Mackenzie is a cosponsor of the federal 'Back the Blue Act of 2025' (H.R. 4310), whose actual sponsor is a representative from Nebraska. Mackenzie did not sponsor or author this legislation; he supports and has publicized his backing of it, but describing him as having 'sponsored' it overstates his role.

inaccurate_statement: In a candidate interview, Brooks was particularly critical of infrastructure-heavy data centers and favored tighter/slower approvals
description: The knowledge base explicitly flags a near-identical claim as a confirmed misattribution: an AI-generated summary attributed a data-center 'self-generate power' remark from a primary debate to Brooks when it actually belonged to a different candidate, Carol Obando-Derstine. While Brooks does have a general platform statement about curbing warehouse/data-center growth on his campaign site, the specific framing here of a distinct 'candidate interview' comment being 'particularly critical of infrastructure-heavy data centers and favored tighter/slower approvals' does not match any documented direct statement and appears to conflate sources.

inaccurate_statement: Bob Brooks has not articulated as direct an anti-warehouse record as Lamont McClure.
description: Bob Brooks's campaign platform includes a fairly explicit, directly quoted anti-warehouse statement: he pledges to 'curb the growth of warehouses' and work with local officials to prevent warehouses and data centers from being built too close to homes and schools while preserving farmland, citing New Jersey as a cautionary example. Characterizing his record as lacking a 'direct' anti-warehouse position compared to McClure understates this documented, on-the-record platform commitment, though it does not reverse the overall accurate point that Brooks frames the issue somewhat differently (emphasizing project benefits/jobs) than McClure did.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie supports Gov. Shapiro's 2026 executive order tightening oversight of data-center development, including greater local authority and environmental/energy scrutiny
description: No statement from Ryan Mackenzie naming or addressing data centers, let alone endorsing Governor Shapiro's data-center executive order, has been found in his official House site, campaign materials, or press coverage. In fact, reporting has specifically noted this as a gap in his record, contrasting him with his mother, state representative Milou Mackenzie, who did make a public statement on this exact executive order in her own state-legislative capacity. Attributing support for Shapiro's order to Ryan Mackenzie is not supported and appears to conflate him with a different officeholder or invent a position he has not taken, directly undermining the response's central claim that the two candidates are closely aligned on data centers.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie sponsored the Back the Blue Act.
description: Ryan Mackenzie is a cosponsor of the federal Back the Blue Act of 2025 (H.R. 4310) after joining Congress in 2025, not its sponsor. The bill was introduced by a different representative (from Nebraska's 2nd district). This overstates Mackenzie's role from cosponsor to sponsor, though his substantive support for the bill's goals is accurately conveyed.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie sponsored the Back the Blue Act, which increases penalties for assaults on law-enforcement officers.
description: Ryan Mackenzie is a cosponsor of the federal Back the Blue Act of 2025 (H.R. 4310), not its sponsor — the bill was introduced by a different member of Congress. Describing him as having 'sponsored' the act overstates his role, though he has publicly backed and highlighted support for the legislation.

inaccurate_statement: Bob Brooks says data centers should generate their own power rather than heavily drawing from the existing grid
description: This specific 'self-generate power' requirement was said by primary candidate Carol Obando-Derstine, not Bob Brooks, according to direct debate-coverage sourcing. This is a known misattribution that has been specifically checked and excluded as inaccurate, and using it here as a central justification for recommending Brooks on this exact issue is a material error.

inaccurate_statement: Bob Brooks would use federal authority over electricity markets where possible to address data centers
description: Available reporting indicates Brooks himself has acknowledged that decisions about things like data-center development are largely local, which limits the federal government's role in regulating electricity markets or approvals — the opposite framing from the claim that he would lean on federal authority over electricity markets to address the issue.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie says he supports a pause on data centers, local zoning approval, and making data centers account for the electricity, noise, and infrastructure burdens they create
description: There is no located direct statement from Ryan Mackenzie (the PA-07 congressman) naming data centers by name or endorsing a pause, local zoning approval requirement, or burden-accounting policy. A direct search of his official House site turns up no mentions of data centers outside a transparency-study bill. This appears to be either a fabrication or a conflation with his mother, State Rep. Milou Mackenzie, who has made her own on-the-record statements favoring local control over data centers in her separate state-legislative capacity — those statements are not Ryan Mackenzie's. Attributing an entire restrictive policy position on the central topic of the question to Mackenzie when no such position exists materially misleads the reader about where he actually stands.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie has clearly hardened his position and now says a pause and stronger local control are needed
description: This repeats the same unsupported claim that Ryan Mackenzie has taken a specific restrictive stance (a 'pause,' stronger local control) on data centers. No such statement from Ryan Mackenzie has been found; his only documented data-center-adjacent action is a transparency/study bill on electricity pricing, not a policy of pausing or restricting data-center development. This risks conflating him with a same-surname family member or fabricating a position outright, which is central to the question being asked.

inaccurate_statement: Bob Brooks has argued that data centers should generate their own power rather than place heavy demands on the existing grid
description: This specific claim about requiring data centers to 'self-generate power' does not belong to Bob Brooks — it is a documented misattribution. The actual source of that position is Carol Obando-Derstine, a rival Democratic primary candidate and former electric-utility engineer, not Brooks. Brooks's own documented position is limited to curbing warehouse/data-center growth near homes and schools and holding developers accountable, without a specific self-generation requirement. Presenting this as Brooks's own stated position is a core factual error in a response whose entire premise is comparing the candidates' data-center positions.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie co-sponsored legislation addressing fentanyl in prison mail.
description: There is a real, specific bill addressing fentanyl smuggled through prison mail — the "Interdiction of Fentanyl in Postal Mail at Federal Prisons Act" (H.R. 5266 in the 118th Congress, reintroduced as H.R. 1046, the "Marc Fischer Memorial" Act, in the 119th Congress), led by Rep. Don Bacon. However, neither the bill's official press releases (which list named cosponsors such as Reps. Moore, Moskowitz, Cuellar, Horsford, Miller, Pappas, Weber, Fitzpatrick, Gottheimer, Lawler, Edwards, Malliotakis, D'Esposito, and Davis) nor Mackenzie's own official House press release listing all the fentanyl- and law-enforcement-related bills he co-sponsors (Fight Fentanyl Act, Protecting First Responders from Secondary Exposures Act, Combating Illicit Xylazine Act, etc.) mention Ryan Mackenzie as a cosponsor of this prison-mail-specific fentanyl bill. Mackenzie has cosponsored several other fentanyl-related bills, but no evidence supports this specific claim about prison mail legislation, and his own comprehensive list of cosponsored public-safety/fentanyl bills notably omits it. Because Mackenzie's broader record of supporting anti-fentanyl legislation is real and well-documented, this appears to be a narrow misattribution/fabricated specific rather than a wholesale fabrication of his stance on the issue, making it a minor rather than critical inaccuracy.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks supports speeding up visa processing.
description: Bob Brooks's official campaign platform page (brooksforcongress.com/issues) contains a detailed immigration section stating he wants a system that 'deters illegal entry and secures our border, while treating people humanely and give law-abiding folks a shot at earning citizenship,' but makes no mention of visa processing, visa backlogs, or speeding up visas anywhere on the site. Broader web searches (including issue-tracker summaries of his platform) likewise only turn up his positions on border security and a pathway to citizenship, with no reference to visa processing speed. Since this is a specific, checkable policy claim that would likely appear on his campaign materials if true, and no supporting evidence exists, it appears to be fabricated rather than a paraphrase of a real position. It is scored as minor rather than critical because it is a narrow add-on to an otherwise accurately characterized general immigration stance, not a claim that would change the overall picture of the candidate.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks wants to repeal Trump's tariffs on allies, arguing that broad tariffs are raising grocery and energy prices for consumers, and supports targeted trade policies that protect American manufacturing rather than across-the-board tariffs
description: Brooks has criticized Trump-era tariffs generally as raising consumer costs, but there is no record of him framing his opposition specifically around tariffs 'on allies' as a distinct policy position — that qualifier appears to be an invented specificity not found in his actual statements or campaign platform.

inaccurate_statement: In June, Mackenzie introduced a bipartisan bill aimed at lowering grocery costs by providing tax incentives for small independent food retailers in underserved areas
description: Mackenzie backed and cosponsored the bipartisan Grocery Affordability Act (H.R. 9378), which provides a 30% tax credit to qualifying independent grocery stores, butcher shops, and bakeries in food deserts — but he was a cosponsor of this legislation, not its introducer/lead sponsor.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie has helped secure more than $585 million in federal pandemic-era assistance for Pennsylvania health-care providers, including hospitals in the Lehigh Valley and Poconos.
description: Available reporting on Mackenzie's health-care-provider funding cites a figure of more than $103 million, not $585 million. The $585 million figure does not match documented sources on his office's reported health-care funding totals.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie calls Medicaid work requirements 'commonsense guardrails'
description: Mackenzie has repeatedly framed Medicaid/SNAP work requirements as "common sense" — his official House site states the budget "protects and strengthens Medicaid with common sense reforms—limiting benefits for illegal immigrants and adding work requirements for able-bodied adults," and in a direct quote to a reporter he said "These are common-sense work requirements again that are in place for every other human services program." However, no source found attributes the specific phrase "commonsense guardrails" to him — he consistently uses "reforms" or "requirements," not "guardrails." The core sentiment (he calls the requirements commonsense) is accurate, but the specific quoted phrase is not verified and appears to be an invented wording rather than an actual quote, making this a minor factual/quotation inaccuracy rather than a mischaracterization of his position.

inaccurate_statement: The November 3, 2026 PA-07 race is primarily a rematch between Republican incumbent Ryan Mackenzie and Democrat Bob Brooks
description: This is not a rematch. Ryan Mackenzie's 2024 race was against then-incumbent Democrat Susan Wild, whom he defeated by about one point. Bob Brooks is a first-time candidate for any elected office and has never run against Mackenzie before; he only became the Democratic nominee after winning a five-way primary in May 2026. Describing this as a 'rematch' misrepresents both candidates' electoral history and the nature of the race.

inaccurate_statement: The November 3, 2026 PA-07 race is primarily a rematch between Republican incumbent Ryan Mackenzie and Democrat Bob Brooks
description: This is not a rematch. Ryan Mackenzie's 2024 race was against then-incumbent Democrat Susan Wild, whom he defeated by about one point. Bob Brooks is a first-time candidate for any elected office and has never run against Mackenzie before; he only became the Democratic nominee after winning a five-way primary in May 2026. Describing this as a 'rematch' misrepresents both candidates' electoral history and the nature of the race.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks has 'no similarly specific proposal' comparable to Mackenzie's specific call for increasing highway capacity on I-78/I-476, and the comparison table states there is no similarly specific Brooks proposal for I-78/I-476 congestion
description: Bob Brooks's own transportation platform explicitly names Route 22, Route 33, and I-78 improvements as priorities, in addition to airport expansion and passenger rail restoration. The response's central claim and comparison table state that Brooks lacks a proposal as specific as Mackenzie's on I-78/I-476, but Brooks does have a direct, named-highway position that includes I-78 specifically. Since the entire premise of the response's 'bottom line' (that Mackenzie has the more road-specific plan) rests on this incorrect comparison, it materially misleads a reader about Brooks's actual platform.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie has an explicit plan for improving freight-rail safety, including grade crossings and infrastructure
description: No evidence supports freight-rail safety (grade crossings, track upgrades, derailment-prevention technology) as one of Mackenzie's stated infrastructure priorities. He does not serve on the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee with jurisdiction over rail safety, and his documented transportation record focuses on roads, bridges, and passenger-rail restoration, not freight-rail safety specifically.

inaccurate_statement: PA-07 covers all of Lehigh, Northampton and Carbon counties plus part of Monroe County
description: PA-07's actual composition (post-2022 redistricting) is the reverse of what's claimed: the district covers all of Northampton and Monroe counties, plus only part of Lehigh County. Carbon County is not part of PA-07 at all — it falls within PA-08. The claim incorrectly lists Carbon County as fully included, incorrectly states Lehigh County is entirely included (it's only partial), and incorrectly states Monroe is only partial (it's fully included). This is a significant geographic/factual error about the district's composition that would mislead readers about which counties and voters the district represents.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie also emphasizes freight-rail improvements, including grade-crossing safety and track upgrades, partly as a way of reducing truck/road congestion
description: No evidence supports Mackenzie advocating for freight-rail safety, grade-crossing improvements, or track upgrades. His documented transportation priorities focus on roads, bridges, and highway/pedestrian funding, and he does not serve on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee's rail-safety jurisdiction. This appears to be a fabricated addition to his actual transportation record.

inaccurate_statement: PA-07 covers all of Lehigh, Northampton and Carbon counties plus part of Monroe County
description: Under Pennsylvania's current congressional map (in effect since the 2022 elections and used in Ryan Mackenzie's 2024 election to PA-07), the district consists of all of Lehigh, Northampton, and Carbon counties, but it does not include any part of Monroe County. Monroe County is instead part of PA-08, represented by a different member of Congress. The claim correctly identifies Lehigh, Northampton, and Carbon as fully included, but incorrectly adds Monroe County as partially included. This is a narrow geographic error that doesn't undermine the overall point that PA-07 covers the Lehigh Valley area, so it is a minor rather than critical inaccuracy.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie sponsored the Back the Blue Act, which would increase penalties for assaulting or killing law-enforcement officers and expand certain firearms-carry rights for active and retired officers
description: Ryan Mackenzie is a cosponsor of the federal Back the Blue Act (H.R. 4310) in the 119th Congress, not its sponsor — the bill was introduced by a different member of Congress. Describing him as having 'sponsored' the bill overstates his role, though his substantive support for the legislation and its tougher-penalty provisions is accurate.

inaccurate_statement: His record includes sponsoring the Back the Blue Act
description: Ryan Mackenzie is a cosponsor of the federal Back the Blue Act of 2025 (H.R. 4310), not its sponsor — the bill was introduced by a member of Congress from Nebraska. Describing Mackenzie as having sponsored this legislation overstates his role in it.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie is sponsoring the Back the Blue Act
description: Ryan Mackenzie is a cosponsor of the federal Back the Blue Act of 2025 (H.R. 4310), not its sponsor — the bill's actual lead sponsor is a member from Nebraska. Describing Mackenzie as 'sponsoring' this bill overstates his role, though his support for it is genuine.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie has sponsored legislation providing mortgage assistance for teachers and first responders
description: The proposal for VA-style zero-down mortgage assistance for teachers, nurses, and first responders (the HELPER Act) is part of Bob Brooks's housing platform, not Ryan Mackenzie's. Mackenzie's documented housing initiatives are the Make American Housing Affordable (MAHA) Act, co-introduced with Rep. Tom Kean Jr., and a separate Housing Affordability Tax Credit bill offering a $5,000/$10,000 tax credit for primary-home purchasers generally — neither is targeted specifically at teachers or first responders. This appears to conflate Brooks's proposal with Mackenzie's record.

inaccurate_statement: Reuters reported 68,000 fewer U.S. manufacturing jobs from January 2025 through May 2026
description: The 68,000 figure was an earlier BLS estimate covering roughly Trump's first year in office and was already revised upward to 108,000 by early 2026; by May 2026 manufacturing employment had actually gained about 7,000 jobs that month, and cumulative losses since inauguration were later reported around 75,000. No Reuters report combining '68,000 jobs' with a 'through May 2026' timeframe and declining truck production has been found. This is a national economic statistic used as background context rather than a claim central to either candidate's record.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks supports job training in manufacturing, construction and clean-energy industries, according to his campaign's policy positions summarized by MoveOn
description: The underlying claim that Brooks supports job training in manufacturing, construction and clean-energy sectors matches his campaign platform, but attributing this summary specifically to MoveOn is unsupported — MoveOn's current Pennsylvania endorsement/issue pages do not list Brooks or PA-07, and no record connects MoveOn to summarizing his platform. This is a narrow sourcing detail, not a claim that changes the substance of his position.

inaccurate_statement: Reuters reported 68,000 fewer U.S. manufacturing jobs from January 2025 through May 2026
description: The 68,000 figure was an earlier BLS estimate covering roughly Trump's first year in office and was already revised upward to 108,000 by early 2026; by May 2026 manufacturing employment had actually gained about 7,000 jobs that month, and cumulative losses since inauguration were later reported around 75,000. No Reuters report combining '68,000 jobs' with a 'through May 2026' timeframe and declining truck production has been found. This is a national economic statistic used as background context rather than a claim central to either candidate's record.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie supports Gov. Shapiro's August executive order slowing data-center approvals and giving local communities more authority
description: Ryan Mackenzie has no located direct statement naming data centers as a policy target, and no evidence he has commented on or supported Governor Shapiro's data-center executive order. This appears to be exactly the kind of fabrication/conflation previously identified, where statements or positions by his mother Milou Mackenzie, a Pennsylvania state representative, get incorrectly attributed to Ryan Mackenzie, or where a data-center quote is invented outright. Ryan Mackenzie's own record shows no comment on this executive order.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie currently supports Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro's new restrictions/oversight on large data-center projects in the Lehigh Valley
description: No direct statement from Ryan Mackenzie supporting Governor Shapiro's data-center restrictions has been found. Mackenzie's own congressional website contains no statements naming data centers as a policy target, and a direct site search turns up nothing on the topic beyond an unrelated electricity-transparency bill. It is his mother, State Representative Milou Mackenzie, who has publicly criticized unrestricted data-center growth and referenced Shapiro's executive order — a statement that belongs to her, not to Congressman Ryan Mackenzie. Attributing a data-center policy position to Ryan Mackenzie appears to conflate him with his mother, a distinct public official with the same surname.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie supports Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro's recent measures increasing oversight of data-center development
description: No statement from Ryan Mackenzie (the PA-07 congressman) endorsing Gov. Shapiro's data-center oversight order or any data-center policy by name has been found; a direct search of his official site turns up no mention of data centers outside an unrelated transparency bill. It is his mother, State Rep. Milou Mackenzie, who publicly commented on Shapiro's data-center order — a distinct person in a different office — and that statement should not be attributed to the congressman. Presenting Ryan Mackenzie as supporting Shapiro's data-center measures conflates the two officials and asserts a position for which no supporting record exists.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks proposes capping out-of-pocket medical costs
description: No source in the available material documents Bob Brooks proposing a specific cap on out-of-pocket medical costs. His documented healthcare platform includes Medicare-for-All-style expanded coverage, negotiating drug prices, and reducing insulin/beta-blocker costs, but a distinct 'capping out-of-pocket costs' proposal is not corroborated.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie has sponsored the Back the Blue Act.
description: Ryan Mackenzie is a cosponsor of the federal Back the Blue Act (H.R. 4310) in the 119th Congress, not its original sponsor — that bill was introduced by a representative from Nebraska's 2nd district. Mackenzie's support for tougher penalties for assaults on law enforcement and expanded firearm-carrying rights for officers is accurate, but describing him as having 'sponsored' rather than cosponsored the bill overstates his role.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie sponsored the Back the Blue Act
description: Ryan Mackenzie is a cosponsor of the federal Back the Blue Act (H.R. 4310) introduced in the 119th Congress, not its sponsor. The bill's actual sponsor is a representative from Nebraska's 2nd district; Mackenzie joined as a cosponsor after taking office in 2025. Describing him as having 'sponsored' the bill overstates his role in originating this legislation.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie has advocated for freight rail connections as part of his transportation priorities
description: No evidence supports Mackenzie advocating for freight-rail improvements, grade-crossing safety, or freight connections; his documented transportation priorities focus on roads, bridges, and highway capacity, not freight rail, and he does not serve on the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee. This appears to be an unsupported addition to his actual transportation record.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie's current platform is less specific about new housing-supply policies
description: Mackenzie actually has a fairly concrete, specific housing agenda, including co-introducing the Make American Housing Affordable (MAHA) Act and a separate Housing Affordability Tax Credit bill, and has cited specific Allentown-area data (rents up 45%, home prices up 64% since the pandemic). Characterizing his housing platform as vague or unspecific compared to Brooks's is not supported and understates a documented, concrete part of his platform.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks has been endorsed by the League of Conservation Voters Action Fund, which specifically frames its agenda around lowering energy costs and expanding clean energy
description: The League of Conservation Voters (LCV) Action Fund is a progressive environmental advocacy organization that has a long-standing, well-documented pattern of endorsing almost exclusively Democratic candidates and frequently opposing Republican candidates based on their environmental voting records via its 'Dirty Dozen' campaigns. Bob Brooks is the Republican candidate/nominee in PA-07. There is no credible basis to expect LCV Action Fund would endorse a Republican candidate in a competitive race, and no evidence supports this specific endorsement claim. This appears to be a fabricated or misattributed endorsement claim that, if false, would materially mislead readers about Brooks's environmental positioning and coalition support.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie's housing proposal is less specific than Brooks's, with Mackenzie only saying housing, transportation and energy-permitting legislation can reduce costs over the long run
description: Ryan Mackenzie has a concrete, detailed housing agenda that includes co-introducing the Make American Housing Affordable (MAHA) Act with Rep. Tom Kean Jr. and a separate Housing Affordability Tax Credit bill, complete with specific dollar figures ($5,000 individual/$10,000 joint filer tax credits) and cited local data (Allentown rents up 45%, home prices up 64% since the pandemic). Characterizing his housing plan as vague or less specific than Brooks's, rather than acknowledging it as a named, detailed legislative proposal, misrepresents his actual record on this issue.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie voted in January 2026 to restore ACA premium tax credits after previously voting for funding packages that didn't extend them.
description: Mackenzie's break from House GOP leadership on ACA premium tax credits is documented as signing a Democratic-led discharge petition on December 17, 2025 for a 3-year clean extension of the credits — not a January 2026 vote to 'restore' them. The general direction (breaking ranks to support extending ACA subsidies) is accurate, but the specific date and legislative mechanism described are incorrect.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie sponsored the Back the Blue Act.
description: Mackenzie is a cosponsor, not the sponsor, of the federal Back the Blue Act of 2025 (H.R. 4310), which was introduced by a member of Congress from Nebraska's 2nd district. Mackenzie joined Congress in 2025 and signed on as a cosponsor after the bill's introduction. Describing him as having 'sponsored' the bill overstates his role, though his general support for tougher penalties for crimes against law enforcement is accurately characterized elsewhere in his record.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie... sponsored the Back the Blue Act, which would increase penalties for assaulting or killing law-enforcement officers
description: Ryan Mackenzie is a cosponsor of the federal Back the Blue Act (H.R. 4310, 119th Congress), not its sponsor. The bill's actual sponsor is a representative from Nebraska's 2nd district, and Mackenzie joined as a cosponsor after entering Congress in 2025. Describing him as having 'sponsored' the bill overstates his role, though the substance of his support for the legislation is accurate.

inaccurate_statement: One legislative tracker records Mackenzie voting for 25 of 25 bills categorized as 'Crime and Law Enforcement' during his House tenure
description: No legislative tracker found in search (Congress.gov, GovTrack, Legisletter.org, Ballotpedia) records a '25 of 25' voting statistic for Mackenzie specifically categorized as 'Crime and Law Enforcement.' Congress.gov does tag 14 pieces of sponsored/cosponsored legislation under that policy area, but this is unrelated to a vote count of 25/25. Legisletter.org, a legislator-tracking site, does not categorize Mackenzie's votes by 'Crime and Law Enforcement' at all, and lists his focus areas as taxation, immigration, and national security. GovTrack tracks missed votes generally, not by policy category in this way. This specific, checkable statistic does not appear to exist on any tracker, suggesting it was fabricated. However, this is a narrow, specific statistical embellishment rather than a claim that fundamentally mischaracterizes Mackenzie's record or positions, so severity is minor rather than critical.

inaccurate_statement: Bob Brooks favors better technology as part of his border-security approach
description: Bob Brooks's official campaign platform (brooksforcongress.com), corroborated by BallotReady and other election-tracker summaries, describes his border-security position solely in terms of deterring illegal entry, securing the border, treating migrants humanely, and creating a pathway to citizenship. There is no mention of 'technology' as part of his border-security approach in his platform statement, campaign press releases, or any news coverage found. This specific detail does not appear to be part of his actual stated position, though the broader claim that he supports border security generally is accurate. Given the claim adds a specific, unverified detail not found anywhere in his platform, it is best characterized as a minor fabrication that doesn't undermine the broader accurate characterization of his border stance.

inaccurate_statement: Both Mackenzie and Brooks currently support Pennsylvania's effort to increase oversight of data centers, including requiring them to account for their power needs and giving local authorities more say
description: No direct statement from Ryan Mackenzie naming or addressing data centers, supporting increased oversight, or requiring them to account for power needs has been found. Research specifically confirms this is a genuine gap in his record — he has no located position on data centers by name, and a similar fabricated data-center quote attributed to 'Mackenzie' was previously identified as a hallucination during research on this exact topic. It is Mackenzie's mother, state representative Milou Mackenzie, who has made public statements supporting local control over data centers, not Ryan Mackenzie. Presenting this as a shared, confirmed position of both candidates create a false equivalence and inaccurately attributes a specific policy stance to Ryan Mackenzie that he has not taken.

inaccurate_statement: Bob Brooks appears stronger on explicit small-business support
description: Research on Brooks's platform found no direct statement from him addressing small-business policy specifically — his lawn-care business surfaces only as personal biography, never as the basis for a small-business platform (no stated position on small-business taxes, regulation, or lending). By contrast, Ryan Mackenzie has a confirmed record of explicit small-business support, including hosting a joint visit with SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler to Lehigh County business owners, a Chamber of Commerce tax-reform roundtable focused on small businesses, an NFIB 'Guardian of Small Business' award, and promotion of the 20% qualified-business-income deduction. This response's central claim reverses the documented reality of which candidate has an established small-business record.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks has specifically campaigned on economic development and small businesses
description: Brooks has general economic-development and 'good local jobs' talking points, but no sourced statement specifically addressing small-business policy was found — this is a confirmed, genuine gap in his platform research, not a documented campaign focus.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks has explicitly argued that data centers should generate their own power, rather than shifting infrastructure and electricity costs onto ordinary ratepayers.
description: This specific claim traces to a quote made by a different Democratic primary candidate, Carol Obando-Derstine, not Bob Brooks. Brooks's actual documented position on data centers focuses on curbing warehouse/data-center growth near homes and schools and holding developers accountable to communities, not requiring data centers to self-generate power. This misattribution is central to the response's entire argument that Brooks has the more restrictive position.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks' proposal that data centers pay their own way for power goes beyond merely supporting the new state rules.
description: This repeats and builds on the same misattributed 'self-generate power' claim, which actually belongs to a different candidate (Carol Obando-Derstine) from the Democratic primary, not Bob Brooks.

inaccurate_statement: The PA-07 race is currently a competitive Brooks–Mackenzie rematch.
description: This is not a rematch. Ryan Mackenzie defeated then-incumbent Democrat Susan Wild in November 2024; Bob Brooks is a first-time candidate for any office and has never previously run against Mackenzie. Describing 2026 as a 'rematch' mischaracterizes the electoral history of the race.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie has also recently taken a tougher position than a simple pro-development stance. He supports Shapiro's executive order and has publicly pushed back against criticism of residents who question data-center projects.
description: Ryan Mackenzie, the PA-07 congressman, has no located direct statement naming data centers by name, and a direct search of his official House website finds zero pages mentioning 'data center' outside of an unrelated electricity-transparency bill. A similar AI-generated fabrication attributing a data-center quote to 'Mackenzie' was previously identified as tracing to no real, findable source from either Ryan Mackenzie or his mother, state representative Milou Mackenzie. There is no record of Mackenzie supporting Shapiro's executive order on data centers or publicly defending residents who question data-center projects.

inaccurate_statement: Both major-party candidates now support stronger oversight [of data centers], so this isn't a straightforward pro- vs. anti-data-center race.
description: This claim rests on the fabricated assertion that Mackenzie supports Shapiro's data-center executive order; no such position by Mackenzie has been documented, so the framing that both candidates now share similar oversight positions is unsupported.

inaccurate_statement: The PA-07 race is currently a competitive Brooks–Mackenzie rematch.
description: This is not a rematch. Ryan Mackenzie defeated then-incumbent Democrat Susan Wild in November 2024; Bob Brooks is a first-time candidate for any office and has never previously run against Mackenzie. Describing 2026 as a 'rematch' mischaracterizes the electoral history of the race.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie has said there needs to be a pause to figure out who pays for the enormous electricity demand, has backed Shapiro's new guardrails, and in a recent interview said communities need to determine how data centers will pay for the electricity they consume
description: No direct statement from Ryan Mackenzie naming data centers as a policy target, calling for a 'pause,' or endorsing Governor Shapiro's data-center guardrails has been found, despite repeated searches of his official House site, campaign materials, and news coverage. A direct site-search of his official House page returns no pages mentioning data centers apart from an unrelated electricity-transparency bill, and coverage of the nearby Project Atlas data-center controversy specifically noted the absence of any Mackenzie quote on the topic. A prior instance of an AI research tool fabricating a similar Mackenzie data-center quote has already been identified and flagged as unreliable. Attributing a specific 'recent interview' comment and a policy shift toward supporting new restrictions to Mackenzie when no such statement exists significantly misrepresents his actual, undocumented position on the central topic of the question.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks joined Mackenzie in responding to Gov. Josh Shapiro's new data-center rules
description: Ryan Mackenzie, the PA-07 congressman, has no located direct statement naming data centers by name or responding to Governor Shapiro's data-center executive order. The only Mackenzie to publicly react to that specific policy was his mother, State Representative Milou Mackenzie, in her separate state-legislative capacity — a statement that must not be attributed to Ryan. Claiming Ryan Mackenzie 'joined' in responding to the data-center rules appears to conflate the two Mackenzies and misrepresents Ryan's actual public record, which contains no data-center-specific statement.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie has generally taken a more pro-development approach on data centers
description: Ryan Mackenzie has no documented direct statement on data centers specifically, either supporting or opposing their development; this is a confirmed research gap, not evidence of an affirmatively pro-development stance. Coverage instead frames him as caught between the Trump administration's energy agenda and local constituent opposition, without a clear personal position on record.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie held a district-wide telephone town hall event in July 2026 where residents could ask questions directly
description: The documented large-turnout telephone town hall matching this description took place on July 23, 2025 (drawing 7,000+ participants), not in July 2026. No July 2026 telephone town hall of this description is documented. This appears to be an off-by-one-year date error rather than a fabricated event, since Mackenzie's practice of holding telephone town halls is real and well-documented.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie held a district-wide telephone town hall in July 2026 where residents could ask questions
description: The documented telephone town hall drawing large participation (7,000+ callers) occurred on July 23, 2025, not July 2026. The response appears to have misdated this event by a year.

inaccurate_statement: The Democratic primary candidates participated in a February town-hall-style event
description: Bob Brooks is a Republican candidate/officeholder associated with PA-07, not a Democratic primary candidate. The claim describes Democratic primary candidates participating in a February town-hall event, which does not pertain to Bob Brooks at all. Attributing this event or characterization to Bob Brooks conflates him with candidates from the opposing party's primary, making this a clear misattribution that would mislead a reader about which race and which candidates were involved.

inaccurate_statement: Bob Brooks has repeatedly said he does not accept corporate PAC contributions, and takes no corporate PAC money according to his campaign.
description: Reporting from a PA-07 primary debate directly contradicts this claim: Brooks was confronted for having taken in more PAC money than the other three candidates despite having suggested he'd like to ban PAC money in politics. Rather than denying taking corporate PAC money, he defended accepting it ('Don't hate the player, hate the game... you can't fund a campaign on 20 bucks'). There is no evidence he signed a no-corporate-PAC pledge or that his campaign claims to take no corporate PAC money; the available evidence shows the opposite is true. This is a critical inaccuracy because it reverses the actual fact pattern about his campaign finance practices.

inaccurate_statement: MoveOn has endorsed Brooks
description: No evidence supports a MoveOn endorsement of Bob Brooks in PA-07. MoveOn's own current Pennsylvania endorsements list PA-1, PA-3, PA-8, and PA-12 candidates but not Brooks, and Brooks's own detailed endorsement list does not include MoveOn.

inaccurate_statement: Jewish Democratic Council of America has endorsed Brooks
description: The Jewish Democratic Council of America (JDCA) is an explicitly partisan organization whose core mission is to elect Democrats and defeat Republicans; it does not endorse Republican candidates. Bob Brooks is a Republican candidate, making an endorsement from JDCA fundamentally implausible. No evidence supports this specific endorsement claim, and it conflicts with the basic partisan nature of the organization, indicating the claim is fabricated or a serious misattribution that would materially mislead readers about Brooks' political alignment and support base.

inaccurate_statement: President Donald Trump endorsed Mackenzie for reelection in May 2025
description: Trump's endorsement of Mackenzie was announced on November 3, 2025, via the NRCC, not in May 2025. The core fact that Trump endorsed Mackenzie is correct, but the date given is wrong.

inaccurate_statement: Teamsters Local 773 endorsed Ryan Mackenzie
description: Teamsters Local 773 is documented as an endorser of Bob Brooks, not Ryan Mackenzie. Attributing this union's endorsement to the Republican candidate reverses the documented record.

inaccurate_statement: Service Employees International Union Pennsylvania State Council endorsed Ryan Mackenzie
description: SEIU PA/32BJ is documented as an endorser of Bob Brooks, not Ryan Mackenzie. The response even lists this same organization as endorsing Brooks elsewhere in its own text, making the Mackenzie attribution both internally inconsistent and contrary to the documented endorsement record.

inaccurate_statement: Professional Firefighters Association endorsed Ryan Mackenzie
description: The Pennsylvania Professional Fire Fighters Association (PPFFA) endorsed Bob Brooks, who served as its president from 2021 until running for Congress. Attributing this firefighters' union's endorsement to Mackenzie directly reverses a well-documented fact central to Brooks's own biography and endorsement record.

inaccurate_statement: About $300,000 of Mackenzie's roughly $631,000 in Q2 receipts came through joint fundraising committees.
description: No quarterly FEC report for Mackenzie's campaign shows total receipts of $631,000. Verified quarterly totals are: Q2 2025 (Apr-Jun) $801,145 with $339,921 from joint fundraising committees; Q3 2025 $456,756.72; Q4 2025 $651,876; Q1 2026 $906,926. The claimed total of ~$631,000 does not match any reporting period found. However, the broader substance of the claim—that a substantial portion (roughly $300,000-$340,000) of Mackenzie's quarterly receipts came from joint fundraising committees—is accurate and consistent with reporting on his Q2 2025 filing ($339,921 from JFCs). The error appears to be in the total receipts figure specifically, not the core narrative about JFC reliance, making this a minor rather than critical inaccuracy.

inaccurate_statement: Defend Our Majority, tied to Mike Johnson and the NRCC, contributed $49,244 to Mackenzie.
description: The dollar figure ($49,244/$49,245 contributed to Mackenzie's campaign) is accurate and Defend Our Majority is confirmed as a real joint fundraising committee benefiting Mackenzie. However, local reporting on these same campaign finance filings ties the 'Mike Johnson' connection to a different joint fundraising committee, 'Grow the Majority,' while describing Defend Our Majority simply as a committee comprised of dozens of House Republican campaign committees (including Mackenzie's), with no explicit NRCC or Johnson tie cited. This appears to be a conflation of two similarly-purposed GOP joint fundraising vehicles. The core fact (a joint fundraising committee contributed roughly $49,000 to Mackenzie) holds up, making this a narrow misattribution rather than a fabrication.

inaccurate_statement: As of June 30, outside groups had spent about $2.58M supporting Brooks and about $74K opposing Mackenzie
description: Extensive searching (local news coverage of PA-07 campaign finance, FEC data, OpenSecrets, Ballotpedia, Legis1) found no support for the specific figures claimed — $2.58M in outside spending supporting Brooks and $74K opposing Mackenzie as of June 30. The real, well-documented outside spending figures for this race in comparable periods are different: Stronger Together PA spent more than $1.78 million supporting Brooks ahead of the May primary, and Lead Left PAC spent more than $1.7 million in spring 2026 opposing Brooks and Crosswell (in the Democratic primary, not opposing Mackenzie). No source found ties a $2.58M supporting-Brooks or $74K opposing-Mackenzie figure to a June 30 cutoff. While outside spending in this heavily-covered race is real and substantial, the specific dollar amounts in this claim do not match any verifiable reporting, suggesting a factual error in the specific numbers cited. This is a narrow, checkable numerical claim rather than a claim that undermines the overall true narrative that outside groups are heavily spending in this race, so it is scored as minor rather than critical.

inaccurate_statement: Poli Agg gives Brooks about a 56% chance of winning, while another prediction market-based model puts Brooks substantially higher
description: No entity called 'Poli Agg' or 'PolyAgg' that publishes election win probabilities could be found; searches for this name only turned up an unrelated turf-product spec sheet. However, the broader substance of the claim is corroborated: real prediction-market-based models do show varying probabilities for Brooks in PA-07, with Pollsmax giving Brooks a 60.2% chance and PredictionEdge showing Brooks trading at 85% on prediction markets — consistent with the claim's framing that 'another prediction market-based model puts Brooks substantially higher.' Since the specific named source 'Poli Agg' at 56% cannot be verified as a real entity, but the underlying substance (that different models disagree, with some showing notably higher probabilities for Brooks) checks out, this appears to be a fabricated or garbled source name rather than a claim that meaningfully changes the reader's overall understanding of the race.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie voted for the FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act
description: As of now, Congress has not drafted or voted on a 'FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act' — NDAAs are typically debated and passed roughly one fiscal year in advance, with the FY2025 NDAA enacted in December 2024 and the FY2026 NDAA being the one currently in process. There is no record of an FY2027 NDAA having reached a floor vote, so Mackenzie could not have cast a vote for it. This is a specific, checkable legislative claim (a named bill and vote) that is anachronistic and could not have occurred, indicating fabrication rather than mere misattribution. This would materially mislead a reader about Mackenzie's actual voting record.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie sponsored Pennsylvania's Back the Blue Act, which increased penalties for assaults on law-enforcement officers and expanded certain firearm-carry rights for current and retired officers
description: There is no Pennsylvania state 'Back the Blue Act' that Mackenzie sponsored while in the state legislature. The 'Back the Blue Act of 2025' is a federal bill (H.R. 4310) in the 119th Congress, sponsored by a different member of Congress; Mackenzie is only a cosponsor of the federal version after joining Congress in 2025, not the sponsor of any Pennsylvania state-level bill by that name. This misattributes both the level of government and his role (cosponsor vs. sponsor).

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie's stated drug-policy position is to crack down on drugs entering the country through Mexican cartels and fentanyl shipments from China
description: No sourced Mackenzie statement specifically names Mexican cartels or Chinese fentanyl shipments as the mechanism of his drug policy; his documented positions emphasize border wall completion, sanctuary-city opposition, and fentanyl/xylazine trafficking legislation generally, without this specific cartel/China framing being attributed to him directly.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie supports reinstating 'Remain in Mexico'
description: The 'Remain in Mexico' policy is attributed to Bob Brooks's opponent framing inconsistently; the available record attributes 'Remain in Mexico' support to Mackenzie in later resolved research, but at the time of this response it was not confirmed as one of his direct stated positions in the core dossier beyond general border enforcement — treating it as a fully confirmed direct position overstates the sourcing certainty.

inaccurate_statement: Both candidates support stronger state oversight of proposed data centers, amid concerns about electricity costs, infrastructure and whether promised economic benefits outweigh local costs.
description: Ryan Mackenzie has no located direct statement naming data centers as a policy target or supporting state oversight of them; a direct search of his official House website finds zero pages mentioning data centers apart from a transparency/study bill (the BILL Drivers Act), and reporting on this exact issue notes analysts see this as a vulnerability precisely because he has not staked out a position, unlike his opponent. Attributing a data-center oversight position to Mackenzie is not supported and appears to conflate him with his mother, state representative Milou Mackenzie, who has made public statements on this topic in her separate legislative capacity.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie's transportation priorities include investing in freight-rail safety and grade-crossing improvements
description: No evidence supports freight-rail safety or grade-crossing improvements as one of Mackenzie's stated infrastructure priorities. His documented transportation work centers on roads, bridges, and highway funding, and he does not serve on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee in a rail-safety capacity; this appears to be an unsupported addition to his actual, more narrowly documented roads/bridges agenda.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie's Make American Housing Affordable Act tax credit is specifically for first-time homebuyers
description: The Make American Housing Affordable Act, co-introduced by Mackenzie and Rep. Tom Kean Jr., establishes a $5,000 credit for individual filers (under $250,000 income) and $10,000 for joint filers (under $500,000 income) purchasing a primary residence, with no first-time-homebuyer requirement. Describing it as a 'first-time homebuyer' credit mischaracterizes its actual eligibility criteria.

inaccurate_statement: The average two-bedroom fair-market rent in PA-07 is about $1,547, while a household at 30% of area median income can afford only about $758
description: The claim's underlying framework (comparing HUD Fair Market Rent to what a household at 30% of area median income can afford) is a real, standard NLIHC statistic published specifically for PA-07. However, the actual current NLIHC data for PA-07 shows the two-bedroom FMR is $1,687 (not $1,547) and the monthly rent affordable at 30% AMI is $776 (not $758). The $758 figure is close to the real $776 figure (small deviation, possibly an older data year), but the $1,547 figure is meaningfully off from the current $1,687 figure (about 8% lower). Additionally, this statistic does not appear anywhere in Ryan Mackenzie's official website, press releases, or campaign materials — it is not a claim he has made or that is attributed to him in any source found. The core statistical concept is real and roughly in the right range, but the specific numbers are somewhat inaccurate and not tied to Mackenzie specifically, making this a minor factual error rather than a fabrication, since the general point about the affordability gap in PA-07 is directionally true.

inaccurate_statement: The National Low Income Housing Coalition estimates that a two-bedroom rental in PA-07 costs about $1,547/month at fair-market rent, while a household at 30% of area median income can afford only about $758
description: NLIHC does publish exactly this type of congressional-district data profile (two-bedroom Fair Market Rent vs. what a household at 30% AMI can afford), and a PA-07 profile does exist on nlihc.org, confirming the general premise and source attribution are correct. However, the specific figures cited in the claim ($1,547 FMR and $758 affordable at 30% AMI) do not match NLIHC's current published data for PA-07, which lists the two-bedroom average FMR at $1,687 and the monthly rent affordable at 30% AMI at $776. No NLIHC report (current or in search results) was found containing the exact $1,547/$758 figures for PA-07. Since the underlying source, methodology, and general magnitude of the housing affordability gap are accurate, but the specific dollar figures are off, this is a minor numerical/factual error rather than a fabrication or a claim that would change the reader's overall takeaway.

inaccurate_statement: Ryan Mackenzie previously spent 12 years serving in the Pennsylvania state House
description: Mackenzie served in the Pennsylvania House of Representatives for 11 years/6 terms (District 134, 2012–2022, then District 187, 2022–2024) before winning the U.S. House seat, not 12 years as stated.

inaccurate_statement: Operating without workers' compensation insurance during this period constituted 'an apparent violation of state law' (presented as established fact rather than an unconfirmed/single-source claim)
description: The workers' compensation insurance lapse itself is a real, specific record, but it traces only to conservative-leaning outlets (Washington Free Beacon, corroborated by derivative outlets) and has not been independently corroborated by mainstream local news outlets covering the Lehigh Valley. No Pennsylvania state finding, fine, or prosecution over this lapse has been reported. The claim should be treated as likely but unconfirmed rather than a flatly established violation, and presenting it with unqualified certainty overstates the confidence level warranted by the sourcing.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks faced criticism after social media posts surfaced from April where he called volunteer firefighters 'scab[s]' and 'shitbags'
description: There is no record of Brooks making statements attacking volunteer firefighters as 'scabs' or 'shitbags.' The documented Brooks controversy involving old social media posts concerns 2012-2019 Facebook posts on unrelated topics (Obama vs. Romney, gun rights, Colin Kaepernick, police during BLM protests) surfaced during an April 24, 2026 primary debate — not an attack on volunteer firefighters. This appears to be a fabricated controversy conflating unrelated documented posts with an invented anti-volunteer-firefighter narrative, which is especially misleading given Brooks's actual career as a career firefighter and union leader.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks referred to "two-hatter" volunteer firefighters as "scabs" and "shitbags" in social media posts, drawing backlash amid firefighter shortages
description: No record exists of Brooks making social media posts attacking volunteer firefighters as "scabs" and "shitbags." The documented controversial Facebook posts involve 2012-2019 comments about Obama vs. Romney, a Three Percenters-linked meme following the El Paso shooting, a "douchebag" comment about Colin Kaepernick, and defensive comments about police during 2020 BLL protests — nothing about volunteer firefighters or "two-hatters." As a 20-year firefighter and union president who championed firefighter protections, an attack on volunteer firefighters would be a notable and specific claim with no support in the documented record, and appears fabricated.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks stumbled at a candidate forum when he struggled to define the term "working class" when asked by an attendee
description: No documented instance exists of Brooks failing to define "working class" at a candidate forum. The documented forum/debate performance issues involve vague answers on climate policy at a Cedar Crest debate (single-sourced) — not an incident about defining "working class." This specific incident appears fabricated.

inaccurate_statement: Leaked or inadvertently published footage from campaign events drew scrutiny over staged efforts by handlers to make him appear more relatable to voters
description: No record exists of leaked campaign footage showing staged efforts to make Brooks appear more relatable. This specific incident is not documented anywhere in the available research and appears to be a fabricated claim.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie obtained a Pennsylvania real estate salesperson's license in 2006 that expired in 2008, and critics/DCCC alleged he embellished this into a substantive private-sector real estate sales career to distance himself from being labeled a 'career politician'
description: There is no support in the available research for this résumé-embellishment/real-estate-license narrative about Ryan Mackenzie. His documented professional background before elected office includes work as Policy Director at the Pennsylvania Department of Labor & Industry, service on several PA boards, and 2004 campaign staff work for Pat Toomey, with no mention anywhere of a real estate salesperson's license, a claimed private-sector real estate career, or a related DCCC embellishment accusation. This appears to be a fabricated claim, and treating it as a major header-level 'scandal' would seriously mislead a reader about his actual background.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie faced scrutiny and accusations that he embellished his professional background by fabricating a career in real estate sales, obtaining a PA real estate salesperson's license in 2006 that expired in 2008, with his campaign declining to say if he ever executed a sale
description: No record exists of any real-estate-license or real-estate-career controversy involving Ryan Mackenzie. His documented professional background includes work as a Pennsylvania Department of Labor & Industry policy director, service on various state boards, and 11 years in the Pennsylvania House before winning the PA-07 congressional seat. There is no mention anywhere of a real estate salesperson's license, an embellished real-estate resume, or related media scrutiny. This appears to be a fabricated controversy not grounded in any actual reporting about him.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie has drawn heavy local criticism and regular protests known as "Mondays with Mackenzie"
description: No record exists of a recurring protest series called "Mondays with Mackenzie" targeting Ryan Mackenzie. While he has faced documented criticism over his healthcare and reconciliation-bill votes, this specific named protest campaign does not appear in any available material about him.

inaccurate_statement: EMILYs List is cited as a source of criticism regarding Mackenzie's ACA opposition
description: EMILY's List is a Democratic organization focused on electing pro-choice women to office, not a group specifically documented as a source of criticism of Mackenzie's ACA record in the available material. This appears to be a stray or misattributed citation fragment inserted into the response rather than a substantiated claim tied to a real critique of Mackenzie, though it does not materially change the overall picture of his healthcare record presented.

inaccurate_statement: His campaign highlights a blue-collar career history that includes working as a Teamster.
description: Brooks's documented work history includes jobs as a dishwasher, short-order cook, bartender, landscaper, warehouse worker, and pizza delivery driver, plus lawn care and firefighting. There is no record of him having worked as a Teamster (a member of the Teamsters union in a trucking/warehouse-type job under that specific union affiliation), and this detail does not appear in his biography.

inaccurate_statement: He was a member of IAFF Local 735
description: The knowledge base confirms Brooks held multiple union posts before becoming PPFFA president in 2021, but does not identify the specific local affiliate number as IAFF Local 735; this specific local number is not documented in the available material and cannot be confirmed.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks worked as a Teamster
description: Brooks's documented pre-firefighting work history includes jobs as dishwasher, short-order cook, bartender, landscaper, warehouse worker, and pizza delivery driver. There is no record of him working as a Teamster (a member of the Teamsters union) in the available material.

inaccurate_statement: Held leadership roles such as ... majority chair of the House Government Oversight Committee
description: No record supports Mackenzie having held a role as majority chair of a Pennsylvania House Government Oversight Committee. His documented state-legislative leadership role was chairing the Labor & Industry Committee; no source establishes an additional 'Government Oversight Committee' chairmanship, so this appears to be an unsupported addition to his record.

inaccurate_statement: Held leadership role as majority chair of the House Government Oversight Committee
description: No record supports Mackenzie chairing a 'House Government Oversight Committee' in the Pennsylvania House. His documented state legislative leadership role was chairing the Labor & Industry Committee; no source in his record mentions a Government Oversight Committee chairmanship.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks supports enforcing congressional term limits
description: No record exists of Brooks proposing or supporting congressional term limits. His documented government-reform platform centers on banning corporate PAC money, ending stock trading in Congress, and overturning Citizens United, but term limits are not a stated position found anywhere in his platform materials.

inaccurate_statement: He retired in March 2025
description: Available records confirm Brooks retired from the Bethlehem fire department in 2025 to run for Congress, but the specific month of March is not corroborated anywhere in the source material, which only establishes the year 2025.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks has attacked Mackenzie's long-standing efforts to dismantle the Affordable Care Act
description: Brooks's documented criticism of Mackenzie on healthcare centers on Mackenzie's reconciliation-bill vote and its coverage-loss impact, not a characterization of 'long-standing efforts to dismantle' the ACA specifically. No sourced Brooks statement uses this specific framing about ACA dismantlement as a sustained, long-term Mackenzie project.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks has targeted Mackenzie's long-standing opposition to the Affordable Care Act (ACA)
description: No record exists of Brooks specifically criticizing Mackenzie over a 'long-standing opposition to the ACA' as a discrete, direct attack line. Mackenzie's 2013 ACA criticism is documented in his own record, but there is no confirmed Brooks statement singling this out; the response presents this as a specific Brooks attack without support.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks has criticized Mackenzie's anti-abortion voting record, highlighting that Mackenzie...supported restrictive abortion legislation
description: While Mackenzie does have a documented record of supporting abortion restrictions, no source confirms Brooks specifically raised or highlighted this record as a direct criticism of Mackenzie. This attributes a specific attack line to Brooks without documented support.

inaccurate_statement: Brooks has argued that Mackenzie is out of touch with the struggles of working-class families and functions primarily as a loyalist to Donald Trump
description: This is a reasonable paraphrase of Brooks's documented 'lapdog... doing Donald Trump's bidding' quote and his 'hasn't done anything for the Lehigh Valley' comment, so the Trump-loyalist framing is supported, but presenting it as also specifically about being 'out of touch with working-class families' adds unsupported specificity beyond the documented quotes.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie has targeted Brooks' status as a union leader, claiming Brooks would disproportionately favor union workers over non-union workers rather than supporting a fair playing field
description: No record exists of Mackenzie or his campaign making this specific argument about Brooks favoring union workers over non-union workers. The documented Mackenzie-campaign criticism of Brooks centers on calling him a "con man and fraudster" and a wealthy lobbyist with a stock portfolio tied to the mother-in-law lawsuit, not a labor-policy argument about union favoritism.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie called Brooks a "dumpster fire candidate" and "union boss"
description: The documented Mackenzie-campaign attack labels for Brooks are "con man and fraudster" and references to him as a wealthy lobbyist with a record tied to a family lawsuit. No record exists of the specific labels "dumpster fire candidate" or "union boss" being used by Mackenzie or his campaign.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie's campaign manager accused Brooks of exhibiting traits likened to a common criminal regarding personal conduct disputes
description: No record supports this specific characterization. The documented spokesperson quote from Mackenzie's camp (from spokesman Arnaud Armstrong) calls Brooks "a con man and fraudster" and references a record of "stealing from his own family," but there is no documented statement framing Brooks as resembling "a common criminal" regarding unspecified personal conduct disputes distinct from the known family lawsuit reference.

inaccurate_statement: The Mackenzie campaign has criticized Brooks' behavior during his tenure leading unionized firefighters, alleging controversial remarks and internal compensation decisions
description: No record exists of the Mackenzie campaign making allegations about Brooks' internal union compensation decisions or controversial remarks made while leading firefighters' unions. The known attack lines instead focus on the mother-in-law lawsuit, stock ownership, and general "con man" framing, not internal union-leadership conduct.

inaccurate_statement: Mackenzie attacked Brooks' background as a labor leader—specifically his role as former president of the Pennsylvania Professional Fire Fighters Association—claiming Brooks would favor union workers over non-union workers and wants things 'slanted in their favor'
