The Rural Health Transformation Program is a real national initiative, but no source ties a $50 billion national total specifically to Van Orden's own claimed role in securing it; his own claims center on Wisconsin-specific dollar figures. This overstates the scope of what he has claimed credit for.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden approaches healthcare from a free-market and cost-reduction perspective rather than expanding government-backed coverage programs.
description: This oversimplifies a genuinely mixed record. While Van Orden's campaign site does use repeal-and-replace, free-market framing, he was also one of only 17 House Republicans nationally to cross the aisle in January 2026 to vote to extend expiring ACA subsidies, has touted securing roughly $1 billion annually for BadgerCare (Wisconsin's Medicaid program) and $500 million for rural hospital infrastructure, and secured CMS approval preserving Wisconsin's hospital provider tax to protect enhanced federal Medicaid funding. His record shows substantial direct engagement with expanding or protecting government health program funding, not merely a hands-off free-market approach, so characterizing him as solely emphasizing cost-reduction over government program expansion is a misleading oversimplification, though not a fabrication.

inaccurate_statement: Derrick Van Orden favors reducing the regulatory burden on healthcare and relying on tax relief to put money back into family budgets to pay for care, rather than growing the size of public programs.

Presenting his position as purely about shrinking public programs versus expanding private-market solutions understates this more complicated record.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden's approach aligns with mainstream conservative principles that look to lower costs through market competition rather than expanding government programs, with his focus resting on managing the budget rather than expanding government health programs.
description: Van Orden's actual healthcare record shows substantial direct engagement with government health programs rather than an approach focused mainly on broader budget/economic policy: he worked with CMS and the Trump administration on Medicaid reimbursement rates for Wisconsin providers, secured CMS approval to preserve Wisconsin's hospital provider tax (protecting enhanced Medicaid funding), and was one of a small number of House Republicans who voted in January 2026 to extend expiring ACA subsidies. This directly contradicts the characterization that his focus is mainly on managing the budget rather than expanding or protecting government health programs, though the response's broader point that he favors market-competition-oriented, cost-focused approaches is not entirely baseless given his campaign-site repeal-and-replace language.

inaccurate_statement: Critics from the Democratic Party have pointed to Van Orden's votes supporting broader spending reform bills that opponents argue could reduce ACA subsidies or limit safety-net funding.
description: This omits that Van Orden's healthcare/ACA record is genuinely mixed rather than one-directional: while he voted for the 2025 reconciliation law that included Medicaid work-requirement tightening (which critics say could reduce coverage), he was also one of only 17 House Republicans nationally who crossed party lines in January 2026 to vote with Democrats to extend expiring ACA subsidies for three years, stating he would not watch constituents lose coverage. Presenting only the critical framing without this cross-party vote gives an incomplete picture of his actual record on this specific issue.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke favors collaborative international diplomacy and expressed reservations regarding unilateral or sudden U.S. military interventions abroad.
description: The claim asserts a general foreign-policy posture favoring collaborative diplomacy and reservations about unilateral/sudden military interventions, but reporting contradicts this generalization. While Cooke did express reservations about further U.S. military aid to Israel's government, she notably supported the 2026 U.S. military intervention in Venezuela and the ousting of President Maduro — a unilateral, sudden military action — with her criticism limited only to the lack of a post-intervention stability plan, not to the intervention or its unilateral character itself. This is a direct counterexample to the claim's core assertion. There is also no clear, attributable statement from Cooke articulating a general doctrine of preferring collaborative diplomacy over unilateral force; if anything, she was criticized publicly for not clearly articulating any foreign policy position during a major military crisis (Iran-related strikes). Given that a specific, notable instance shows her supporting rather than opposing a unilateral intervention, the claim's overall characterization is inaccurate and would meaningfully mislead readers about her actual foreign policy stance.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke made her immigration statement in an August 2026 interview
description: The claim cites an August 2026 interview as the source of Cooke's immigration statement, but this date appears to be erroneous or fabricated — it references a future date that could not have already occurred at the time such a claim would be made about a current political race. Without tool access to verify further, the specific dating of this interview cannot be confirmed as accurate, and a future-dated citation is a clear factual/sourcing error. This is treated as minor rather than critical because the underlying substance of Cooke having made some public statement on immigration may still be true; it is the specific attribution of date/interview that is unsupportable.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden joined Trump for the June 2026 signing of the Secure America Act, which his office says provides full funding for ICE and related immigration enforcement
description: The claim describes a specific event — Van Orden joining Trump for a signing of the 'Secure America Act' — dated June 2026, which is in the future relative to verifiable current events. No such bill named the 'Secure America Act' providing 'full funding for ICE' is known to exist or to have been signed into law. Presenting a future-dated, unconfirmed event as an already-completed fact with specific attributed details (that 'his office says' it provides full ICE funding) is a hallmark of a fabricated claim. No corroborating evidence exists for this specific bill, signing ceremony, or Van Orden's attendance at it, and the claim is specific enough that real evidence would appear if true. This is a critical inaccuracy because it fabricates a concrete legislative achievement and presidential event that would materially shape a reader's view of Van Orden's record.

inaccurate_statement: Property taxes were named by 7% of respondents as their top issue in the July 2026 Marquette poll
description: The claim cites a 'July 2026 Marquette poll' — a specific, checkable data point (a named poll with a specific date and statistic). This date is in the future and no such poll could have been conducted, reported, or cited as a factual basis for this claim at the time this response was generated. There is no evidence any Marquette Law School poll from July 2026 exists showing 7% of respondents naming property taxes as their top issue. This appears to be a fabricated statistic attributed to a poll that has not occurred, which would materially mislead a reader into thinking this is verified, current polling data about voter priorities in WI-03.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden opposes federal subsidies for electric-vehicle purchases
description: No record in the available material documents Van Orden taking a specific stance opposing EV purchase subsidies. His confirmed energy platform centers on expanding domestic oil, gas, and ethanol production and opposing regulatory constraints, but this specific EV-subsidy opposition claim is not substantiated by any sourced statement.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke proposes to extend enhanced ACA premium tax credits for three years as an immediate way to reduce premiums
description: The three-year extension of enhanced ACA premium tax credits is documented as something Van Orden voted for in January 2026 (one of 17 House Republicans crossing party lines), not a Cooke campaign proposal. Cooke's own platform language is to 'improve the Affordable Care Act and healthcare exchange as it exists by providing more tax credits' without the specific three-year extension framing attributed to her here.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke puts 'healing our healthcare system' first among her campaign priorities.
description: Healthcare/affordability is genuinely one of Cooke's most emphasized campaign themes, but her platform lists it alongside several other substantial priority areas (economy, farming, seniors, unions, reproductive rights, education, environment, small business), and no source frames it as her single top or 'first' priority to the exclusion of others. The specific phrase 'healing our healthcare system' also does not appear in her documented platform language.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke's 2026 platform explicitly calls for investment in rural roads and bridges, describing safe roads and bridges as essential to rural economic growth and keeping communities connected.
description: Rebecca Cooke's actual campaign platform page has no 'Rural Infrastructure,' roads, or bridges plank. The near-verbatim phrase used here ('safe roads and bridges... essential for economic growth and keeping our communities connected') traces to a typosquat/phishing site impersonating her campaign, not her real platform. Her only verified, on-record infrastructure-adjacent comment concerns broadband access, not roads or bridges. Since this is the central topic the user asked about, presenting a fabricated roads/bridges platform position as her stated plan is a significant inaccuracy.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden voted against the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, despite subsequently highlighting federal infrastructure dollars delivered to WI-03.
description: Derrick Van Orden was not a member of Congress in November 2021 when the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law passed — he lost his first congressional bid to incumbent Ron Kind in 2020 and did not take office until January 3, 2023, after winning the 2022 open-seat race. He therefore could not have cast a vote on that 2021 legislation, and no vote record exists showing he opposed it. This claim, presented as 'one important distinction' central to the response's comparison, fabricates a nonexistent voting record.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke's campaign explicitly says that 'safe roads and bridges' are essential investments in rural Wisconsin and economic growth
description: Rebecca Cooke's official campaign platform page has no 'Rural Infrastructure,' 'roads,' or 'bridges' plank. This specific 'safe roads and bridges... essential for economic growth' phrasing traces to a typosquat/phishing site impersonating her real campaign, not her actual platform. Her only genuine, verified infrastructure-adjacent statement is a single recorded comment about broadband access, not a formal roads/bridges commitment. This overstates her documented position but does not fundamentally alter the reader's overall understanding of her candidacy.

inaccurate_statement: In June, Cooke highlighted her backing from 13 labor unions and specifically talked about the people who 'build our bridges' and 'pave our highways'
description: No record exists of Cooke making a specific roads/bridges/highways-themed statement tied to labor union endorsements in June, and her verified platform does not contain a formal roads or bridges commitment. This appears to be an unconfirmed overreach consistent with a broader pattern of AI-generated content mistakenly attributing a roads/bridges platform position to her.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke's campaign explicitly lists 'safe roads and bridges' alongside broadband as investments needed to strengthen rural communities and economic growth.
description: Rebecca Cooke's official campaign platform page has no confirmed 'Rural Infrastructure,' roads, or bridges plank. Her only verified, on-the-record statement in this area is specifically about broadband access (comparing it to rural electrification), not roads and bridges. A 'roads and bridges' framing attributed to her campaign traces to language found on a typosquat site impersonating her campaign, not her actual platform, so presenting this as her stated position overstates what is actually confirmed.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke: I'm not finding a comparably detailed, current crime-reduction agenda
description: Cooke does have documented statements specifically on crime/policing, including comments favoring reallocation of some funding toward social workers, mental health services, and root-cause programs, alongside a stated position that police departments should be fully funded. The response's framing that she has no findable crime-related positioning at all overstates the silence — while she lacks a formal, itemized 'crime plan' comparable to Van Orden's platform page, there is a real, sourced record of her views on policing and public safety that the response fails to surface.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke's Red Letter Grant has helped launch more than 60 businesses
description: Cooke's campaign has claimed Red Letter Grant helped over 50 small businesses launch in rural communities, a figure noted as not independently verified. The response's figure of 'more than 60' does not match this documented claim and appears to be an inflated or incorrect number.

inaccurate_statement: WI-03's unemployment rate is about 3.4% in the latest district-level Census data cited by Project Curia
description: No evidence exists that 'Project Curia' is a real organization or data source that publishes district-level Census unemployment statistics for WI-03. The specific unemployment figure (3.4%) cannot be verified against any legitimate source, and the attribution to 'Project Curia' appears fabricated. However, this is a narrow statistical/sourcing detail rather than a claim that fundamentally mischaracterizes Rebecca Cooke's positions, record, or candidacy, so it does not rise to a critical severity on its own.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden's CNA Workforce Improvement Act would broaden who can supervise CNA training, with the stated goal of getting more workers into rural health-care jobs
description: No record of a 'CNA Workforce Improvement Act' sponsored or supported by Van Orden appears in his documented legislative record, which covers agriculture, veterans affairs, PFAS/water funding, small-business tax provisions, and immigration/workforce measures like the Agricultural Workforce Reform Act. This specific bill name and health-care-training mechanism cannot be corroborated and appears to be an invented legislative item.

inaccurate_statement: WI-03's unemployment rate is about 3.4% in the latest district-level Census data cited by Project Curia
description: The 3.4% unemployment rate figure for WI-03 is factually accurate and matches U.S. Census Bureau ACS 5-Year Estimates data found via other district-profile trackers (e.g., legisletter.org, which explicitly cites 'U.S. Census Bureau ACS 5-Year Estimates' for this exact 3.4% figure). However, the attribution to 'Project Curia' is not supported. Project Curia's own site describes its scope as tracking 'how they voted, who paid for their campaigns, whether they trade stocks, which bills they have signed' and its published data catalog (votes.csv, issues.json, etc.) contains only legislative voting/finance data, with no district-level Census demographic or unemployment statistics. This appears to be a case of a real, verifiable statistic being misattributed to the wrong source rather than a fabricated number, and it's a narrow attribution error rather than a claim that would change the overall takeaway about the candidate.

inaccurate_statement: Rebecca Cooke's campaign specifically calls for investment in regional mass transit, including high-speed rail.
description: There is no record of Cooke's platform including a mass-transit or high-speed rail proposal. Her documented infrastructure-related position is limited to a single verified comment favoring broadband expansion (comparing it to rural electrification), and her official campaign priorities page contains no roads, transit, or rail plank. A high-speed rail proposal is not part of her confirmed platform and appears fabricated.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke has highlighted investments in regional transportation and mass transit as part of her infrastructure approach
description: There is no confirmed formal platform plank from Cooke on roads, bridges, or mass transit/regional transportation. Her official campaign site has no infrastructure section on roads or transit, and her one verified statement in this area is specifically about broadband access, not mass transit or regional transportation options. Presenting a transit/mass-transit-specific policy focus as her stated infrastructure approach overstates what is actually documented.

inaccurate_statement: Wisconsin received $203.7 million through the Rural Health Transformation Program
description: The documented figure for Wisconsin's Rural Health Transformation Fund allocation is $204 million annually for five years (over $1 billion total), not $203.7 million as a apparently one-time or differently-scoped figure. This is a very close approximation of the correct number and does not materially mislead, but it doesn't precisely match the sourced figure.

inaccurate_statement: Wisconsin's 2025–27 state budget includes $150 million for the Agricultural Roads Improvement Program, including $30 million specifically for bridge and culvert repairs
description: The dollar figures are correct: Wisconsin's 2025-27 state biennial budget does include $150 million for the Agricultural Roads Improvement Program (ARIP), with $30 million earmarked for bridge and culvert repairs via the Local Small Structures Improvement Program. However, this is exclusively a Wisconsin state government program — created by state Senate Bill 247/Act 13 and funded through the state budget signed by Gov. Tony Evers, with credit given to state legislators (Sens. Marklein, Tomczyk, Ballweg and Reps. Tranel, VanderMeer). Derrick Van Orden is a U.S. House Representative (federal office) with no role in the state budget process. No search result connects him to ARIP in any capacity; his own website and campaign materials discuss separate federal rural-roads legislation (e.g., the Rural Surface Transportation Grant Program bill), not this state program. Attributing this state budget achievement to Van Orden would be a significant misattribution that conflates state and federal action.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke explicitly supports rural infrastructure—safe roads/bridges—as part of her platform
description: Cooke's official campaign platform page has no 'Rural Infrastructure,' 'roads,' or 'bridges' plank. The only verified statement on this general topic is a single recorded comment specifically about broadband (comparing it to rural electrification), not a roads/bridges commitment. A near-identical 'safe roads and bridges' phrase attributed to her elsewhere traces to a typosquat site impersonating her campaign, not a genuine platform statement. The broadband-specific claim is real; the roads/bridges claim is not supported.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden co-sponsored legislation to make federal rural transportation grants easier for small communities to access
description: No record of this specific legislative co-sponsorship on rural transportation grant accessibility exists in the available material on Van Orden's record; his confirmed rural infrastructure credential is limited to a documented $8.4 million funding event in Sparta, WI with the U.S. Transportation Secretary, not a described grant-accessibility bill.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke explicitly supports investment in safe roads and bridges
description: Cooke's official campaign platform page has no 'Rural Infrastructure,' 'roads,' or 'bridges' plank. While she has made a real, verified statement about broadband (comparing it to rural electrification), no formal roads/bridges commitment has been confirmed for her, and presenting this as an explicit position overstates her documented record.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke's health-care plan includes lowering costs through extended ACA premium tax credits
description: Cooke's confirmed healthcare platform includes a public option, expanded Medicare benefits (vision/dental/hearing), prescription drug price negotiation, and working to 'improve the Affordable Care Act and healthcare exchange as it exists by providing more tax credits' — this is close to but not precisely 'extended ACA premium tax credits' as a distinct named policy; it is a reasonable paraphrase of her general ACA tax-credit position rather than a fabrication, so while checkable, it is not a clear contradiction.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden supported the Healthy H2O Act, which helps communities test and filter contaminated drinking water
description: No record exists of Van Orden supporting or being associated with legislation called the 'Healthy H2O Act.' His confirmed PFAS/water-related record includes securing $350 million to transition firefighting foams away from PFAS, and FY24 Interior Appropriations funding for PFAS-filtration equipment in Eau Claire and a new municipal water system for the Town of Campbell. No bill by this specific name appears in his documented record.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden has opposed broader federal Waters of the United States (WOTUS) regulation, arguing that it places excessive burdens on farmers and that Wisconsin farmers are already good environmental stewards
description: No record of a specific Van Orden statement characterizing Wisconsin farmers as 'already good environmental stewards' in the context of WOTUS opposition exists in the available material. General concern about WOTUS regulations affecting farmers is documented, but this specific framing and quote attribution is unverified.

inaccurate_statement: The 2026 district housing profile puts the fair-market rent for a two-bedroom at about $1,109/month, while a household at 30% of area median income can afford only about $732
description: This cites a since-superseded NLIHC figure for WI-03; the profile was updated in August 2026 to $1,155 for average two-bedroom fair-market rent and $749 affordable at 30% of area median income.

inaccurate_statement: The 2026 district housing profile puts the fair-market rent for a two-bedroom at about $1,109/month, while a household at 30% of area median income can afford only about $732

inaccurate_statement: Her approach also puts substantial emphasis on workforce development, infrastructure, broadband, transportation and American-made products
description: Cooke's campaign site has no formal 'Rural Infrastructure,' roads, or bridges platform plank; her only independently verified statement in this space is a single broadband comment comparing it to rural electrification. Characterizing infrastructure and transportation as areas of 'substantial emphasis' for her overstates this to a formal platform commitment beyond what is confirmed.

inaccurate_statement: Independent tracking shows roughly $58 million in FY2026 community-project requests across 15 projects for Van Orden
description: Multiple sources, including Van Orden's own official press releases and local Wisconsin news outlets (WEAU, WXOW, La Crosse Tribune), consistently report that Van Orden's FY2026 Community Project Funding totaled just over $22 million, not $58 million. His house.gov FY26 CPF page also lists projects consistent with this ~$22M figure. While each House member can request up to 15 projects (a detail confirmed across many congressional offices' FY2026 CPF pages), no source found corroborates a $58 million figure specifically for Van Orden's FY2026 requests or awards. For comparison, in FY2024 Van Orden requested approximately $73 million but ultimately secured about $26 million, showing his 'request' and 'secured' figures for other years also don't match $58 million. The $58 million figure for FY2026 appears to be a fabricated or erroneous statistic not found in any earmark-tracking database, news coverage, or official record for Van Orden. This is a specific, checkable claim that a genuine search failed to substantiate, though the broader point that Van Orden participates in the earmark/CPF process for a comparable number of projects (13-15) is accurate, making this an inaccurate dollar figure rather than a wholesale fabrication of the underlying practice.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden's campaign says 15 western Wisconsin sheriffs endorsed him in his first congressional campaign
description: The '15 Sheriffs in Wisconsin's 3rd District' endorsement is documented on his current campaign materials without a specific tie to his 2022 ('first congressional campaign') race specifically; the knowledge base does not confirm this endorsement occurred during his first campaign rather than a later one, making the added timing detail an unsupported specific.

inaccurate_statement: The Congressional Research Service estimates the 2025 reconciliation law will reduce federal health outlays by about $1.1 trillion over 10 years and result in roughly 10 million additional uninsured people by 2034 compared with the baseline
description: The $1.1 trillion reduction in federal health outlays and ~10 million additional uninsured by 2034 figures are correct as policy estimates for the 2025 reconciliation law (H.R. 1/OBBBA), but they were produced by the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), not the Congressional Research Service (CRS). A CRS report (R48633) on the law's health provisions explicitly states 'The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates that, together, the health provisions in P.L. 119-21 will reduce federal outlays by $1.1 trillion...over 10 years,' and CBO separately estimated the 10 million increase in uninsured by 2034. CRS merely reported/cited CBO's numbers rather than generating its own independent estimate. This is a misattribution of the source agency, not a fabrication of the underlying facts, and does not change the overall substance of the claim as it relates to Van Orden's vote for the reconciliation law.

inaccurate_statement: His actual congressional record includes support for a House resolution backing local law enforcement and opposing efforts to defund police departments.
description: No record exists of a specific House resolution backing local law enforcement and opposing defunding police departments that Van Orden supported. His documented public-safety record includes voting for funding for local first responders and supporting the HALT Fentanyl Act, but no such specific resolution is confirmed. This is a narrow, unverified specific claim layered onto an otherwise accurate general characterization of his pro-police stance.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke has explicitly said she would 'stand up to Democrats to fight for a secure border.'
description: No record exists of Cooke using this specific phrasing. Her documented direct statements on immigration frame the issue as 'a commonsense immigration policy that includes a secure border and a pathway to citizenship,' citing the bipartisan Dignity Act, without the 'stand up to Democrats' framing attributed here. This particular quote is not corroborated by any source in the record and appears to be an invented quote, though it is directionally consistent with her genuine support for border security.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke previously owned a retail business that grew to four Wisconsin locations
description: Cooke founded Red's Mercantile, a single home-goods retail store in Eau Claire that operated from 2014 to 2022 and closed. There is no record of it expanding to four locations across Wisconsin.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden voted for the 2025 tax law that increased the small-business deduction from 20% to 23%
description: Van Orden's confirmed position and voting record involve making the existing 20% small-business deduction permanent, not increasing it to 23%. No source supports a 23% figure.

inaccurate_statement: Red Letter Grant has helped launch 60+ businesses
description: Cooke's campaign claims Red Letter Grant helped over 50 small businesses launch, not 60+ as stated in the response; this figure is also noted as not independently verified, but the response's number exceeds even the campaign's own claimed figure.

inaccurate_statement: PolitiFact rated claims that Van Orden 'participated in the insurrection' as misleading because the evidence showed attendance at the rally, not participation in the violence.
description: The fact-check finding that the 'participated in the Jan. 6 insurrection' characterization was overstated came from a Milwaukee Journal Sentinel fact-check (October 2023), which rated that specific claim 'mostly false' — not from PolitiFact, and not with a 'misleading' rating label. The substantive point that his actual documented conduct (rally attendance, presence in a restricted area) fell short of 'participating in the insurrection' is accurate, but the source and the specific rating terminology are incorrect.

inaccurate_statement: AP noted criticism of Van Orden's inflammatory posts and AI-generated attack ads targeting Cooke.
description: The substance of the claim is well-supported: Van Orden's AI-generated videos targeting Rebecca Cooke drew extensive criticism from Democrats, ethicists, and media outlets in Wisconsin's 3rd District race. Multiple sources confirm Van Orden posted AI-generated deepfake videos of Cooke, and that this drew rebuke — for example, one outlet reported Van Orden 'has posted countless AI-generated videos of his opponent, Rebecca Cooke, across multiple social media platforms, putting false, inflammatory statements in her mouth.' However, extensive searching found no evidence that the Associated Press (AP) specifically authored or published a story on this topic. All the substantive reporting found traces to Wisconsin Public Radio (WPR), Spectrum News 1, Wausau Pilot & Review, Urban Milwaukee, the Badger Herald, and other local/regional outlets — not AP. The core fact (widespread criticism of Van Orden's AI attack ads on Cooke) is accurate, but attributing this specifically to 'AP' appears to be a misattribution of the source, rather than a fabrication of the underlying event.

inaccurate_statement: J Street PAC is Cooke's biggest identified PAC contributor, with roughly $219,000 in direct contributions
description: JStreetPAC's documented contributions/bundled payments to Cooke totaled approximately $91,295–$93,941, not $219,458 (or the rounded $219,000 cited here). JStreetPAC's support for Cooke is real, but the specific dollar figure is overstated by more than double.

inaccurate_statement: One notable PAC contributor is JStreetPAC, which has provided about $219,000 in direct contributions
description: Independent sources tracking Rebecca Cooke's FEC filings show JStreetPAC's contributions/bundled payments to her campaign totaled approximately $91,295–$93,941, not $219,458 or $219,000. The relationship (JStreetPAC supporting Cooke) is real, but the specific dollar figure cited is more than double the documented amount.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke has about $2.5 million versus Van Orden's $4.68 million cash on hand comparison [implied by using both figures as of the same July 22 filing point]
description: The response's actual figures ($1.83M for Cooke and $4.68M for Van Orden) are both correctly drawn from the same July 22, 2026 filing period, so this specific pairing in the response is accurate; however, other circulating comparisons pairing Van Orden's $4.68M with a $2.5M Cooke figure from an earlier period are a known mismatch. This item is included for completeness but the response itself did not make that specific error.

The broader point that a large majority of his itemized money comes from out-of-state donors is directionally accurate, but the specific percentages are incorrect.

This directly contradicts the response's bottom-line answer to the core question being asked.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke raised about $1.1 million versus roughly $1.0 million for Van Orden in one recent reporting period, marking her second consecutive quarter ahead of him
description: The claim's core narrative—that Cooke outraised Van Orden for a second consecutive quarter—is accurate and confirmed by multiple sources (WPR, Urban Milwaukee, NOTUS, WisPolitics all report this for Q1 2026). However, the specific dollar figures cited are wrong: in that quarter, Cooke actually raised approximately $2.4 million and Van Orden raised approximately $1.3 million, not $1.1 million and $1.0 million as claimed. The '$1.1 million' figure appears to be a conflation with press coverage describing the *margin* by which Cooke outraised Van Orden that quarter ('outraises Van Orden by nearly $1.1 million'), not her total fundraising haul. Since the overall directional claim (second consecutive quarter, Cooke ahead) holds up and only the specific dollar amounts are wrong, this is a narrow factual error rather than one that changes the reader's overall takeaway.

inaccurate_statement: October 30, 2026 at 5 p.m. — Last day to register in person at your municipal clerk's office
description: This claim is generic voter-registration deadline information rather than a substantive claim about Rebecca Cooke's record, positions, or actions — it's not really 'about' her in a way that reflects on her candidacy. More importantly, the specific date appears incorrect: under Wisconsin law (Wis. Stat. § 6.29), the deadline to register in person at the municipal clerk's office is the Wednesday before the election, by 5:00 p.m. For a November 3, 2026 general election, that Wednesday would be October 28, 2026, not October 30, 2026 (which falls on a Friday). Since I was unable to complete additional verification searches due to tool limits this turn, and this is a narrow, non-attributable procedural detail rather than a core claim about Cooke herself, this is best treated as a minor factual error rather than one that changes the overall takeaway about the candidate.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden appeared at the Republican convention in Dallas this September despite being in a competitive race
description: No record exists of Van Orden attending a Republican convention in Dallas in September. The documented 2024 RNC-week event involving Van Orden took place in Milwaukee in July 2024 (where he reported being assaulted by an activist outside the Pfister Hotel), not Dallas in September. This appears to be a confused or fabricated detail about the location, timing, and nature of the event.

inaccurate_statement: First elected in 2022, defeating Democratic incumbent Ron Kind's successor, Brad Pfaff
description: This mischaracterizes the 2022 race. Ron Kind was the retiring incumbent (he did not lose to Van Orden or to anyone else — he chose not to run again), and Brad Pfaff was not Kind's 'successor' since Pfaff never held the House seat. The 2022 race was an open-seat contest after Kind's retirement, in which Van Orden defeated Democratic state senator Brad Pfaff, who was not an incumbent of any kind in this seat.

inaccurate_statement: She previously ran for the same congressional seat in 2022 and 2024, narrowly losing to Republican incumbent Derrick Van Orden in 2024.
description: In 2022 Cooke ran only in the Democratic primary, which she lost to Brad Pfaff; that year's general election was between Pfaff and Van Orden, not Cooke and Van Orden. Her only general-election matchup against Van Orden prior to 2026 was in 2024. Describing 2022 as a race against Van Orden misstates the electoral history, though the overall point that she has run for this seat multiple times and lost the 2024 general to Van Orden is accurate.

inaccurate_statement: Describes herself as a sixth-generation Wisconsinite.
description: No record of Cooke describing herself with this specific "sixth-generation Wisconsinite" phrasing exists in available biographical material, which documents her as being from a dairy-farming family in Eau Claire but does not include this specific generational claim.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden supports expanded fossil-fuel/coal production
description: Van Orden's documented energy platform emphasizes expanding U.S. oil, natural gas, and other domestic energy production, along with ethanol/E15 expansion, and maintaining conventional power generation for grid reliability. There is no specific documented statement or record of him emphasizing coal production specifically; his stated priorities center on oil, gas, and biofuels rather than coal.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke makes healthcare her top priority
description: Healthcare/cost reduction is genuinely one of Cooke's most emphasized issues, and she has called it a top-of-platform priority, but her campaign platform lists healthcare alongside numerous other substantial priority areas (economy, farming, seniors, unions, reproductive rights, education, environment, small business). No source frames healthcare as her single, exclusive top priority, so presenting it that way overstates what the record supports, even though healthcare is a leading emphasis for her.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden's healthcare approach is characterized as 'More conservative approach; supported major Trump-era healthcare cuts' without noting he also crossed party lines to vote to extend ACA subsidies
description: Van Orden's healthcare record is genuinely mixed: he voted for the 2025 reconciliation law that included Medicaid work-requirement tightening, but he was also one of only 17 House Republicans nationally (and the only one from Wisconsin's delegation) to vote in January 2026 to extend expiring ACA subsidies, stating he would not watch constituents lose coverage. Presenting his healthcare position as simply supporting 'major Trump-era healthcare cuts' omits this cross-party vote and gives an incomplete picture of a documented, conflicting record.

inaccurate_statement: Heritage Action gives him a 62% score for the current congressional session and a 64% lifetime score
description: Heritage Action's official scorecard confirms Van Orden received a 62% score, but that was for the 118th Congress (previous session), not the current 119th Congress session, which shows 73%. Additionally, in both the 118th and 119th Congress scorecards, his lifetime score is listed as 68%, not 64% as claimed. The response appears to have pulled the correct session score from an outdated (118th Congress) page while also stating an incorrect lifetime score that doesn't match either session's page.

inaccurate_statement: The confrontation occurred while Van Orden was standing in line at a restaurant
description: The well-documented April 2023 confrontation involving Derrick Van Orden occurred on the steps of the U.S. Capitol, where he yelled profanities at a group of teenage Senate pages who were taking a group photo in the early morning hours. It did not occur at a restaurant or while he was standing in line. None of these sources use the terms 'community activist' or 'community organizer' to describe her. Her career centers on running a retail store (Red's Mercantile), founding a nonprofit supporting female business owners, serving on the WEDC board, and political consulting/fundraising for campaigns—not grassroots community organizing. While she is often described as committed to 'community advocacy' or being a 'community leader,' this is a distinct characterization from being a professional 'community organizer/activist,' so the claim as phrased is not well supported and appears to be a mischaracterization of her actual background. This is a relatively narrow mislabeling rather than one that changes the overall picture of her (business owner, nonprofit leader), so it is minor rather than critical.

The 2022 date itself matches when he was first elected to office, so this is accurate rather than an error — no correction needed.

inaccurate_statement: Rebecca Cooke is described as Derrick Van Orden's 'primary challenger.'

Presenting 2022 alongside 2024 as consecutive campaigns for the same seat without clarifying this distinction risks implying she ran against Van Orden in 2022, which is inaccurate.

This is a minor imprecision in phrasing rather than a substantive factual error about the race's outcome or dynamics.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke centers her platform on community-level prevention... to address public safety
description: No direct statement from Cooke on crime/public safety as a broad platform priority framed around 'community-level prevention' was found in available research; her documented, confirmed position on this topic is specifically about gun policy (background checks, red-flag laws), not a stated general public-safety/crime-prevention platform plank. Presenting gun policy as her overall 'approach to community safety and crime' overstates what is actually confirmed, though the specific gun-policy details cited are accurate.

inaccurate_statement: The WI-03 general-election ballot includes independent candidates named Alexander Valiensi Kent and Rustin Provance
description: The names 'Alexander Valiensi Kent' and 'Rustin Provance' do not correspond to any known candidates in the WI-03 congressional race. The 2024 WI-03 general election ballot featured Republican incumbent Derrick Van Orden and Democrat Rebecca Cooke as the principal candidates; there is no record of independent candidates by these names appearing on the ballot. This appears to be a fabricated detail with no supporting evidence, though it is a tangential claim about the ballot composition rather than about Cooke's own record, positions, or conduct, so it does not change the overall takeaway about her candidacy.

inaccurate_statement: The WI-03 general-election ballot includes independent candidates named Alexander Valiensi Kent and Rustin Provance
description: No evidence exists for independent candidates named 'Alexander Valiensi Kent' or 'Rustin Provance' appearing on the WI-03 general election ballot. The WI-03 race has been characterized in reporting as a contest primarily between incumbent Republican Derrick Van Orden and Democrat Rebecca Cooke, with no documented independent candidates by these unusual names. These names appear to be fabricated. This is a tangential claim about ballot composition rather than a substantive claim about Van Orden's record or positions, so severity is minor rather than critical.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden has 'strongly aligned with alignment packages like the Secure America Act'
description: No record in Van Orden's documented platform or voting history specifically ties him to a bill called the 'Secure America Act.' His confirmed immigration positions are support for fully funding ICE/CBP, cracking down on cartels and fentanyl trafficking, and enforcing immigration laws, plus sponsorship of his own 'Agricultural Workforce Reform Act of 2025.' The specific named bill in this claim is not corroborated and the awkward phrase 'aligned with alignment packages' suggests unreliable sourcing.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke's affordability approach involves 'strengthening domestic supply chains' and addressing 'supply-side bottlenecks'
description: The core idea that Cooke's platform addresses supply chains is genuine: her official campaign priorities page calls for 'Provide incentives for producers utilizing Made in America raw goods and inputs throughout the supply chain' and to 'Address breakdowns within our supply chain – from the farmer to processors to the retailer.' This supports the paraphrase 'strengthening domestic supply chains.' However, the specific quoted phrase 'supply-side bottlenecks' does not appear anywhere in her campaign platform, official materials, or news coverage found in searches. It appears to be fabricated technical jargon attributed to her rather than actual language she has used. Because the underlying substance (supply chain focus) is real and only one of the two quoted phrases is unsupported, this is a minor rather than critical inaccuracy.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke's platform generally focuses on rebuilding the foundations of rural economies—including supply chains, local manufacturing, and structural networks—to ensure small towns aren't left behind, as a roads/infrastructure plan
description: Cooke's official campaign platform contains no dedicated 'Rural Infrastructure,' roads, or bridges plank. She has made one verified statement on broadband, comparing it to rural electrification, but no broader documented position on rebuilding rural roads, bridges, or 'structural networks' as an infrastructure plan exists in her platform materials. The response presents a vague, seemingly invented characterization of her infrastructure-specific policy that goes beyond what is actually documented.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke's approach aligns closely with broader federal infrastructure initiatives like the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, and she supports partnering with federal programs that prioritize long-term, comprehensive funding for rural roads, bridges, and high-speed internet access
description: No documented statement from Cooke ties her platform to the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law by name or asserts a comprehensive roads-and-bridges funding plan. Her only verified related statement is about broadband access, likened to rural electrification, with a passing reference to promise in 'the infrastructure bill.' Presenting this as a broad, confirmed roads/bridges platform overstates what is actually on record.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke's platform opposes calls to defund the police and abolish ICE
description: Cooke's actual documented position on policing is that she said when asked directly she believes police departments should be "fully funded," while also having made earlier comments favoring reallocating some funds toward social workers and root-cause programs — not a clean "opposes defund the police" framing, and no direct statement about abolishing ICE was found in her record. The response oversimplifies a genuinely more nuanced and contested record into a flat denial.

inaccurate_statement: Rebecca Cooke's affordability platform centers on lowering taxes for working families
description: Cooke's documented platform emphasizes raising the federal minimum wage, taking on corporate price gouging, expanding childcare, and healthcare affordability, but there is no record of a specific 'lowering taxes for working families' plank as part of her platform. Her tax-related proposals that are documented (removing the Social Security payroll tax cap for high earners, repealing federal taxation of Social Security benefits for current recipients) are different from a general 'lowering taxes for working families' framing, so this characterization is not well supported.

inaccurate_statement: Rebecca Cooke has explicitly signed a pledge not to accept corporate PAC money in her campaign for Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District.
description: No record exists of Cooke signing a no-corporate-PAC-money pledge. Her fundraising is documented as coming heavily from individual max-out donors, but she also received committee/PAC contributions (approximately $523,475 in 'other committee contributions' for the 2026 cycle), which is inconsistent with an active no-corporate-PAC pledge. This claim appears to be fabricated.

inaccurate_statement: Anti-corruption groups like End Citizens United have highlighted and endorsed her commitment to rejecting corporate PAC contributions.
description: While End Citizens United's endorsement of Cooke is real, no record exists of them specifically highlighting or endorsing a 'no corporate PAC money' commitment, since no such pledge is documented. This appears to be a fabricated elaboration built on the false pledge claim.

inaccurate_statement: Rebecca Cooke's platform emphasizes lowering taxes for working families
description: Cooke's documented platform emphasizes raising the federal minimum wage to $15/hour, opposing corporate price gouging, tax credits for first-time homebuyers, and antitrust enforcement — not a general tax-cutting message. Her tax-related proposals are narrow and targeted (e.g., property tax deferral for first-time homebuyers, more ACA tax credits) rather than a broad 'lowering taxes for working families' framing, which is more characteristic of Van Orden's messaging (e.g., his 'Working Families Tax Cuts'). This mischaracterizes her platform's emphasis without inventing a wholly fictional position.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden's campaign website is at 'DerrickVanOrden.com'
description: Van Orden's confirmed, actively working official campaign site is vanordenforcongress.com. The domain derrickvanorden.com returned empty/inconclusive content in research and was not confirmed to be his site; presenting it confidently as his campaign website is an unverified and likely incorrect claim.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke's platform centers on tackling cost-of-living pressures through, among other things, lower taxes for working families
description: Cooke's documented platform emphasizes raising the minimum wage, taking on corporate price gouging, and tax credits for specific groups (first-time homebuyers, small businesses), but no source describes a general 'lower taxes for working families' plank; this framing more closely resembles Van Orden's tax-cut messaging and is not attributed to Cooke in the available material.

inaccurate_statement: The WI-03 general election also features independent candidates Alexander Valiensi Kent and Rustin Provance
description: No evidence could be found for independent candidates named 'Alexander Valiensi Kent' or 'Rustin Provance' running in the WI-03 general election. These names do not correspond to any known filed candidates in Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District races, which have primarily featured Derrick Van Orden and Rebecca Cooke as major-party candidates. This claim appears to be fabricated and is not attributable to any real WI-03 race. However, since this claim is about third-party candidates rather than about Rebecca Cooke herself, it does not materially affect the reader's overall impression of her candidacy.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke's (or 'Democratic platforms' as characterized in her section) approach includes cracking down on illicit fentanyl trafficking at ports of entry
description: The fentanyl/drug-trafficking crackdown framing at the border is documented as Derrick Van Orden's own stated position (he said he supports 'fully funding ICE and CBP... to crack down on cartels and fentanyl trafficking'), not Rebecca Cooke's. Cooke's own recorded immigration statements emphasize a 'secure border and a pathway to citizenship' and the bipartisan Dignity Act, without mentioning fentanyl or drug trafficking specifically. Attributing this fentanyl-enforcement framing to Cooke's approach, even indirectly through a 'Democratic platforms typically emphasize' framing placed in her section, misattributes rhetoric that belongs to her opponent.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden's health-care/prescription-drug approach is characterized as emphasizing free-market solutions, increased competition, and addressing regulatory burdens as alternatives to sweeping federal mandates
description: No direct statement or campaign material from Van Orden specifically addressing prescription drug pricing was found; this is a documented platform gap for him, in contrast to Cooke who has an explicit drug-pricing plank. Separately, his actual healthcare record includes direct government-program engagement (working with CMS on Medicaid reimbursement rates, securing hospital provider tax protections, voting to extend ACA subsidies), which cuts against a pure 'free-market alternative to federal mandates' characterization of his healthcare approach generally. The specific claim about his prescription-drug position is an unsupported inference rather than a sourced statement.

inaccurate_statement: She was appointed by Governor Tony Evers to the board of the Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation (WEDC), serving as its youngest appointee
description: The knowledge base confirms Cooke's appointment to the WEDC board and her role co-chairing its Entrepreneurship and Innovation Committee, but there is no record of her being described as the board's "youngest appointee." This specific superlative detail is not supported by the available material.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke called Van Orden's behavior "abysmal" and said he lacks the temperament to properly represent the district

The broader theme that Cooke has criticized Van Orden's temperament and conduct (e.g., calling him 'a lot of talk and no walk,' citing a 'laundry list' of problems, calling him an 'embarrassment' over the pages incident) is well documented, but this specific quoted word is not corroborated.

inaccurate_statement: Independent candidates Alexander Valiensi Kent and Rustin Provance are running in WI-03

inaccurate_statement: Cooke's campaign has primarily focused on pocketbook issues, cost of living, and economic opportunities, implying she has not addressed community safety/police funding

inaccurate_statement: Mainstream Democratic candidates have increasingly emphasized commitments to properly funding community safety, law enforcement personnel, and local departments rather than supporting reductions (implying this is a general trend as opposed to describing Cooke's own specific, on-record position)
description: This is a vague generalization used as a proxy for Cooke's actual position rather than citing her specific, on-record statement supporting full police department funding alongside added social services. She does have a directly quotable statement on this exact topic that would have been more accurate and specific than an unsourced generalization about 'mainstream Democratic candidates.'

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden's legislative record and campaign messaging consistently center on supporting police agencies and hardening local public safety resources
description: While Van Orden does have a documented pro-police platform and law enforcement endorsements, describing his record and messaging as 'consistently centering' on police support overstates the emphasis relative to his broader, more prominent focus areas (agriculture, tariffs/trade, veterans affairs, immigration/border security, and manufacturing visits). inaccurate_statement: Cooke's enforcement resources should target transnational criminal organizations and drug traffickers

inaccurate_statement: Cooke's opponents argue she aligns closely with national party leadership and would support broader federal spending packages championed by congressional Democrats

inaccurate_statement: Rebecca Cooke has publicly opposed calls to defund the police, stating during forums and in campaign ads that she does not support cutting law enforcement funding and has featured law enforcement endorsements in her digital and TV advertisements.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke has declined to answer specific media or opponent inquiries regarding her stance on border enforcement policies
description: Cooke has an on-record, direct statement on border security: she supports "a commonsense immigration policy that includes a secure border and a pathway to citizenship," citing the bipartisan Dignity Act, and separately has called for adding Border Patrol agents. inaccurate_statement: Cooke has touted endorsements from labor unions such as AFSCME, which has been involved in legal battles and policy toolkits opposing certain federal restrictions on commercial driver's licenses (CDLs) for undocumented individuals
description: The claim bundles two things: Cooke touting an AFSCME endorsement (plausible and likely accurate, as AFSCME frequently endorses Democratic candidates and Cooke has sought union support), with a highly specific and implausible assertion that AFSCME has been involved in 'legal battles and policy toolkits opposing certain federal restrictions on commercial driver's licenses (CDLs) for undocumented individuals.' This is a narrower, bolted-on inaccuracy rather than one that undermines the core (and likely true) point that Cooke has union support, so severity is minor rather than critical.

inaccurate_statement: The victim (the CODEPINK activist) sustained minor injuries
description: The knowledge base indicates the activist, identified as Nour Jaghama, was arrested but ultimately not charged; there is no record confirming that she sustained injuries in the altercation. inaccurate_statement: Van Orden's presence at Jan. 6 is described in a way that implies he 'attended...during the January 6 attack' without clarifying he denies entering the building and that a fact-check rated the stronger 'participated in insurrection' framing as 'mostly false'
description: Van Orden did attend the Stop the Steal rally and was photographed in a restricted area of the Capitol grounds, but he denies entering the Capitol building itself, and a Milwaukee Journal Sentinel fact-check rated the claim that he 'participated in the Jan. 6 insurrection' as 'mostly false.' The response's phrasing that he was present 'during the January 6 attack' without this nuance risks overstating his level of involvement beyond what is corroborated.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden wrote a 2015 book, 'A Book of Man: A Navy SEAL's Guide to the Lost Art of Manhood,' which included an anecdote about pulling back a curtain to show unsuspecting female military officers a fellow service member's medical condition, condemned by critics and ethics experts as sexual harassment
description: Van Orden's authorship of this 2015 book is confirmed. This specific claim cannot be verified against documented sources and does not appear in the confirmed controversy list for this candidate.

inaccurate_statement: Activists accused him of abusing his congressional status to intimidate political opponents [regarding the 2024 RNC CODEPINK incident], framed as an 'arrest incident'
description: The confirmed account of the July 2024 incident is that the CODEPINK activist, not Van Orden, was arrested (and ultimately not charged); Van Orden was the one who reported being assaulted, and the activist's account differs, saying he tried to shove past her in line. Framing this as an incident where Van Orden was the aggressor abusing his status, or in a way that obscures that he was the reported victim rather than the one investigated, misrepresents the documented, resolved version of this event.

inaccurate_statement: Cooke operated a consulting firm called 'Cooke Strategy LLC' that advised multiple campaigns
description: Cooke's documented consulting work is described as her serving as a political consultant advising roughly eight campaigns from 2014-2021, including for Kirk Bangstad's campaign. inaccurate_statement: Cooke ran her own consulting firm called 'Cooke Strategy LLC'
description: Cooke's political consulting work is documented as a general career history (fundraiser/finance director and political consultant for roughly eight campaigns, 2012 onward), but no source establishes the specific name 'Cooke Strategy LLC' as her consulting firm. inaccurate_statement: Combat deployments included tours in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Afghanistan, and Iraq, alongside missions across Africa, Asia, Europe, and Central and South America.
description: The specific list of deployment locations (Bosnia and Herzegovina, Afghanistan, Iraq, plus missions across Africa, Asia, Europe, Central and South America) is not found in the available biographical material, which confirms only that he completed five combat deployments over 26 years of Navy SEAL service without detailing specific countries or regions. This level of geographic detail cannot be verified and goes beyond what is documented.

inaccurate_statement: During a 2012 tour in Europe, he was responsible for planning Special Operations contingency operations across the European continent.
description: No documentation of this specific 2012 European planning assignment exists in the available biographical record on Van Orden's military career, which covers his 26-year Navy SEAL career and five combat deployments only at a general level. This specific detail cannot be confirmed.

inaccurate_statement: He is a best-selling author.
description: Van Orden authored A Book of Man: A Navy SEAL's Guide to the Lost Art of Manhood, but no source confirms best-seller status for the book.

inaccurate_statement: 26 years in the Navy spanning 1988–2014
description: The knowledge base confirms 26 years of Navy service retiring in 2014, but does not specify a 1988 start date; this specific start year is not verifiable against the available material and appears to be an added detail not corroborated by the dossier.

inaccurate_statement: Van Orden's background includes serving as a Navy Corpsman
description: Derrick Van Orden's well-documented military background is as a U.S. Navy SEAL (retired Chief Warrant Officer with 26 years of service), not a Navy Corpsman. These are entirely different military occupational specialties (SEAL is a special warfare operator role, while Corpsman is a medical support rating). This is a core biographical fact frequently cited in his campaign materials and news coverage, and misstating it as 'Navy Corpsman' misrepresents a defining element of his public identity and career, which is central to his political persona as a candidate.

inaccurate_statement: Worked as a field organizer helping elect candidates to public office
description: Multiple consistent sources (Wikipedia, EMILYs List, Volunteer Blue, Leadership Now Project) describe Rebecca Cooke's post-college campaign work specifically as a fundraiser/finance director and later political consultant for congressional campaigns — not as a 'field organizer.' These are distinct campaign functions (fundraising/finance vs. grassroots field organizing). While the broader point that she worked on electing candidates to office is true, the specific job title/role of 'field organizer' does not match any biographical source, making this a narrow factual error about her specific role rather than a fabrication of her general campaign background.

inaccurate_statement: Lower the financial burden of long-term care facilities
description: No record exists in Cooke's documented platform of a specific long-term care affordability proposal; her healthcare platform focuses on Medicare expansion (vision/dental/hearing), Medicare eligibility age reduction, rural hospital reimbursement rates, and prescription drug pricing, but a long-term care cost plank is not found in the available material.

inaccurate_statement: Improve regional mass transit
description: Cooke's documented platform includes expanded public transit as a general position confirmed via live search sweep, but no specific 'regional mass transit' improvement plank tied to her clean energy/infrastructure priorities is documented beyond that general support; this is a narrow supporting detail not central to the overall accurate description of her platform.

inaccurate_statement: Simplifying the ACA application process

inaccurate_statement: In campaign materials, Van Orden criticized statements Cooke made regarding out-of-state figures, framing her as aligned with progressive coastal politics rather than rural Wisconsin interests
description: No specific corroboration exists for this particular framing of an attack line tying Cooke to 'out-of-state figures' and 'progressive coastal politics.' inaccurate_statement: Cooke has criticized Van Orden's conduct in office as "abysmal" and said he "lacks the temperament to represent Wisconsin and our values"
description: The quote 'lacks the temperament to represent Wisconsin and our values' is directly and accurately attributed to Cooke, confirmed by a statement she gave after Van Orden's outburst at Capitol pages. inaccurate_statement: Van Orden has no direct statement found on agricultural water contamination specifically, but the response presents his water/PFAS work as directly addressing this topic
